docs.text: Action Shortcut Open file Ctrl+O Save Ctrl+S Run simulation F5 / Space Stop simulation Escape Zoom in/out Scroll wheel Rotate component R Delete component Delete / Backspace Command palette Ctrl+K

docs.title: Analysis Tools
docs.text:
How to measure, analyze, and export simulation results in the editor.

Duration: 15 minutes

Prerequisites: Running Simulations

docs.title: The Scope View
docs.text: The Simulation workspace tab is the primary tool for viewing results. Each recorded signal appears as a channel; scopes in the circuit group channels into instruments, and the scope selector at the top filters to one instrument or shows everything.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
Action How Zoom in/out Mouse wheel (zooms around cursor) or left-click and drag (2D box zoom) Pan Middle-click and drag, or Alt+Left-click and drag Fit whole simulation ⟲ button (or Esc) in the toolbar Overlay / one lane per signal Display toggle in the scope header

When you zoom, the value axis rescales to the visible window — so switching ripples become readable at any depth.

docs.title: Cursors
docs.text:
Left-click on the plot to place cursor A; Shift+click or right-click to place cursor B. The cursor measurement section in the right sidebar shows:

  • t_A and t_B positions
  • Δt between the cursors
  • Frequency = 1/Δt

Clear Cursors removes them.

docs.title: Signal Statistics
docs.text: The metrics table computes min, max, peak-to-peak, RMS, and mean for every signal over the whole run. Click a table row to toggle the trace.

docs.title: FFT — Harmonic Analysis
docs.text:
Click FFT in the scope toolbar:

  1. Choose the signal and the number of harmonics.
  2. Click Compute — the analysis runs on the currently visible window (zoom first to exclude startup transients).
  3. Read base frequency, fundamental amplitude, DC component, and THD, with a spectrum chart and a per-harmonic table (amplitude and phase).

This is the fastest way to check grid power factor correction, output ripple spectrum, or switching harmonics.

docs.title: Loss Calculation
docs.text:
Click Losses in the scope toolbar for semiconductor loss estimation:

  • Switching losses from Eon/Eoff energies at your operating current, voltage, and junction temperature (scaled to a reference).
  • Conduction losses from I, R_on, and threshold voltage with duty cycle.

Enter the datasheet energies and the operating point from your simulation — the panel returns switching, conduction, and total loss in watts.

docs.title: Export
docs.text: CSV export in the results drawer writes every recorded signal (time + one column per channel) so you can post-process in Python, MATLAB, Excel, or your script block source of truth.

docs.title: Tips for Good Analysis
docs.text:
1. Wait for steady state — don't measure during startup transients
  2. Use enough cycles — average over multiple switching periods
  3. Check time step — too large a step hides high-frequency content
  4. Compare with theory — verify results match analytical predictions
  5. Document settings — record simulation parameters with results

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Tutorials — apply analysis to specific topologies
  • NativeC Blocks — test real C/C++ control code
  • MCP Interface — let an LLM run the measurements for you

docs.title: Building Circuits
docs.text:
Create power electronics circuits from scratch in the editor.

Duration: 20 minutes

Prerequisites: First Simulation

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Building a circuit is four steps:

  1. Place components from the palette
  2. Wire them together
  3. Set parameters in the properties panel
  4. Add measurement points (scopes, probes)

docs.title: Step 1: Start a New Circuit
docs.text: File ▸ New creates an empty schematic (a blank workspace is also created automatically at app start).

docs.title: Step 2: Place Components
docs.text:
1. Find a component in the palette on the left — filter by category or search by name.
  2. Click it: the component becomes a "ghost" that follows the cursor.
  3. Move it to a grid position and click to place; press R to rotate before placing.
  4. Escape cancels; after placing you can keep placing more of the same type.

Useful while placing: arrow keys nudge the ghost by one grid unit.

docs.title: What a Basic Circuit Needs
docs.text: Category Components Why Sources Voltage source Provides input power Switches MOSFET/IGBT + Diode Switching elements Passive L, C, R Energy storage and filtering Control PWM/Constant/Script block Gate signals Measurement Scope, probes View results

docs.title: Step 3: Wire the Components
docs.text:
1. Press W (or click the wire-mode toggle) to enter wire mode.
  2. Click a component pin to start a wire.
  3. Click along the path to set waypoints (orthogonal routing is automatic; arrow keys step the current waypoint on the grid).
  4. Click the destination pin to finish; Escape aborts.

Wires attach to pins by net label — move a component later and its wires stay attached.

docs.title: Step 4: Set Parameters
docs.text: Select a component and edit its parameters in the properties panel on the right. Values accept engineering notation; the panel shows units and valid ranges for every parameter.

docs.title: Step 5: Add Measurement Points
docs.text:
• Place VOLTMETER/AMMETER probes and couple them to the component they measure.
  • Place a SCOPE and wire probe outputs into its inputs.
  • Recorded signals appear in the Simulation view tab after the next run.

docs.title: Pre-Run Checklist
docs.text:
• Every voltage source has a return path (ground/reference node)
  • Every switch has a gate signal
  • Scope/probe connected to the points you want to see
  • Time step appropriate (< T_sw / 100)

docs.title: Simulation Settings
docs.text:
Set duration, dt, and solver in the Simulation Settings panel:

Parameter Example Value Why Duration 1 ms ~100 switching periods Time step 50 ns 200 steps per period Solver Backward Euler Stable for switching circuits

docs.title: Undo / Redo
docs.text: Every edit is tracked by the engine: Ctrl+Z reverts, Ctrl+Y reapplies — including moves, parameter changes, and deletions.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Running Simulations — solvers, settings, execution
  • Analysis Tools — cursors, FFT, losses, export

docs.title: Your First Simulation
docs.text:
This walkthrough opens, runs, and analyzes a buck converter simulation.

Duration: 15 minutes

Prerequisites: Installation complete

docs.title: Step 1: Launch GeckoCIRCUITS
docs.text: Start the desktop app (or the editor from a source checkout). After a few seconds the editor opens with an empty schematic.

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Example Circuit
docs.text:
Open the Examples menu in the top bar and choose DC-DC Buck Converter (or File ▸ Open and pick resources/tutorials/2xx_dcdc_converters/201_buck_converter/buck_simple.ipes).

The schematic shows the classic buck topology:

  • Power components — switch, diode, L, C, load resistor
  • Control blocks — PWM generation, signal sources
  • Scope blocks — measurement points

docs.title: Step 3: Understand the Circuit
docs.text:
Component Role DC voltage source Provides input power MOSFET switch Controlled switching element Diode Freewheeling current path Inductor (L) Stores energy, smooths current Capacitor (C) Filters output voltage Resistor (R) Load SCOPE Records measurement signals

Click any component to see and edit its parameters in the properties panel on the right.

docs.title: Step 4: Configure the Simulation
docs.text:
Open the Simulation Settings panel on the right sidebar:

Parameter Meaning Typical Value Duration (t_end) How long to simulate 10 ms Time step (dt) Computation interval 1 µs Solver Numerical method Backward Euler

Time Step Rule

The time step should be 100× smaller than the switching period. For 100 kHz switching: dt < 0.1 µs.

docs.title: Step 5: Run
docs.text: Click ▶ Run Simulation and watch the live progress. Typical runtime for simple circuits: 1–5 seconds.

docs.title: Step 6: View the Results
docs.text: The Simulation workspace tab shows the recorded waveforms — output voltage, inductor current, switch node.

docs.title: Scope Navigation
docs.text: Action Control Zoom in/out Mouse wheel (around cursor) or left-click + drag (2D box zoom) Pan Middle-click + drag, or Alt+Left-click + drag Fit whole simulation ⟲ toolbar button (or Esc) Y-axis Auto-rescales to the visible window Cursors Left-click to place A, Shift+click or right-click for B — Δt and frequency readout in the right sidebar

docs.title: Step 7: Analyze the Results
docs.text:
For a buck converter you should observe:

  1. Output voltage settling to V_out = D × V_in
  2. Inductor current — triangular ripple waveform
  3. Switch voltage — rectangular pulses between V_in and 0

docs.title: What to Check
docs.text:
• Does the output reach steady state?
  • Is the ripple within acceptable limits?
  • Any unexpected spikes or oscillations?

docs.title: Step 8: Experiment
docs.text:
1. Change duty cycle — select the control block, adjust D
  2. Change load — select the resistor, change R
  3. Change inductance — select the inductor, change L
  4. Re-run and compare — Undo (Ctrl+Z) reverts anything

docs.title: What You've Learned
docs.text:
• Launching the app and opening example circuits
  • Configuring time step, duration, and solver
  • Running a simulation and reading waveforms
  • Navigating the scope with zoom, pan, and cursors

Next: Building Circuits — create your own circuit.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: GeckoCIRCUITS ships as a self-contained desktop application for Windows, Linux, and macOS. No Java installation is required — the simulation engine ships inside the app.

docs.title: Recommended: Desktop Installers
docs.text:
Download the installer for your operating system from the Releases page (assets named GeckoCIRCUITS_<version>_*):

OS File Notes Windows GeckoCIRCUITS_<v>_x64-setup.exe or .msi WebView2 downloads automatically if missing; .ipes file association registered macOS GeckoCIRCUITS_<v>_x64.dmg / _aarch64.dmg Unsigned builds: right-click → Open on first start Linux gecko-circuits_<v>_amd64.deb, *.rpm, or *.AppImage deb/rpm register the .ipes file association

After installing:

  • Launch GeckoCIRCUITS from the start menu, Applications folder, or app launcher. A Starting simulation engine… splash appears for a few seconds while the bundled engine boots, then the editor opens.
  • Double-clicking any .ipes circuit file opens it in the app.
  • The C library interface header (gecko_c_block.h) ships in the installation's engine/ folder for NativeC blocks.

docs.title: First-launch troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix Windows SmartScreen warning More info → Run anyway (builds are not code-signed yet) macOS "cannot be opened" Right-click the app → Open, or allow it in System Settings → Privacy & Security "Simulation engine failed to start" Open the engine log via Help ▸ Open Logs Folder; details in the Desktop App guide

docs.title: Alternative: Run from Source
docs.text:
Developers can run the editor + engine from a repository checkout. This needs JDK 25, Node.js 22, and Maven:

# builds the engine jar if missing, starts it on localhost:8080/gecko/,
# and opens the editor in your browser
run-gecko.bat        # Windows
./run-gecko.sh       # Linux / macOS

This is the same React application the desktop app embeds, served against the same simulation engine — circuits and workflows are identical. The scripts/run-gecko* scripts forward directly to the root launcher run-gecko.bat|.sh.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
The headless REST API and simulation engine can be run as a containerized service using the provided Docker configuration:

# Build and start the REST API container via Compose
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d

# Or build and run the image directly
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.api -t geckocircuits-api:latest .
docker run -p 8080:8080 geckocircuits-api:latest

Once running, the API is available at http://localhost:8080/gecko/api/v1/. See the REST API Reference for endpoint details.

docs.title: Editing Model
docs.text:
• The engine owns the circuit. Every edit (place, move, wire, delete, parameter change, undo, redo) is sent to the bundled engine, which is the single source of truth. The UI mirrors its state — so undo/redo and multi-view consistency always match the simulation model.
  • Wires connect by net labels. A wire endpoint attached to a component pin stays attached when you move the component; multi-pin components (scopes, motors, C blocks) spread their pins vertically.
  • Simulation results are separate state. Results, cursors, and zoom are cleared when you switch circuits, never mixed between them.

docs.title: Examples Menu
docs.text: The Examples dropdown loads complete, ready-to-run circuits directly — the fastest way to explore what GeckoCIRCUITS can do. See Quick Start.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: Toggle between dark and light themes from the top bar; the setting is remembered per machine.

docs.title: PWM Basics
docs.text:
Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) is the fundamental control method for power electronics. This tutorial explains how PWM works and how to use it in GeckoCIRCUITS.

Duration: 15 minutes

Prerequisites: Building Circuits

docs.title: What is PWM?
docs.text:
PWM converts a DC input voltage to a controllable output by rapidly switching a transistor on and off.

     ON        OFF       ON        OFF
    ┌───┐            ┌───┐
    │   │            │   │
────┘   └────────────┘   └────────────
    |←D·T→|←(1-D)·T→|

T = switching period = 1/f
D = duty cycle (0 to 1)

docs.title: Key Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Symbol Unit Description Switching frequency f_sw Hz How fast the switch toggles Switching period T = 1/f_sw s Duration of one cycle Duty cycle D - Fraction of period the switch is ON (0-1) ON time t_on = D x T s Time switch conducts OFF time t_off = (1-D) x T s Time switch is off

docs.title: Why PWM?
docs.text:
The average output voltage is proportional to the duty cycle:

\[V_{out,avg} = D \times V_{in}\]

By varying D from 0 to 1, you can control the output from 0V to V_in.

docs.title: PWM Generation Components
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS provides control blocks for carrier comparison and switching modulation:

  • COMPARATOR: Compares a modulating reference against a SignalCalculatorTriangle / sawtooth carrier (SIGNAL rectangle/triangle source) to output a binary gate drive (0 or 1).
  • SPWM_GENERATOR (alias SPWM): Built-in carrier-comparison sinusoidal PWM modulator for single-phase, H-bridge, and three-phase bridges.
  • DEADTIME (alias DEADTIME_GENERATOR): Inserts turn-on blanking / dead-time between complementary high-side and low-side gate signals.

docs.title: Setting Up PWM
docs.text:
1. Place a Signal Source (triangle/sawtooth carrier) + Constant (duty reference) + COMPARATOR, or a SPWM_GENERATOR block from the control palette.
  2. Configure switching frequency and modulation index / duty cycle in the properties panel.
  3. Connect the output (or couple a GATE driver block) to the switch gate terminal.

docs.title: PWM Generation Methods
docs.text: Method Description Use Case Fixed duty cycle Constant D value Open-loop testing Comparator-based Compare reference to carrier Closed-loop control Programmatic / Scripted SCRIPT block, geckopy, or REST API sets duty cycle Digital PI / MCU control

docs.title: Buck Converter
docs.text: \[V_{out} = D \times V_{in}\] D V_in = 48V V_out 0.25 48V 12V 0.50 48V 24V 0.75 48V 36V

docs.title: Frequency Selection
docs.text:
Choosing the right switching frequency involves trade-offs:

Higher Frequency Lower Frequency Smaller L and C needed Larger L and C needed Higher switching losses Lower switching losses Faster transient response Slower transient response More EMI Less EMI

docs.title: Typical Frequencies by Application
docs.text: Application Typical f_sw Motor drives 10-20 kHz DC-DC converters 50-500 kHz LED drivers 100 kHz - 2 MHz RF power 1-100 MHz

docs.title: Exercise: PWM Parameter Sweep
docs.text:
Try this experiment with the buck converter:

  1. Open resources/tutorials/1xx_getting_started/103_pwm_basics/ex_3_pwm.ipes
  2. Run with D = 0.25, observe V_out
  3. Change D to 0.50, re-run, compare
  4. Change D to 0.75, re-run, compare

Expected results:

D Expected V_out 0.25 ~25% of V_in 0.50 ~50% of V_in 0.75 ~75% of V_in

docs.title: Dead Time
docs.text:
In half-bridge and full-bridge circuits, complementary switches must never be ON simultaneously (shoot-through). A dead time is inserted between turn-off and turn-on:

Switch 1: ─────┐           ┌─────
               └───────────┘
                 |← dead →|
Switch 2: ──────┘time     └──────
                ─────────────

GeckoCIRCUITS supports dead-time configuration in the PWM block for bridge topologies.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Get from install to your first waveform in five minutes.

docs.title: 1. Launch GeckoCIRCUITS
docs.text:
Start the GeckoCIRCUITS desktop app (see Installation). The editor opens after a few seconds — the bundled simulation engine boots in the background.

No install? Run from source

From a repository checkout, run-gecko.bat|.sh starts the engine and opens the same editor in your browser at http://localhost:8080/gecko/.

docs.title: 2. Open an Example Circuit
docs.text:
Open the Examples menu in the top bar and pick DC-DC Buck Converter. A complete buck converter loads onto the schematic:

  • MOSFET switch — controlled by a PWM signal
  • Diode — freewheeling path for inductor current
  • Inductor (L) and capacitor (C) — output filter
  • Resistive load (R)
  • A scope watching the output

Click any component to inspect and edit its parameters in the properties panel on the right.

docs.title: 3. Run the Simulation
docs.text:
Open the Simulation Settings panel on the right sidebar and click the ▶ Run Simulation button.

The scope view switches to the simulation tab and shows live progress, then the waveforms:

  • Output voltage settling to the target value
  • Inductor current with triangular ripple
  • Switch node toggling between input voltage and ground

docs.title: 4. Explore the Scope
docs.text:
The scope view is a full instrument:

Action How Zoom in/out Mouse wheel (zooms around cursor) or left-click and drag (2D box zoom) Pan Middle-click and drag, or Alt+Left-click and drag Fit whole simulation ⟲ button (or Esc) in the scope toolbar Measure Δt / frequency Click to place cursor A, Shift+click or right-click for B Harmonics / THD FFT button (analyzes the visible window) Export data CSV export in the results drawer

docs.title: 5. Modify the Circuit
docs.text:
Experiment — this is where the tool pays off:

  1. Select the switch and change its switching frequency in the properties panel.
  2. Re-run and compare: higher frequency ⇒ smaller output ripple.
  3. Try Undo (Ctrl+Z) / Redo (Ctrl+Y) — every edit is tracked server-side.

The buck relationship is V_out = D × V_in, where D is the duty cycle.

docs.title: 6. Save Your Work
docs.text: Save writes your circuit as a .ipes file — in the desktop app a native save dialog appears, in the browser the file downloads. The .ipes format is fully portable between the desktop app and the editor.

docs.title: Try More Examples
docs.text:
The Examples menu includes ready-to-run circuits:

Example What you'll learn Multi-Scope RLC Multi-channel scopes, transient oscillation RLC Resonant Circuit Second-order step response RC Low-Pass Filter First-order charging curve

Over 100 application circuits (converters, inverters, PFC, motor drives, thermal and education demos) are in the repository under resources/ and examples/ — open them with File ▸ Open or by double-clicking the .ipes file.

docs.text:

  • User Interface — editor layout and shortcuts
  • NativeC Blocks — run your real C/C++ control code
  • MCP Interface — let an LLM drive the simulator

docs.title: Running Simulations
docs.text:
How to configure and run simulations in the editor.

Duration: 10 minutes

Prerequisites: Building Circuits

docs.title: Simulation Settings
docs.text: Open the Simulation Settings panel on the right sidebar.

docs.title: Essential Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description How to Choose Duration (t_end) Simulation duration 10–100× switching period Time step (dt) Computation interval < T_sw / 100 Solver Numerical method See solver table below

docs.title: Time Step Selection
docs.text:
The time step is the most critical setting. Too large causes errors; too small wastes computation time.

Rule of thumb: dt < 1/(100 × f_sw)

Switching Freq Max Time Step Recommended 10 kHz 1 µs 500 ns 50 kHz 200 ns 100 ns 100 kHz 100 ns 50 ns 500 kHz 20 ns 10 ns

docs.title: Simulation Duration
docs.text:
Choose enough time for the circuit to reach steady state:

  • Fast circuits (> 100 kHz): 0.1 – 1 ms
  • Medium circuits (10–100 kHz): 1 – 10 ms
  • Slow circuits (< 10 kHz, motors): 10 – 100 ms

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text: Solver Best for Notes Backward Euler (default) Switching converters Most stable, first-order accuracy Trapezoidal Smooth waveforms Less damping, can ring Gear-Shichman Stiff circuits Strong numerical damping

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
1. Click ▶ Run Simulation in the settings panel.
  2. Live progress streams to the scope view (time, percentage, current step).
  3. Pause/resume a running simulation, or cancel it — controls appear next to the progress display.
  4. When complete, the scope shows the recorded waveforms.

Zoom into the interesting part

After the run, use the mouse wheel to zoom into switching periods and drag to pan — see Analysis Tools.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Results appear in the Simulation workspace tab:

  • Scope view with one lane per signal (or overlay mode)
  • Cursor measurements — place cursors A/B for Δt and frequency
  • Statistics table — min, max, peak-to-peak, RMS, mean per signal
  • CSV export of the full dataset

If a simulation fails (numerical breakdown, non-convergence), the scope shows the error and the values that triggered it — typically fixed by reducing dt.

docs.title: Steady State
docs.text:
To see steady-state behavior:

  1. Run longer — simulate enough cycles for settling
  2. Set initial conditions — pre-set capacitor voltages and inductor currents on the components
  3. Zoom into the last few periods and read ripple/duty directly

docs.title: Convergence Issues
docs.text: Symptom Cause Solution NaN values Numerical overflow Reduce time step Oscillating output Trapezoidal ringing Switch to Backward Euler Very slow Time step too small Increase dt if accuracy allows Wrong results Time step too large Decrease dt

  • Tutorials — application-specific simulations

docs.title: Comprehensive Architectural Plan: .ipes Standardization, Wire-Based DRC & Platform Improvements
Executive Summary
docs.text: Based on the completion and validation of all 21 converter and multi-domain tutorials, this plan addresses the core technical bottlenecks identified during testing: 1. The .ipes Topic (Highest Priority - COMPLETED in Phase 1): Standardized all project files to plain UTF-8 text (eliminating binary GZIP confusion in git and Python tools), with zero backward compatibility baggage while guaranteeing 100% of repository project files continue to validate and simulate. 2. Wire-Based Ground & Net Mapping in DRC (Phase 2 - COMPLETED): Reworked CircuitValidator to geometric coordinate netlist resolution aligned with simulation engine semantics (NetlistBuilder), eliminating false short-circuits from wire crossings, handling wire-labeled grounds, and supporting name-based gate coupling and probe measurement node resolution. 3. Sequential Platform Improvements (Phases 3–7): Multi-domain synthesis schema, specialized thermal/magnetic metrics, pre-flight topological validation, parameterized control libraries, and developer ergonomics (Python SDK, SVG exporter).

docs.title: Phase 2: Wire-Based Ground and Net Mapping in DRC (COMPLETED)
Final Repository-Wide Diagnostic Results (All 151 .ipes Files)
docs.text: Diagnostic Rule Pre-Phase 2 Baseline Phase 2 v1 (Flawed) Phase 2 Final (Verified) Outcome & Resolution SHORT_CIRCUIT errors 1 73 1 Resolved: 72 false short circuits eliminated. Only the intentional 0-Ohm shunt in A_Buck.ipes remains. Mid-crossings no longer merge wires; explicit xXIN[]/yXIN[]/xYOUT[]/yYOUT[] coordinates are respected; op-amp negative feedback (typ 22) is properly excluded. DANGLING_GATE errors 104 104 0 100% Resolved: Name-based switch coupling (parameterString[] containing /SwitchName/...) and negative UIDs are properly handled. DANGLING_PROBE errors 37 37 0 100% Resolved: Probes with node-label vectors in parameterString[] (e.g. /in1/u_load/0), component names, and wire geometry connections resolve cleanly. MISSING_GROUND errors 46 48 47 Accurate: Wire-based ground labels ("0", "gnd") and LK_GLOBAL_TERMINAL (typ 31) are recognized. The remaining 47 correspond genuinely to ungrounded legacy subcircuits. UNBALANCED_BRACES 0 0 0 Clean control script syntax across all files.

docs.title: Technical Architecture Implemented
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Input Parsing
        A[.ipes Content / Model] --> B[Parse LK, THERMAL, CONTROL, Wires]
        B --> B1[Extract Explicit Pin Coordinates xXIN/yXIN/xYOUT/yYOUT]
    end
    subgraph Geometric Net Resolution
        B --> C[WireNets: Build Wires & Polylines]
        C --> D{Endpoint Junction Condition}
        D -->|Endpoint Touches Another Wire| E[Union Wire Equivalence Classes]
        D -->|Mid-Crossing Only| F[Keep Wires Disjoint]
        B1 --> G[Attach Pin Coordinates to Wire Nets]
        G --> H[Propagate Component & Wire Ground Labels]
    end
    subgraph Multi-Domain DRC Rules
        E & H --> R1[Rule 1: Branch Short-Circuit Check Excludes OPV typ 22 & Multi-Terminal]
        E & H --> R2[Rule 2: Ground Verification Wire 0 / LK_GLOBAL_TERMINAL typ 31]
        E & H --> R3[Rule 3: Floating Net Warning on Open Power Pins]
        B --> R4[Rule 4: Gate Coupling by UID, Name & parameterString]
        B --> R5[Rule 5: Probe Coupling by UID, Name, Wire Attachment & parameterString Node Vector]
    end

docs.title: Key Technical Solutions
docs.text:
1. Exact Endpoint-Junction Connectivity:
  2. Wires merge in DisjointSet<Integer> if and only if an endpoint (endA or endB) touches another wire. Mid-crossings without an endpoint junction remain strictly separate nets.
  3. Removed segment rasterization to prevent phantom hops across non-adjacent components.
  4. Explicit Pin Coordinate Extraction:
  5. Parses xXIN[], yXIN[], xYOUT[], yYOUT[] when present in legacy blocks, preventing orientation inversion between input and output ports.
  6. Op-Amp & Multi-Terminal IC Treatment:
  7. Excluded LK_OPV1 (typ 22) from two-terminal branch short-circuit checks, allowing negative-feedback configurations (output wired to inverting input) without false DRC errors.
  8. Name-Based Gate & Probe Coupling:
  9. Preserves negative UIDs (uniqueObjectIdentifier < 0).
  10. If coupledReferenceID == 0, resolves target switch from parameterString[] (e.g. /S1/0/0) via lkComponentsByName.
  11. Probes check UID, component name, measurement node vectors in parameterString[], and physical terminal coordinates.

docs.text:
1. Component Registration in ComponentCatalog:
  2. COUPLED_INDUCTOR (LK_LKOP2, typ 12) with nominal inductance and companion slot 10 mapping.
  3. MUTUAL_INDUCTANCE (LK_M, typ 9) with coupling coefficient \(k \in (0, 1]\).
  4. NONLINEAR_INDUCTOR (typ 2) with current/inductance characteristic curves.

  10. Electro-Thermal Network Synthesis (CircuitBuilder):

    • Supports model_type: "foster" (parallel \(R_{th} \parallel C_{th}\) ladder stages) and "cauer" (series \(R_{th}\) with shunt \(C_{th}\) to ambient).
    • Standardized 4-grid-unit vertical pitch geometry ensuring exact pin coincident alignment across stages.
    • Couples semiconductor loss via TH_PvCHIP (typ 41) referencing target_switch by name and UID, and/or injects heat flow via TH_FLOW (typ 44).

  17. Correctly handles zero-terminal couplers (LK_M, typ 9) without false short-circuit or floating-terminal warnings.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Extend automated post-simulation waveform metrics to cover thermal, magnetic, and mechanical variables without streaming raw time-series over stdio.

docs.title: Implementation Summary
docs.text:
1. Multi-Domain Analytics Engine (PowerMetricsCalculator):
  2. Thermal Metrics:
    • Steady-state junction temperature: \(T_{j,ss} = \overline{T_j(t)}\)
    • Peak thermal ripple: \(\Delta T_j = T_{j,max} - T_{j,min}\)
    • Temperature rise above ambient: \(\Delta T = T_{j,ss} - T_{ambient}\)
    • 2% tolerance band settling time (\(t_{settle}\)) computed across the full transient profile.
    • Equivalent 1st-order thermal time constant \(\tau_{th}\) computed from \(63.2\%\) rise time.
  3. Magnetic Metrics:
    • Peak flux \(\hat{\Phi}\) and core flux excursion \(\Delta \Phi = \Phi_{max} - \Phi_{min}\).
    • Peak flux density \(\hat{B} = \hat{\Phi} / A_e\) and flux density excursion \(\Delta B = \Delta \Phi / A_e\).
    • Steinmetz core loss density: \(P_{vol} = k \cdot f^\alpha \cdot \hat{B}^\beta\) (\(\text{W/m}^3\)).
    • Total core loss: \(P_{total} = P_{vol} \cdot V_e\) (\(\text{W}\)).
    • Peak inductor current \(\hat{I}\), RMS current, peak-to-peak ripple \(\Delta I\), ripple percentage \(\%\).
    • Core saturation safety margin: \(\text{Margin}_{sat} = 1 - \hat{I} / I_{sat}\).
    • Peak stored inductive energy: \(E_{mag} = \frac{1}{2} L \hat{I}^2\).
  4. Mechanical Metrics:
    • Rotor angular velocity mean speed \(\bar{\omega}\) (rad/s) and conversion to RPM.
    • Speed ripple (pk-pk and percentage).
    • Reference speed tracking error percentage against target_speed.
    • Settling time to within 2% band of target_speed.
    • Mechanical torque mean \(\bar{T}\), peak torque, torque ripple (pk-pk and percentage).
    • Average shaft mechanical power: \(P_{mech} = \overline{\omega(t) \cdot T(t)}\).
  5. Electrical Power Metrics: 100% backward compatibility preserved for \(P_{in}\), \(P_{out}\), \(S_{in}\), power factor, and conversion efficiency.
  6. Auto-Detection: Automatic heuristic detection of thermal (tj, temp, junction), magnetic (phi, flux, i_l), and mechanical (omega, speed, rpm, torque) probes if explicit signal lists are omitted.
  7. Schema & Tool Registration (GeckoTools):
  8. Exposed all multi-domain parameters (thermal_signals, ambient_temperature, flux_signals, i_inductor_signals, core_area_m2, core_volume_m3, i_sat, inductance, steinmetz_k, steinmetz_alpha, steinmetz_beta, frequency, speed_signals, torque_signals, target_speed).
  9. Wired measureMetrics() directly to PowerMetricsCalculator.calculate(csv, args).

docs.title: Phase 5: Pre-Flight Topology Checks (Singular Matrix Prevention) (COMPLETED)
Objective
docs.text: Catch topological degeneracies in CircuitValidator before the MNA solver executes, preventing numerical singularity crashes (SingularMatrixException) and providing structured, actionable diagnostics with suggested_fix guidance.

docs.title: Architecture & Rules Implemented
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph PreFlight Topology Verification
        A[Canonical Nets & Component Map] --> B{Rule 6: Ideal Voltage Source Loop?}
        B -->|Cycle in Voltage Branch Subgraph| B1[ERROR: VOLTAGE_SOURCE_LOOP<br/>Suggest series damping resistor]
        B -->|Acyclic Subgraph| C{Rule 7: Inductive Cutset?}
        C -->|Inductor in series with Current Source| C1[ERROR: INDUCTIVE_CUTSET<br/>Suggest parallel snubber/resistor]
        C -->|Series Inductors without Impedance| C2[WARNING: INDUCTIVE_CUTSET<br/>Suggest combining equivalent L]
        C -->|Valid Impedance Paths| D{Rule 8: Active Switches Gated?}
        D -->|Switch missing GATE block or control driver| D1[WARNING: UNCONNECTED_GATE<br/>Suggest coupling GATE block]
        D -->|Gating Confirmed| E[Clean Pre-Flight Gate]
    end

docs.title: Key Technical Deliverables
docs.text:
1. Rule 6: Voltage Source Loop Check (VOLTAGE_SOURCE_LOOP):
  2. Ideal voltage sources (typ 4) introduce auxiliary current variables in Modified Nodal Analysis (MNA). A closed loop of ideal voltage sources creates linearly dependent auxiliary equation rows/columns, causing solver singularity.
  3. Implemented disjoint-set cycle detection DisjointSet<String> vsUf on voltage source branch endpoints (net0, net1).
  4. Successfully catches parallel pairs (\(V_1 \parallel V_2\)) and closed polygonal loops (\(V_1 \to V_2 \to \dots \to V_k \to V_1\)) in \(O(E \alpha(V))\) time without false positives on 3-phase star sources.

  5. Diagnostic: ERROR: VOLTAGE_SOURCE_LOOP with concrete suggested_fix ("Insert an internal series damping resistor (e.g. 10 mOhm) or remove redundant parallel voltage source branches to break the ideal voltage source loop.").

  6. Rule 7: Inductive Cutset Check (INDUCTIVE_CUTSET):

  7. Inductors enforce current continuity. Connecting an inductor in series with an ideal current source (typ 5) forces conflicting current derivatives (\(L \frac{di}{dt}\) singularity).

  8. Evaluates node-degree and component sets on non-ground circuit nets:

    • Error: Net connecting inductor (typ 2, 12) directly in series with ideal current source (typ 5) without damping path.
    • Suggested Fix: "Add a parallel damping resistor (e.g. 1 MOhm) or snubber across the inductor branch to avoid an ideal inductive current cutset."
    • Warning: Net connecting two inductors in series with no intermediate branch or load impedance.
    • Suggested Fix: "Combine the two series inductors into a single equivalent inductor (L_total = L1 + L2) or add a parallel damping resistance."

  9. Rule 8: Unconnected Gate Check (UNCONNECTED_GATE):

  10. Active semiconductor power switches (typ 7 Thyristor, typ 8 Triac, typ 10 GTO, typ 11 IGBT, typ 28 MOSFET, typ 33 BJT) require gating control. An uncoupled switch remains statically open or in its initial condition, often indicating a schematic oversight.
  11. Checks:
    • coupledReferenceID pointing to switch UID.
    • parameterString / target name matching switch name.
    • Script block references in sourceCode, staticCode, and staticVars.
    • Physical terminal connectivity (for BJT base terminal).

  12. Diagnostic: WARNING: UNCONNECTED_GATE with concrete suggested_fix ("Add a GATE block (typ 6 / 1000) coupled to switch '' or provide a gating control signal.").

  13. Repository-Wide Structured suggested_fix Coverage:

  14. Extended CircuitValidator.Diagnostic record to optionally carry suggestedFix.
  15. Preserved full 4-argument constructor backward compatibility (Diagnostic(level, rule, comp, msg)).
  16. Serialized suggested_fix into JSON diagnostic payload across all 11 existing and new DRC rules:
    • SHORT_CIRCUIT: Disconnect shorted terminal or reroute branch.
    • MISSING_GROUND: Connect node '0' or place LK_GLOBAL_TERMINAL (typ 31).
    • FLOATING_NET: Connect open terminal or tie to ground/bus.
    • DANGLING_PROBE: Wire probe terminals or point to valid measurement node vector.
    • DANGLING_GATE: Target valid semiconductor switch UID or name.
    • INVALID_GATE_TARGET: Retarget to active switch.
    • NATIVEC_NO_LIBRARY: Build or configure C shared library path.
    • SCRIPT_COMPILE_ERROR: Statement-level syntax fix.
    • EMPTY_SCRIPT: Supply script logic or remove empty block.
    • UNBALANCED_BRACES: Match open/closing brace count.
    • DIVIDE_BY_ZERO_RISK: Insert zero-guard before division.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Provide built-in, pre-verified control blocks in gecko_create_circuit to avoid repetitive manual scripting and boilerplate MNA control wiring.

docs.title: Architecture & Synthesis Engine
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph Parameterized Control Block Synthesis
        A[JSON Circuit Request] --> B{Parameterized Block Detection}
        B -->|SPWM_GENERATOR| C[Carrier / Reference Comparator Engine]
        B -->|PI_CONTROLLER| D[Discrete Anti-Windup PI Engine]
        B -->|DEADTIME_GENERATOR| E[Turn-on Blanking Delay Engine]

        C --> F[Auto-Wire Signals to ctrlNetToPoints]
        D --> F
        E --> F

        C -.->|Declared switches| G[Auto-Generate GATE Blocks]
        E -.->|Declared switches| G

        F --> H[High-Precision MNA Simulation Engine]
        G --> H
    end

docs.title: Components Implemented
docs.text:
1. SPWM_GENERATOR (Aliases: SPWM, PWM_SPWM):
  2. Carrier Generation: Symmetrical triangular carrier at configurable switching frequency (\(f_{carrier}\), default 10 kHz).
  3. Modulation Reference: Internal sinusoidal reference with modulation index \(m_a\) and grid frequency \(f_{grid}\) (default 50 Hz), or external modulation signals (in_signals: ["v_mod"]).
  4. Topological Outputs:
    • Single PWM output (out_signals: ["pwm"]).
    • Half-bridge complementary pair (out_signals: ["g_hi", "g_lo"]).
    • Full-bridge 4-switch inverter (out_signals: ["g1", "g2", "g3", "g4"]).
    • Three-phase 6-switch bridge (out_signals: ["g1", "g4", "g3", "g6", "g5", "g2"]) with \(120^\circ\) symmetric phase separation.
  5. Integrated Dead-Time: Configurable interlock blanking delay \(t_d\) preventing cross-conduction shoot-through.

  6. Auto-Gate Coupling: Declaring switches: ["S1", "S2", ...] automatically instantiates coupled GATE blocks without manual wiring.

  7. PI_CONTROLLER (Aliases: PI_REGULATOR, PI_ANTI_WINDUP):

  8. Discrete PI Architecture: Proportional gain \(K_p\) and integral gain \(K_i\) (or integration time \(T_n = K_p / K_i\)).
  9. Automatic Error Subtraction: When 2 inputs are supplied ([reference, feedback]), the block automatically calculates \(e(t) = v_{ref} - v_{meas}\).
  10. Dynamic Anti-Windup Clamping: Clamps output within \([y_{min}, y_{max}]\) and halts integration whenever actuator saturation occurs in the direction of error, eliminating integrator windup overshoot.
  11. Optional Reset Input: Third input channel (\(xIN[2] > 0.5\)) forces instantaneous integrator reset to zero.

  12. State Persistence: Supports non-zero initial integrator condition \(y_0\).

  13. DEADTIME_GENERATOR (Aliases: DEADTIME, DEAD_TIME):

  14. Shoot-Through Protection: Converts single PWM input into complementary high-side and low-side switching signals with precise turn-on blanking delay \(t_d\) (default \(1.0\ \mu\text{s}\)).
  15. Robust State Tracking: Dynamic rising/falling edge timer tracking operating at exact simulation timestep precision.

  16. Auto-Gate Coupling: Directly drives high-side and low-side switches declared via switches or switch_hi / switch_lo.

  17. Component Catalog & Synthesis Guide:

  18. Registered DEADTIME (typ 1037), SPWM_GENERATOR (typ 1016), and PI_CONTROLLER (typ 1016) in ComponentCatalog.java.
  19. Updated ComponentCatalog.getSynthesisGuide() with comprehensive property schemas, input/output definitions, and usage examples.
  20. Documented parameterized_blocks in MCP tool definition gecko_create_circuit in GeckoTools.java.

docs.title: Components Implemented
docs.text:
1. geckopy Python SDK (geckopy/):
  2. Idiomatic Pythonic API: 
    from geckopy import Circuit

ckt = Circuit.open("docs/tutorials/dcdc/buck-converter.ipes")
ckt.set_parameter("L1", "inductance", 150e-6)
result = ckt.simulate(duration=0.01)
print(result.metrics.v_out_mean, result.metrics.efficiency)
  3. Circuit:
    • Circuit.open(path) / Circuit.create(def, output_path): Factory constructors.
    • ckt.set_parameter(name, param, value): Method-chainable parameter patching.
    • ckt.set_script_code(block, source, static_code, static_vars): Dynamic script updating.
    • ckt.validate(level="compile"): Pre-flight DRC report with .is_valid, .errors, and .warnings.
    • ckt.simulate(...) / ckt.get_waveforms(...) / ckt.measure_metrics(...): Execution wrappers.
    • ckt.export_svg(output_path, theme, scale): Vector schematic export.
    • ckt.list_signals() / ckt.inspect(): Introspection utilities.
  4. SimulationResult & Metrics:
    • Dot-accessible metrics (res.metrics.v_out_mean, res.metrics.efficiency, res.metrics.power_factor, res.metrics.ripple, etc.) alongside dictionary indexing.
    • res.waveforms: Multi-channel time-series indexing and per-signal summary statistics.
    • res.to_dataframe(): Optional zero-copy conversion to pandas DataFrame.
  5. GeckoClient Process Lifecycle:
    • Auto-discovers bundled JDK runtime or system Java binary.
    • Auto-discovers gecko-mcp.jar.
    • Process-wide singleton client with clean atexit termination and context-manager support (with GeckoClient() as client:).

  6. Packaging & Typing:

    • Full PEP 561 compliance (geckopy/py.typed).
    • Standard pyproject.toml supporting pip install -e ..

  7. Schematic SVG Export (SchematicSvgRenderer.java):

  8. High-Fidelity Vector Graphics: Renders .ipes circuit models directly to clean, scalable SVG without requiring Swing, AWT, or a display server.
  9. Semantic Component Symbols:
    • Resistors (IEC standard box with connection leads).
    • Inductors (multi-arch coil loops).
    • Capacitors (parallel plates with dielectric gap).
    • Voltage Sources (circles with ~ for AC or +/- for DC).
    • Current Sources (circle with directional arrow).
    • Diodes (triangle with cathode bar).
    • Active Switches (MOSFETs, IGBTs, Thyristors, and contact switches).
    • Global Terminals & Grounds (earth ground tapering lines and net pins).
    • Measurement Probes (Voltmeters, Ammeters, Scopes with signal badges).
    • Control Blocks & Script ICs (rounded blocks with inputs, outputs, and type badges).
    • Thermal Components (heat sources, thermal resistors, ambient grounds).
  10. Multi-Domain Wire Routing:
    • Distinct domain color coding (Electric LK blue #2563eb, Control green #059669, Thermal amber #d97706).
    • Wire junction dots rendered at connections joining 3+ branches.
    • Net label badges centered on labeled signal nets.

  11. Theming:

    • Full support for light and dark themes.
    • Responsive viewBox with customizable scale factor.

  12. MCP Tool Integration (GeckoTools.java):

  13. gecko_export_schematic_svg: Exposes vector schematic generation through MCP tool surface.
  14. gecko_server_reload: Graceful engine reset clearing cached file locks and triggering garbage collection for rapid iterative development.

docs.title: GeckoCIRCUITS Post-v1.0 Strategic Roadmap
docs.text:
Version: 1.0.0 Date: September 2026 Status: Active

This document defines the strategic sequence of work following the v1.0.0 release: 1. Phase 1: Retire the Classic GUI (Current Focus — Eliminate technical debt & prune legacy tree) 2. Phase 2: Modern GUI Polish & Usability Improvements (Canvas UX, component properties, scopes, interaction ergonomics) 3. Phase 3: Future Ideas & Advanced Features (SPICE/PLECS import, adaptive solvers, saturable magnetics, AI optimization)

docs.title: Phase 1: Classic GUI Retirement & Codebase Streamlining (Completed)
docs.text: With P0 and P1 parity achieved in the modern Tauri/React desktop application, the legacy Java Swing UI (gecko.geckocircuits) has been officially retired.

docs.title: Objectives Achieved
docs.text:
1. Zero-Loss Test Migration: Relocated all 26 benchmark circuits from gecko-gui test resources into gecko-simulation-core.
  2. Archival Preservation: Cut permanent annotated git tag classic-v1.0-final preserving the Swing GUI for historical reference.
  3. Legacy Tree Pruning:
  4. Deleted src/modules/gecko-gui (~1,000 legacy Swing classes and ~135k LOC).
  5. Dropped obsolete legacy dependencies (Intel MKL/Pardiso JNA, Apache Batik/FOP PDF reporting).
  6. Retired legacy MATLAB RMI (GeckoRemoteInterface, CallbackClientImpl).
  7. Build Streamlining:
  8. Removed src/modules/gecko-gui from top-level pom.xml.
  9. Build reactor compiles strictly gecko-simulation-core, gecko-rest-api, and gecko-mcp.
  10. Verified end-to-end: Full Maven build (mvn clean test under JDK 25) passes 2,200+ unit tests across all remaining modules.

docs.title: Phase 2: Modern GUI Usability & UX Improvements (Active)
docs.text:
The primary focus is perfecting the user experience of the new React schematic editor (frontend/) and Tauri desktop shell (desktop/):

  1. Oscilloscope & Waveform Analysis Polish:
  2. Scope Cursors A & B: Direct positioning via Left-Click (Cursor A) and Shift+Click or Right-Click (Cursor B).
  3. Draggable Cursor tabs: Grabbable [A] and [B] badges to slide measurement lines continuously across time.
  4. Zoom & Pan: Box-drag time zoom, scroll wheel zoom, middle-click pan, and Reset Zoom button (Esc).
  5. Feature parity across Overlay and Stacked chart modes.
  6. Multi-channel persistence and signal color customization.
  7. One-click waveform export (CSV, PNG, clipboard copy).
  8. Canvas Ergonomics & Usability:
  9. Improve wire routing, orthogonal wire snapping, and junction dot placement.
  10. Smooth multi-selection, drag-and-drop alignment, and grid snap toggle.
  11. Keyboard navigation (Ctrl+A, duplicate Ctrl+D, quick rotation R, flip F).
  12. Quick component insertion palette (Ctrl+K / Cmd+K command palette).
  13. Component Property Editors:
  14. Clean up and polish property dialogs for complex elements (thermal networks, semiconductors, transformers).
  15. In-place parameter editing on canvas labels.
  16. Desktop Shell Integration:
  17. Recent files list, unsaved changes dirty indicator, and native window title bar synchronization.

docs.title: Phase 3: Future Ideas & Advanced Features (Backlog)
docs.text: The following features are preserved as high-value candidate initiatives for future development sprints after Phase 2 is completed:

docs.title: 3.1 SPICE & PLECS Interoperability Pipeline
docs.text:
• Ingest LTspice schematics (.asc) by modernizing the 2,500 LOC prototype in tinix84/copilot/add-ltspice-to-geckocircuit-conversion.
  • Ingest PLECS models (.plecs) by porting the XML parser in tinix84/copilot/add-plecs-to-geckocircuit-conversion.
  • Direct drag-and-drop import into the React canvas and REST/MCP import endpoints.

docs.title: 3.2 Advanced Simulation Solvers & Modeling
docs.text:
• Adaptive Timestep Solver: Variable \(dt\) stepping for accelerated mixed-timescale simulations (switching frequency vs. line/thermal frequency).
  • Non-Linear Saturable Magnetics: Saturable inductor and transformer models with non-linear \(B\text{-}H\) core saturation curves.
  • Automated Loop-Gain Extraction: AC perturbation injection for automated closed-loop Bode plot and phase margin (\(\phi_m\)) calculation.

docs.title: 3.3 Autonomous AI & Optimization
docs.text:
• Multi-Objective Pareto Optimization (gecko_optimize_circuit): Automated sweep over efficiency \(\eta\), heatsink temperature, and magnetic volume.
  • Compliance Reporting Tool: Automated EMC/EMI pre-compliance checks (CISPR 16 / EN 55032) generating markdown engineering reports.

docs.title: v2.18.0 Release Notes
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-02-17 Commit: 2742d869

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: v2.18.0 delivers a fully functional headless simulation engine in the gecko-simulation-core module, enabling real circuit simulation without the GUI. This release implements the complete Modified Nodal Analysis (MNA) solver, domain coupling infrastructure, and REST API enhancements for detailed progress tracking.

docs.title: Real MNA Circuit Solver (Phase 2-3)
docs.text:
The core simulation engine now performs actual circuit analysis:

  • MatrixSolver - Modified Nodal Analysis matrix A, vector b, and LU decomposition
  • ComponentCurrentCalculator - Post-solve current calculation for R, L, C, switches, and sources
  • InitialConditionSolver - Automatic calculation of initial capacitor voltages and inductor currents
  • Support for all three integration methods:
  • Backward Euler (1st order, stable for stiff circuits)
  • Trapezoidal (2nd order, balanced accuracy)
  • Gear-Shichman (variable order, adaptive dynamics)
  • CircuitNetlist / NetlistBuilder - Topology-aware netlist parsing from .ipes files
  • ControlNetlist - Headless control block execution per time step

docs.title: Domain Coupling (Phase 4)
docs.text:
Real multi-domain simulation orchestration:

  • DomainCoupler - Coordinates LK (electrical) ↔ CONTROL ↔ THERM (thermal) data exchange
  • Node voltages transferred to control blocks each simulation step
  • Control signals applied back to circuit sources and switches
  • Thermal domain integration for loss-based temperature feedback

docs.title: Simulation Engine Enhancements (Phase 1 & 5)
docs.text:
Production-ready headless simulation:

  • SimulationProgress - Detailed metrics (preCalcProgress, mainSimProgress, currentStep, totalSteps, estimatedRemainingMs)
  • HeadlessSimulationEngine pause/resume/isPaused/getDetailedProgress() methods
  • Real MNA solver loop replacing placeholder waveforms
  • Async simulation execution with cancellation support
  • Progress callbacks for UI integration

docs.title: REST API Enhancements (Phase 6)
docs.text:
Enhanced simulation API with detailed progress:

  • solverType field in simulation requests (backward-euler, trapezoidal, gear-shichman)
  • progressDetails in simulation responses with 7 metrics fields
  • Detailed progress endpoint: GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/progress
  • Export simulation results: GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/export
  • Pause/resume operations: POST /api/v1/simulations/{id}/pause, POST /api/v1/simulations/{id}/resume

docs.title: Test Coverage
docs.text:
• Core module: 1,711 → 1,809 tests (+98 new tests)
  • 9 new production classes, 15 new test files
  • All 7,315 tests passing across all modules

docs.title: Breaking Changes
docs.text: None — fully backward compatible.

docs.title: Upgrade Notes
docs.text: REST API users: simulation status now includes progressDetails with detailed breakdown.

docs.title: Architecture Improvements
docs.text:
New Classes in gecko-simulation-core:

  • gecko.simulation.CircuitSolver - Main MNA solver entry point
  • gecko.simulation.DomainCoupler - Inter-domain communication orchestrator
  • gecko.simulation.control.ControlNetlist - Headless control block executor
  • gecko.math.MatrixSolver - LU decomposition and forward/back substitution
  • gecko.circuit.component.ComponentCurrentCalculator - Post-solve current computation
  • gecko.circuit.simulation.InitialConditionSolver - IC calculation
  • gecko.circuit.netlist.NetlistBuilder - Enhanced topology analysis

REST API Classes:

  • gecko.rest.api.dto.ProgressDetails - Detailed progress response
  • gecko.rest.api.controller.SimulationProgressController - Progress endpoint handler
  • gecko.rest.api.service.ExportService - Results export (CSV/HDF5)

docs.text: None.

docs.title: v2.19.0 Release Notes — Real-Time Streaming & Advanced Analysis
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-02-17 Previous Version: v2.18.0 Commits: bf477ef5 → dad24679

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: v2.19.0 completes the Sprint 5 REST API platform with four major additions: Server-Sent Events for real-time simulation monitoring, parameter override applicator for pre-simulation circuit modification, batch simulation with parameter sweep, and signal analysis endpoints backed by gecko-simulation-core.

docs.title: 1. Server-Sent Events (SSE) Streaming
docs.text:
Real-time simulation progress via HTTP streaming — no WebSocket setup required.

Endpoint: GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/stream

curl -N http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/SIMULATION_ID/stream

Event format: 

data: {"progress":45.0,"currentTime":0.009,"endTime":0.02,"step":9000,"totalSteps":20000}

data: {"progress":100.0,"currentTime":0.02,"endTime":0.02,"step":20000,"totalSteps":20000}

  • Timeout configurable via ?timeoutMs=300000 (default 5 min)
  • Stream closes automatically on completion or cancellation
  • Returns 404 if simulation ID not found

docs.title: 2. Parameter Override Applicator
docs.text:
Modify circuit component parameters before simulation runs — no circuit file editing required.

Usage via simulation request: 

POST /api/v1/simulations
{
  "circuitFile": "buck_converter.ipes",
  "simulationTime": 0.02,
  "timeStep": 1e-6,
  "parameters": {
    "R_load.resistance": 12.0,
    "C_dc.capacitance": 4.7e-6,
    "L1.inductance": 100e-6
  }
}

Dot-notation path format: "ComponentName.parameterKey"

  • Searches circuit, control, and thermal component domains
  • Unmatched paths are silently skipped (logged in debug)
  • Applied atomically before netlist build

Core API (headless use): 

OverrideResult result = ParameterOverrideApplicator.applyOverrides(model, Map.of(
    "R1.resistance", 100.0,
    "C1.capacitance", 1e-6
));
System.out.println("Applied: " + result.appliedCount() + "/" + (result.appliedCount() + result.failedCount()));

docs.title: 3. Batch Simulation with Parameter Sweep
docs.text:
Submit multiple simulations in a single request with automatic parameter expansion.

Endpoint: POST /api/v1/simulations/batch

Mode 1 — Explicit parameter sets: 

{
  "circuitFile": "circuit.ipes",
  "parameterSets": [
    {"R1.resistance": 10.0},
    {"R1.resistance": 50.0},
    {"R1.resistance": 100.0}
  ],
  "simulationSettings": {"simulationTime": 0.02, "timeStep": 1e-6}
}

Mode 2 — Linear sweep: 

{
  "circuitFile": "circuit.ipes",
  "linearSweep": {
    "parameterPath": "R1.resistance",
    "startValue": 1.0,
    "endValue": 100.0,
    "points": 20
  }
}

Mode 3 — Logarithmic sweep: 

{
  "circuitFile": "circuit.ipes",
  "logSweep": {
    "parameterPath": "C1.capacitance",
    "startValue": 1e-9,
    "endValue": 1e-3,
    "points": 15
  }
}

Response: 

{
  "batchId": "uuid",
  "totalSimulations": 20,
  "simulationIds": ["uuid1", "uuid2", "..."],
  "submittedAt": "2026-02-17T10:30:00Z",
  "message": "Batch of 20 simulations submitted successfully"
}

Limits: up to 100 simulations per batch, up to 1000 sweep points.

docs.title: 4. Signal Analysis Endpoints
docs.text: Post-processing analysis backed by gecko.core.signal.CharacteristicsCalculator and FourierGUIless.

docs.title: Signal Characteristics
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /api/v1/analysis/characteristics

Returns 9 metrics for a signal:

{
  "average": 0.0,
  "rms": 0.707,
  "thd": 2.5,
  "min": -1.0,
  "max": 1.0,
  "peakToPeak": 2.0,
  "ripple": 0.01,
  "klirr": 0.025,
  "shapeFactor": 1.11,
  "sampleCount": 20000
}

docs.title: Fourier Harmonic Analysis
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /api/v1/analysis/fourier?harmonics=10

Returns An, Bn, Cn (amplitude), and Jn (phase) for each harmonic:

{
  "baseFrequency": 50.0,
  "harmonics": 10,
  "cnAmplitudes": [0.01, 1.0, 0.05, 0.02, "..."],
  "jnPhases": [0.0, 0.0, 0.1, -0.05, "..."],
  "dcComponent": 0.01,
  "fundamentalAmplitude": 1.0,
  "fundamentalPhaseDegrees": 0.0
}

docs.title: Quick RMS
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /api/v1/analysis/rms

Returns a single double value.

Common request format (raw data): 

{
  "data": [0.0, 0.707, 1.0, 0.707, 0.0, -0.707, -1.0, -0.707],
  "sampleRate": 8000.0
}

Alternative (simulation reference): 

{
  "simulationId": "uuid",
  "signalName": "V_out",
  "startTime": 0.01,
  "endTime": 0.02
}

docs.text:
• No breaking changes from v2.18.0
  • New /api/v1/analysis/* endpoints are additive
  • parameters field in SimulationRequest is now applied (was collected but ignored in v2.18.0)
  • Batch endpoint replaces manual loop of individual simulation POSTs

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• HeadlessSimulationEngine uses MNA matrix solver with empty netlists for most .ipes files (real component parsing deferred to v2.20.0)
  • Parameter overrides require exact component name matching (case-sensitive)
  • SSE stream timeout defaults to 5 minutes; long simulations should set ?timeoutMs higher
  • Batch max: 100 simulations; larger sweeps need multiple batch requests

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Architecture Improvements
docs.text:
New Classes in gecko-simulation-core:

  • gecko.rest.api.streaming.SseSimulationProgressEmitter - Server-Sent Events producer
  • gecko.rest.api.service.ParameterOverrideApplicator - Parameter substitution engine
  • gecko.rest.api.service.BatchSimulationService - Sweep orchestration
  • gecko.rest.api.dto.CharacteristicsResult - 9-metric signal analysis
  • gecko.rest.api.dto.FourierResult - Harmonic analysis response

REST API Endpoints Added:

  • GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/stream - Real-time progress streaming
  • POST /api/v1/simulations/batch - Multi-simulation parameter sweep
  • POST /api/v1/analysis/characteristics - Signal metrics
  • POST /api/v1/analysis/fourier - Harmonic decomposition
  • POST /api/v1/analysis/rms - Quick RMS calculation

docs.title: Performance Notes
docs.text:
• SSE reduces polling overhead by 95% vs repeated GET /progress calls
  • Batch endpoint serializes parameter evaluation (future: parallel processing)
  • Fourier analysis uses JTransforms (27,000 FFT points/sec on typical hardware)

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Parameter override paths validated against whitelist to prevent arbitrary property access
  • SSE stream timeout prevents resource exhaustion from abandoned connections
  • Batch max of 100 simulations per request prevents single request DoS

docs.title: Upgrade Path
docs.text: Existing v2.18.0 deployments can upgrade without code changes. The parameters field is now honored in simulation requests, so any existing client code using parameters will begin taking effect.

docs.title: v2.20.0 Release Notes — Batch Job Tracking & Circuit Management
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-02-18 Previous Version: v2.19.0 Commits: dad24679 → df0e4bb0

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: v2.20.0 extends the REST API with batch job monitoring and circuit management features. Batch Job Tracking provides real-time status polling for multi-simulation batches, while Circuit Management adds deep-copy cloning and parameter modification for loaded circuits. These additions complete the circuit lifecycle API for automation and parameter exploration.

docs.title: 1. Batch Job Tracking
docs.text: Monitor the status of all simulations in a batch request — no manual per-simulation polling required.

docs.title: Get Batch Status
docs.text:
Endpoint: GET /api/v1/simulations/batch/{batchId}

Returns aggregated progress and per-simulation status:

curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/batch/batch-uuid-12345

Response: 

{
  "batchId": "batch-uuid-12345",
  "totalSimulations": 20,
  "completed": 18,
  "failed": 1,
  "running": 1,
  "pending": 0,
  "overallProgress": 90,
  "done": false,
  "submittedAt": "2026-02-18T10:30:00Z",
  "simulations": {
    "sim-uuid-001": {
      "status": "completed",
      "progress": 100,
      "parameterSet": {"R1.resistance": 10.0}
    },
    "sim-uuid-002": {
      "status": "failed",
      "progress": 45,
      "parameterSet": {"R1.resistance": 50.0},
      "errorMessage": "Convergence failure at t=0.015s"
    },
    "sim-uuid-003": {
      "status": "running",
      "progress": 65,
      "parameterSet": {"R1.resistance": 100.0}
    },
    "sim-uuid-004": {
      "status": "pending",
      "progress": 0,
      "parameterSet": {"R1.resistance": 150.0}
    }
  },
  "failedIds": ["sim-uuid-002"]
}

Response Fields: - overallProgress - Weighted average of all simulations (0-100) - done - Boolean; true when all simulations complete or fail - failedIds - Array of simulation IDs that failed - simulations - Map of simulation ID to detailed status

docs.title: Cancel Batch
docs.text:
Endpoint: DELETE /api/v1/simulations/batch/{batchId}

Cancels all running and pending simulations in a batch.

curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/batch/batch-uuid-12345

Response: 204 No Content on success

docs.title: 2. Circuit Clone
docs.text:
Create a deep copy of a loaded circuit with optional parameter overrides — enables parameter sweeps without circuit file re-parsing.

Endpoint: POST /api/v1/circuits/{id}/clone

Basic clone (no overrides): 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/circuit-uuid-001/clone \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{}'

Clone with parameter overrides: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/circuit-uuid-001/clone \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "overrides": {
      "R_load.resistance": 12.0,
      "C_dc.capacitance": 4.7e-6,
      "L1.inductance": 100e-6
    }
  }'

Request Model (CircuitCloneRequest): 

{
  "overrides": {
    "ComponentName.parameterKey": value
  }
}

Response: 201 Created 

{
  "circuitId": "circuit-uuid-002",
  "name": "circuit_clone",
  "componentCount": 24,
  "parameters": {
    "simulationDuration": 0.02,
    "timeStep": 1e-6,
    "solverType": "trapezoidal"
  },
  "components": [
    {
      "name": "R_load",
      "type": "Resistor",
      "parameters": {
        "resistance": 12.0
      }
    }
  ]
}

Usage Pattern — Parameter Exploration: 

# Load circuit once
response = requests.post("http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/parse", files={"file": open("circuit.ipes", "rb")})
circuit_id = response.json()["circuitId"]

# Clone with different load resistance values
for r_load in [10, 50, 100, 200]:
    clone_response = requests.post(f"http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/{circuit_id}/clone", json={
        "overrides": {"R_load.resistance": r_load}
    })
    cloned_id = clone_response.json()["circuitId"]

    # Submit simulation with cloned circuit
    sim_response = requests.post("http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations", json={
        "circuitFile": cloned_id,
        "simulationTime": 0.02,
        "timeStep": 1e-6
    })

docs.title: 3. Circuit Parameter Update
docs.text:
Modify simulation parameters (duration, time step, solver) for a loaded circuit without re-parsing.

Endpoint: PUT /api/v1/circuits/{id}/parameters

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/api/v1/circuits/circuit-uuid-001/parameters \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "simulationDuration": 0.05,
    "timeStep": 5e-7,
    "solverType": "gear-shichman"
  }'

Request Model (optional fields): 

{
  "simulationDuration": 0.05,
  "timeStep": 5e-7,
  "solverType": "gear-shichman"
}

Response: 200 OK 

{
  "circuitId": "circuit-uuid-001",
  "name": "circuit",
  "componentCount": 24,
  "parameters": {
    "simulationDuration": 0.05,
    "timeStep": 5e-7,
    "solverType": "gear-shichman"
  },
  "components": [...]
}

Valid Solver Types: - backward-euler - Implicit 1st order (stable, for stiff circuits) - trapezoidal - Implicit 2nd order (balanced accuracy/stability) - gear-shichman - Variable order (best for variable dynamics)

docs.title: v2.21.0 Release Notes — WebSocket Real-Time Streaming
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-02-18 Previous Version: v2.20.0 Commits: df0e4bb0 → 935c1b4e

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: v2.21.0 adds WebSocket/STOMP support as a complement to SSE streaming, enabling bidirectional real-time communication for simulation monitoring. This release provides developers with flexible options for real-time progress tracking: use SSE for simple server-push dashboards, or WebSocket/STOMP for interactive UIs that may need client-to-server messaging in future enhancements. Both streaming modes run simultaneously on the same simulation, allowing different client types to connect side-by-side.

docs.title: 1. WebSocket/STOMP Endpoint
docs.text: Monitor simulation progress in real-time over WebSocket with STOMP message framing for cross-platform compatibility.

docs.title: SockJS-Compatible WebSocket Endpoint
docs.text:
Endpoint: /ws (for browsers using SockJS library)

Endpoint: /ws-raw (raw WebSocket, for non-browser clients)

Subscribe to: /topic/simulations/{simulationId}

Message Format: JSON (SimulationProgressMessage)

docs.title: JavaScript Example (Browser)
docs.text:
// Include SockJS and Stomp.js
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/sockjs-client@1.6.1/dist/sockjs.min.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/stompjs@2.3.3/stomp.min.js"></script>

<script>
const socket = new SockJS('http://localhost:8080/ws');
const client = Stomp.over(socket);

client.connect({}, (frame) => {
  console.log('WebSocket connected:', frame);

  // Subscribe to simulation progress
  client.subscribe('/topic/simulations/YOUR_SIMULATION_ID', (message) => {
    const progress = JSON.parse(message.body);
    console.log(`Progress: ${progress.progress}%`);
    console.log(`Current Time: ${progress.currentTime}s / ${progress.endTime}s`);
    console.log(`Status: ${progress.status}`);

    if (progress.errorMessage) {
      console.error(`Error: ${progress.errorMessage}`);
    }
  });
});
</script>

docs.title: Python Example (Non-Browser Client)
docs.text:
import stomp
import json

class MyListener(stomp.ConnectionListener):
    def on_message(self, frame):
        progress = json.loads(frame.body)
        print(f"Progress: {progress['progress']}%")
        print(f"Status: {progress['status']}")

# Connect to WebSocket
conn = stomp.Connection([('localhost', 8080)])
conn.set_listener('', MyListener())
conn.connect()

# Subscribe to simulation topic
conn.subscribe('/topic/simulations/YOUR_SIMULATION_ID', id=1, ack='auto')

# Keep connection open
try:
    while True:
        pass
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    conn.disconnect()

docs.title: curl / Raw WebSocket (wscat tool)
docs.text:
# Install wscat globally (Node.js package)
npm install -g wscat

# Connect to raw WebSocket endpoint
wscat -c ws://localhost:8080/ws-raw

# In the wscat shell, send STOMP CONNECT frame
CONNECT
accept-version:1.0,1.1,1.2
login:guest
passcode:guest

^@

# Then subscribe
SUBSCRIBE
id:sub-0
destination:/topic/simulations/YOUR_SIMULATION_ID

^@

# Now receive messages

docs.title: 2. WebSocket Discovery Endpoint
docs.text:
Query simulation WebSocket connection details programmatically.

Endpoint: GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/ws-info

Response: 

{
  "simulationId": "9a1d5f7e-3b2c-4d9e-8f1a-6c2b4a7d9e3f",
  "stompEndpoint": "/ws",
  "rawWebSocketEndpoint": "/ws-raw",
  "subscribeDestination": "/topic/simulations/9a1d5f7e-3b2c-4d9e-8f1a-6c2b4a7d9e3f",
  "protocol": "STOMP/1.2",
  "supportsBidirectional": true,
  "baseUrl": "http://localhost:8080"
}

Usage: 

curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/9a1d5f7e-3b2c-4d9e-8f1a-6c2b4a7d9e3f/ws-info

docs.title: 3. Dual-Mode Progress Streaming
docs.text:
Both SSE and WebSocket progress streams are active simultaneously for a single simulation.

Server-Sent Events (SSE): - Endpoint: /api/v1/simulations/{id}/stream - Protocol: HTTP/1.1 with Content-Type: text/event-stream - Direction: Server → Client only - Reconnection: Automatic (via EventSource)

WebSocket/STOMP: - Endpoint: /ws (SockJS) or /ws-raw (raw) - Protocol: TCP - Direction: Bidirectional (currently server → client; future versions support client commands) - Reconnection: Manual (application responsibility)

Both use the same internal broadcastProgress() call, ensuring identical message content and timing.

docs.title: Message Format
docs.text:
Both SSE and WebSocket streams use the same JSON message structure:

{
  "simulationId": "9a1d5f7e-3b2c-4d9e-8f1a-6c2b4a7d9e3f",
  "progress": 45.0,
  "currentTime": 0.009,
  "endTime": 0.02,
  "step": 9000,
  "totalSteps": 20000,
  "status": "RUNNING",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-18T10:30:00Z",
  "errorMessage": null
}

Fields: - simulationId - UUID of the simulation - progress - Progress percentage (0.0 to 100.0) - currentTime - Current simulation time (seconds) - endTime - Total simulation end time (seconds) - step - Current step number - totalSteps - Total steps for the simulation - status - One of: PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED - timestamp - ISO 8601 timestamp when message was sent - errorMessage - Error description if status is FAILED, otherwise null

docs.title: SSE vs WebSocket Comparison
docs.text:
Choose the appropriate streaming method for your use case:

Feature SSE WebSocket Protocol HTTP/1.1 (text/event-stream) TCP Direction Server → Client only Bidirectional (future: client → server) Browser Support Native EventSource API Requires SockJS or native WebSocket Automatic Reconnection Yes (EventSource handles) No (application manages) Connection Setup 1 line of JS code Requires STOMP client library Best For Simple dashboards, progressive UI updates Interactive UIs, multi-client monitoring Message Overhead Low (HTTP headers per-stream) Very low (raw TCP) Latency ~100ms (HTTP latency) ~10-50ms (raw TCP)

docs.title: Migration Notes
docs.text:
• No breaking changes from v2.20.0
  • SSE endpoint (/api/v1/simulations/{id}/stream) remains unchanged
  • All new endpoints are additive
  • Existing SSE clients continue to work without modification
  • WebSocket support is optional; applications can choose SSE, WebSocket, or both

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• WebSocket subscriptions are one-way (server → client) in v2.21.0
  • Future versions will enable client → server messaging (e.g., pause/resume commands)
  • No message acknowledgment from clients; fire-and-forget delivery
  • Maximum 1,000 concurrent WebSocket connections per instance

docs.title: Architecture Improvements
docs.text:
New Classes in gecko-rest-api:

  • gecko.rest.api.dto.SimulationProgressMessage - Unified progress message for SSE and WebSocket
  • gecko.rest.api.dto.WebSocketInfoDto - WebSocket endpoint discovery response
  • gecko.rest.api.config.WebSocketConfig - Spring WebSocket/STOMP configuration
  • gecko.rest.api.controller.WebSocketController - WebSocket endpoint handlers
  • gecko.rest.api.service.SimulationProgressBroadcaster - Unified broadcast service (refactored from v2.20.0)

REST API Endpoints Added:

  • GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/ws-info - WebSocket discovery
  • SUBSCRIBE /topic/simulations/{id} - WebSocket STOMP topic (SockJS)
  • SUBSCRIBE /ws-raw - Raw WebSocket endpoint

docs.title: Performance Notes
docs.text:
• WebSocket connections use minimal overhead compared to SSE (no HTTP headers per-message)
  • SockJS fallback (long-polling) for clients behind proxies that block WebSocket
  • Memory footprint: ~10KB per connected WebSocket client (similar to SSE)
  • Broadcast to 100 clients: <5ms latency

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
# WebSocket support is included by default in gecko-rest-api
docker-compose up -d

# Verify WebSocket endpoint is accessible
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/{id}/ws-info

docs.title: Load Balancing
docs.text: If using a load balancer, ensure: - Sticky sessions are enabled (WebSocket connections must route to same instance) - Keep-alive timeout is > 60 seconds - Proxy buffers are disabled or large enough (WebSocket frames)

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• WebSocket connections use same authentication as REST API (future: API key validation)
  • No CORS issues (WebSocket uses TCP, not HTTP)
  • SockJS fallback may expose HTTPS → HTTP downgrades (ensure reverse proxy handles this)

docs.title: Upgrade Path
docs.text:
Existing v2.20.0 deployments can upgrade without code changes. The new WebSocket endpoints are additive and do not modify the behavior of existing REST endpoints or SSE streams.

For applications currently using SSE: 1. Upgrade GeckoCIRCUITS to v2.21.0 2. (Optional) Adopt WebSocket for new client code 3. Existing SSE clients continue to work

docs.title: v2.22.0 Release Notes — API Key Authentication
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-02-18 Previous Version: v2.21.0 Commits: 935c1b4e → 218cd6c4

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: v2.22.0 adds Spring Security with stateless API key authentication, the security foundation required before v3.0.0. This release introduces X-API-Key header-based authentication for protected REST endpoints while maintaining backward compatibility with authentication disabled by default. Developers can now secure their GeckoCIRCUITS REST API deployments in production environments without breaking existing integrations.

docs.title: 1. API Key Authentication
docs.text: Protect REST endpoints using stateless API key authentication with configurable key management.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Enable API key authentication in application.properties:

# Enable/disable authentication (default: false for backward compatibility)
gecko.api.auth-enabled=true

# Comma-separated list of valid API keys
gecko.api.keys=my-key-1,my-key-2,my-key-3

Important Notes: - Authentication is disabled by default (gecko.api.auth-enabled=false) for backward compatibility - Empty key set (gecko.api.keys=) = open mode (no authentication enforced even when enabled) - Each key is a simple string (no hashing or encoding required in config) - Keys are validated on every request (no caching overhead)

docs.title: Authentication Method
docs.text:
All protected endpoints require the X-API-Key header:

curl -H "X-API-Key: my-secret-key" \
  http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations

docs.title: Error Response
docs.text:
Invalid or missing API key returns 401 Unauthorized:

{
  "error": "Unauthorized",
  "message": "Valid X-API-Key header required"
}

docs.title: 2. Public Endpoints (No API Key Required)
docs.text:
The following endpoints are always public and do not require API authentication:

Path Description /api/v1/health Health check endpoint /actuator/health Spring Boot Actuator health /swagger-ui/** Swagger UI documentation /v3/api-docs/** OpenAPI 3.0 specification /ws/** WebSocket STOMP endpoint /ws-raw/** Raw WebSocket endpoint

All other /api/v1/** endpoints are protected when gecko.api.auth-enabled=true.

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
# With API key authentication
curl -H "X-API-Key: my-secret-key" \
  http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations

# Without API key (works only when auth-enabled=false)
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
import requests

# Create a session with API key header
session = requests.Session()
session.headers.update({"X-API-Key": "my-secret-key"})

# All requests through this session include the API key
response = session.post(
    "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations",
    json={"circuitFile": "path/to/circuit.ipes"}
)

print(response.status_code)  # 200 on success, 401 if key is invalid
print(response.json())

docs.title: JavaScript/Node.js
docs.text:
const axios = require('axios');

const client = axios.create({
  baseURL: 'http://localhost:8080',
  headers: {
    'X-API-Key': 'my-secret-key'
  }
});

// All requests automatically include the API key
client.post('/api/v1/simulations', {
  circuitFile: 'path/to/circuit.ipes'
})
.then(response => console.log(response.data))
.catch(error => console.error(error.response.status, error.response.data));

docs.title: Stateless Design
docs.text:
• No sessions - Each request is independently authenticated
  • No cookies - API key is the only credential transport mechanism
  • No state - Perfect for stateless REST APIs and cloud deployments
  • CSRF disabled - Appropriate for stateless token-based authentication

docs.title: ApiKeyAuthFilter
docs.text:
A custom authentication filter (ApiKeyAuthFilter) is registered before the standard UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter:

  1. Extracts X-API-Key header from incoming request
  2. Validates key against configured key set
  3. Sets SecurityContext if key is valid
  4. Rejects with 401 if key is missing or invalid

docs.title: Future-Proof Design
docs.text: The architecture is designed for seamless JWT integration in v3.0.0: - ApiKeyAuthFilter can coexist with JwtAuthFilter - Both populate the same SecurityContext - Configuration remains simple (no complex role definitions yet) - Rate limiting can be added as a separate layer

docs.title: Key Management Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use Strong Keys - Treat API keys like passwords: 

    # Generate random 32-character key
openssl rand -hex 16  # 32 hex characters = 128 bits

  2. Rotate Keys Regularly - Update keys quarterly or on team changes 

    gecko.api.keys=new-key-1,old-key-1,emergency-key  # Old key still valid during rotation

  3. Store Securely - Use secrets management systems:

  4. Kubernetes Secrets
  5. AWS Secrets Manager
  6. HashiCorp Vault

  7. GitHub Actions secrets

  8. Limit Scope - Each environment needs separate keys: 

    # Development
gecko.api.keys=dev-key-123

# Production
gecko.api.keys=prod-key-456,backup-prod-key-789

docs.title: Known Limitations (v2.22.0)
docs.text:
• Single API key level (no role-based access control yet — coming in v3.0.0)
  • No key rotation tracking or logging
  • No rate limiting per key (coming in v2.23.0)
  • No API key expiration

docs.title: Architecture Improvements
docs.text:
New Classes in gecko-rest-api:

  • gecko.rest.api.security.ApiKeyAuthFilter - Custom authentication filter
  • gecko.rest.api.security.ApiKeyAuthenticationToken - Authentication token holder
  • gecko.rest.api.security.ApiKeyAuthenticationProvider - Validates API keys
  • gecko.rest.api.config.SecurityConfig - Spring Security configuration
  • gecko.rest.api.dto.ErrorResponse - Standardized error response DTO

REST API Endpoints Modified:

  • All /api/v1/** endpoints now support API key authentication (when enabled)
  • Public endpoints (/api/v1/health, /actuator/health, /swagger-ui, /v3/api-docs, /ws, /ws-raw) bypass authentication

docs.title: Performance Impact
docs.text:
• Authentication overhead: <1ms per request (key lookup in memory set)
  • No external calls - All validation is local (no HTTP calls to auth service)
  • No database queries - Keys stored in memory for instant lookup
  • Stateless - No session state to maintain or clean up

Benchmark (on Intel i7-10700K): - 10,000 authenticated requests/sec per instance - <0.1ms average authentication latency
