docs.title: v3.0.0 Release Notes — Complete REST API Platform
docs.text: Release Date: February 18, 2026 Commit: TBD (tag v3.0.0)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
v3.0.0 is the first major release of the GeckoCIRCUITS REST API platform, marking a significant milestone 12 versions in the making since the Java 21 foundation (v2.10.0). This release transforms GeckoCIRCUITS from a desktop-only simulator into a production-ready web service suitable for cloud deployment, CI/CD automation, batch processing, and real-time data streaming.

The REST API is now production-ready with 32 comprehensive endpoints covering simulation management, circuit file operations, loss calculations, signal analysis, batch operations, and real-time monitoring. Combined with the extracted GUI-free simulation core (183 classes, 1,829 tests), GeckoCIRCUITS v3.0.0 delivers a complete, tested, and deployable platform for power electronics simulation.

This release achieves a critical milestone: 7,426 total tests (5,373 main + 1,829 core + 224 API), with complete segregation of the simulation engine from GUI dependencies. The dual-track development strategy—maintaining the mature desktop application while building a modern REST API—is now complete and validated.

docs.title: Complete v2.18.0 → v2.22.0 Feature Integration
docs.text:
v3.0.0 consolidates all improvements from the v2.18.0–v2.22.0 release cycle:

v2.18.0 - Circuit Management & Parameter Override - Circuit cloning API endpoint - Circuit parameter update API endpoint - ParameterOverrideApplicator for pre-simulation circuit modification - 169 REST API tests (up from 94)

v2.19.0 - Batch Simulation & Parameter Sweep - Batch simulation submission endpoint (POST /api/v1/simulations/batch) - Parameter sweep with linear and logarithmic spacing - Batch status monitoring and cancellation - 191 REST API tests (up from 169)

v2.20.0 - Real-Time Streaming & WebSocket - Server-Sent Events (SSE) progress streaming (GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/stream) - WebSocket STOMP endpoint for bidirectional communication (WS /ws) - Raw WebSocket endpoint for real-time data push (WS /ws-raw) - WebSocket connection info endpoint (GET /api/v1/simulations/{id}/ws-info) - 204 REST API tests (up from 191)

v2.21.0 - Signal Analysis Endpoints - Signal characteristics calculation (POST /api/v1/analysis/characteristics) - Fourier analysis endpoint (POST /api/v1/analysis/fourier) - RMS calculation endpoint (POST /api/v1/analysis/rms) - 204 REST API tests (maintained, pending full integration)

v2.22.0 - Security & Authentication - API key authentication via Spring Security - Header-based authentication (X-API-Key) - Opt-in security model (disabled by default for backward compatibility) - Configuration: gecko.api.auth-enabled, gecko.api.keys - 224 REST API tests (stable, security integration pending)

docs.title: gecko-simulation-core: The Simulation Engine
docs.text:
The extracted core module is the foundation of v3.0.0:

  • 183 classes spanning 11 packages (circuit, control, datacontainer, math, signal, nativec, i18n, allg)
  • 1,829 comprehensive tests (30%+ JaCoCo coverage enforced)
  • Zero GUI imports (validated by CorePackageValidationTest)
  • Headless-ready with injectable dependencies for file I/O and external storage
  • Complete circuit analysis: MNA matrix stamping, LU decomposition, FFT, loss calculations

Key Validated Packages: - circuit.matrix - MNA matrix stampers with caching - circuit.netlist - Netlist building from circuit topology - circuit.simulation.solver - Real MNA solvers (BE, TRZ, GS) with cached LU decomposition - circuit.losscalculation - Power electronics loss lookup tables - control.calculators - 71+ control block implementations - math - Matrix operations, LU decomposition, FFT via JTransforms - datacontainer - Signal caching with IntegerMatrixCache, ShortMatrixCache - signal - Fourier analysis, characteristics calculation, CISPR16 FFT

docs.title: HeadlessSimulationEngine
docs.text:
The REST API uses HeadlessSimulationEngine for deterministic, reproducible simulations:

// Direct MNA solver usage in REST API
MatrixSolver solver = new MatrixSolver(TIME_STEP, SOLVER_TYPE);
Circuit circuit = circuitParser.parse(fileData);
solver.initialize(circuit);
for (int step = 0; step < steps; step++) {
    solver.step(circuit);  // Real MNA simulation
    results.append(solver.getNodeVoltages());
}

docs.title: Spring Boot 3.2.1 REST API
docs.text:
Production-ready REST service built on:

  • Spring Boot 3.2.1 - Latest stable release
  • Spring Security - API key authentication (optional)
  • Spring WebSocket - STOMP/SockJS for real-time bidirectional communication
  • OpenAPI 3.0 / Swagger UI - Auto-generated API documentation
  • Docker Compose - One-command deployment

docs.title: MNA Matrix Solver in Core
docs.text:
The circuit simulation engine is powered by the Modified Nodal Analysis (MNA) solver extracted to gecko-simulation-core:

  • Sparse matrix stamping for efficient representation
  • LU decomposition caching across multiple time steps
  • Automatic sparsity detection for optimal performance
  • Three solver families: Backward Euler (BE), Trapezoidal (TRZ), Gear-Shichman (GS)
  • Initial condition solving for accurate transient startup
  • Component current calculation from node voltages

docs.title: Parameter Override Applicator
docs.text:
The ParameterOverrideApplicator enables pre-simulation circuit modification:

// Override circuit parameters before simulation
ParameterOverrideApplicator applicator = new ParameterOverrideApplicator(circuit);
applicator.setParameter("R1", "Resistance", 1000.0);
applicator.setParameter("L1", "Inductance", 0.001);
applicator.apply();
// Now simulate with modified values

docs.title: Domain Coupling (LK-CONTROL-THERM)
docs.text:
Experimental support for multi-domain coupling:

  • Electrical (circuit simulation)
  • Control (feedback regulators)
  • Thermal (junction temperature, heatsink)

Bidirectional data flow enables co-simulation of interacting physical domains.

docs.title: Known Limitations (Honest Assessment)
docs.text: While v3.0.0 represents a major milestone, several intentional limitations remain:

docs.title: 1. Circuit File Parsing Scope
docs.text:
• CircuitFileParser successfully parses .ipes circuit metadata (name, type, version)
  • Full component topology parsing is incomplete—most real .ipes files result in empty netlists in HeadlessSimulationEngine
  • Workaround: Use API to upload and validate circuits before batch simulation
  • Status: Parser enhancement planned for v3.1.0

docs.title: 2. Parameter Override Name Matching
docs.text:
• ParameterOverrideApplicator requires exact component name matching (case-sensitive)
  • Component names must match exactly as specified in circuit file (e.g., "R1", "L1", "SW1")
  • Workaround: Use circuit validation endpoint to list exact component names first
  • Status: Fuzzy matching planned for v3.1.0

docs.title: 3. WebSocket Authentication
docs.text:
• STOMP/SockJS endpoint is publicly accessible without auth in v3.0.0
  • HTTP header-based authentication (X-API-Key) not yet supported for WebSocket connections
  • Workaround: Deploy REST API behind authenticated proxy/gateway
  • Status: WebSocket auth integration planned for v3.1.0

docs.title: 4. Rate Limiting & Quotas
docs.text:
• No rate limiting on API endpoints (no request throttling)
  • No per-user quota enforcement
  • Batch jobs not limited by request count or computational resources
  • Workaround: Deploy with reverse proxy (nginx, HAProxy) with rate-limit rules
  • Status: Native rate limiting planned for v3.1.0

docs.title: 5. MNA Solver Limitations
docs.text:
• Only three-phase AC and DC circuits tested thoroughly
  • Non-linear devices (diodes, transistors) use simplified models
  • Frequency-dependent components (transformers with frequency loss) use constant impedance
  • Workaround: Use detailed loss lookup tables for accurate loss estimation
  • Status: Component model expansion planned for v3.2.0

docs.title: v3.1.0 Roadmap (Next Release)
docs.text:
• Rate limiting and quota management
  • JWT token authentication (in addition to API keys)
  • Pagination for list endpoints (GET /api/v1/simulations?page=1&size=50)
  • Circuit file parser enhancements (full topology support)
  • Fuzzy component name matching
  • WebSocket JWT authentication
  • Batch job progress webhooks
  • Simulation result caching and expiration policies

docs.title: For Production Use
docs.text:
1. Use Docker deployment with docker-compose up -d
  2. Enable API key authentication: Set GECKO_API_AUTH_ENABLED=true
  3. Set strict simulation timeout: GECKO_SIMULATION_TIMEOUT=60 (adjust for your workloads)
  4. Deploy behind reverse proxy (nginx, HAProxy) with:
  5. SSL/TLS termination
  6. Rate limiting rules
  7. Access logging
  8. Monitor container logs: docker-compose logs -f gecko-rest-api
  9. Use managed storage for circuit files (S3, Azure Blob, GCS)

docs.title: For CI/CD Integration
docs.text:
# Submit batch simulation in CI/CD pipeline
BATCH_ID=$(curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/batch \
  -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  -d @batch-request.json | jq -r '.batchId')

# Poll until complete
while true; do
  STATUS=$(curl -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
    http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/batch/$BATCH_ID | jq -r '.status')
  if [ "$STATUS" = "COMPLETED" ] || [ "$STATUS" = "FAILED" ]; then
    break
  fi
  sleep 5
done

# Fetch results
curl -H "X-API-Key: $API_KEY" \
  http://localhost:8080/api/v1/simulations/batch/$BATCH_ID/results > results.json

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to GeckoCIRCUITS.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Native Desktop File Workflow: Implemented full file lifecycle management (New, Open, Save, Save As, and real-time dirty state tracking) across both the Tauri desktop shell and browser application modes.
  • Integrated Examples Library: Integrated the circuit examples browser directly into the File -> Examples menu, supporting local/disk synchronization, custom example authoring, and collision-free overwriting.
  • 2D Planar Topology Placement & Trunk-and-Stub Manhattan Router: Intelligent collision-free component placement and orthogonal Steiner comb routing in gecko_create_circuit for electrical, control, and thermal domains.
  • Headless Vector SVG Schematic Generator (gecko_export_schematic_svg): Publication-quality vector export of .ipes schematics with IEC 60617 symbols, orthogonal wire polylines, 3-way junction dots, and light/dark themes.
  • SPWM Inverter with Dead-Time Example: Bundled turnkey full-bridge SPWM inverter circuit configuration with active semiconductor freewheeling and dead-time control.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• IEC 60617 / IEEE 315 Semiconductor Symbols: Modernized IGBT, MOSFET, and BJT symbols by removing surrounding circular enclosures and scaling channel bar dimensions to match passive and diode component proportions.
  • Unified Global Ground Terminals: Synchronized LK_GLOBAL_TERMINAL (31), REL_GLOBAL_TERMINAL (32), and TH_GLOBAL_TERMINAL (50) across ComponentTerminals, NetlistBuilder, CircuitValidator, and the web canvas as single-terminal pins at (x, y - 2).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• DRC Dangling Wire Warnings: Resolved ground terminal pin offset bug where wires erroneously routed past the terminal stem to the symbol center.
  • Thermal Domain Wire Routing: Fixed diagonal thermal connection lines by routing thermal RC ladders through orthogonal unit-stepped paths with intermediate obstacle avoidance.
  • Code Review Cleanups: Eliminated dead code, replaced hardcoded grid coordinates and orientation flags with named constants, and completed full Javadoc/TSDoc coverage.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:

  • Pre-Simulation Signal Discovery: Automatic discovery and category filtering of electrical and control signals before running simulations.
  • Interactive Measurement Cursors: Precision drag cursors with delta readouts, 2D box zoom, and collapsible statistical analysis drawer.
  • MCP Server Comprehensive Test Suite: End-to-end automated tests for all 16 Model Context Protocol tools.

docs.title: Build & Test Everything
docs.text:
# Backend engine, REST API, and MCP server (enforces >=30% JaCoCo coverage on core)
mvn clean verify

# View core JaCoCo coverage report:
# backend/gecko-simulation-core/target/site/jacoco/index.html

# Style & static checks on gecko-mcp and gecko-rest-api
mvn checkstyle:check pmd:check \
  -D"checkstyle.config.location=../../checkstyle.xml" \
  -D"pmd.rulesets=../../pmd-ruleset.xml" \
  -pl backend/gecko-mcp,backend/gecko-rest-api

npm --prefix frontend run lint

npm --prefix frontend test

# Python SDK and tooling unit tests
python -m unittest discover -s tests

# Documentation strict link & build check

docs.title: Code Architecture
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS/
├── backend/
│   ├── gecko-simulation-core/   # GUI-free Java 25 MNA solver, stampers, calculators, .ipes I/O, DRC
│   ├── gecko-rest-api/          # Spring Boot 4.1.1 REST/SSE/WebSocket API + embedded frontend assets
│   └── gecko-mcp/               # Stdio MCP JSON-RPC 2.0 server (16 tools) + vector SVG exporter
├── frontend/                    # React + TypeScript schematic editor, scopes, FFT, loss panels
├── desktop/                     # Tauri 2 Rust desktop shell (`gecko-engine` & `gecko-desktop`)
├── geckopy/                     # Python SDK wrapping `gecko-mcp`
├── examples/                    # Curated quick-open circuits + manifest.json
├── resources/                   # Tutorials, application examples, reference projects, newsletters
└── docs/                        # MkDocs documentation site source

docs.title: Architectural Principles
docs.text:
• Strict GUI-Free Simulation Core: backend/gecko-simulation-core never imports Swing, AWT GUI frameworks, or UI libraries (guarded by maven-enforcer-plugin).
  • MNA Solver & Stampers: Components register in StamperRegistry (CircuitTypCore -> IMatrixStamper / IStatefulStamper).
  • Pure-Java Control Calculators: 74 calculator classes in gecko.core.control.calculators implement AbstractControlCalculatable.calculateYOUT(double deltaT).

docs.title: Pull Request Process
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository and create a branch from main (fix/..., feature/..., docs/..., refactor/..., test/...).
  2. Keep changes focused and add unit tests for new behavior.
  3. Run the relevant backend, frontend, desktop, Python, and mkdocs build --strict checks.
  4. Open a Pull Request against main with a clear summary and verification results.

docs.title: Adding Circuit Examples
docs.text:
1. Author and validate your .ipes file in GeckoCIRCUITS (or via geckopy / gecko_validate_circuit).
  2. Verify it simulates cleanly with expected physics behavior.
  3. Add or update documentation in docs/ and run mkdocs build --strict (plus python scripts/verify-examples.py if editing examples/).

docs.text: Domain Package Key Interface / Base Class Control Calculators gecko.core.control.calculators AbstractControlCalculatable, InitializableAtSimulationStart Circuit Stampers gecko.core.circuit.matrix IMatrixStamper, IStatefulStamper, StamperRegistry Solvers & Coupling gecko.core.simulation, gecko.core.simulation.solver HeadlessSimulationEngine, MatrixSolver, DomainCoupler Thermal / Losses gecko.core.circuit.losscalculation VerlustBerechnungDetailed, LossFileAccessor

docs.title: Adding a Control Block Calculator
docs.text:
Control calculators process wired input signals and produce output values on each simulation step in gecko.core.control.calculators:

  • Base class: AbstractControlCalculatable(int noInputs, int noOutputs) (or package-local helpers such as AbstractSingleInputSingleOutputCalculator).
  • Step execution: Override public void calculateYOUT(final double deltaT).
  • Signal arrays: Inputs sit in _inputSignal[port][0] and outputs are written to _outputSignal[port][0].
  • Initialization: Implement InitializableAtSimulationStart (initializeAtSimulationStart(final double deltaT)) when a block needs state reset at t = 0.

docs.title: Example: Gain Amplifier (GainCalculator)
docs.text:
package gecko.core.control.calculators;

public final class GainCalculator extends AbstractSingleInputSingleOutputCalculator {
    private double _gain;

    public GainCalculator(final double gain) {
        super();
        setGain(gain);
    }

    @Override
    public void calculateYOUT(final double deltaT) {
        _outputSignal[0][0] = _gain * _inputSignal[0][0];
    }

    public void setGain(final double gain) {
        _gain = gain;
    }
}

docs.title: Example: Stateful Integrator Pattern
docs.text:
package gecko.core.control.calculators;

public class SimpleIntegratorCalculator extends AbstractSingleInputSingleOutputCalculator
        implements InitializableAtSimulationStart {

    private double state;

    @Override
    public void initializeAtSimulationStart(final double deltaT) {
        state = 0.0;
        _outputSignal[0][0] = 0.0;
    }

    @Override
    public void calculateYOUT(final double deltaT) {
        state += _inputSignal[0][0] * deltaT;
        _outputSignal[0][0] = state;
    }
}

docs.title: Writing Calculator Unit Tests
docs.text:
import gecko.core.control.calculators.GainCalculator;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;

class GainCalculatorTest {
    @Test
    void scalesInputSignal() {
        GainCalculator calc = new GainCalculator(2.5);
        calc._inputSignal[0][0] = 4.0;
        calc.calculateYOUT(1e-6);
        assertEquals(10.0, calc._outputSignal[0][0], 1e-12);
    }
}

docs.title: Adding a Circuit Matrix Stamper
docs.text: Circuit elements stamp Modified Nodal Analysis (A · x = b) contributions into MatrixAccumulator (wrapped around dense or sparse solver matrices) and vector b:

docs.title: IMatrixStamper & IStatefulStamper
docs.text:
• stampMatrixA(MatrixAccumulator a, int nodeX, int nodeY, int nodeZ, double[] parameter, double dt)
  • stampVectorB(double[] b, int nodeX, int nodeY, int nodeZ, double[] parameter, double dt, double time, double[] previousValues)
  • calculateCurrent(double nodeVoltageX, double nodeVoltageY, double[] parameter, double dt, double previousCurrent)
  • getAdmittanceWeight(double parameterValue, double dt)

Switching elements (diodes, ideal switches, IGBTs, MOSFETs, thyristors) implement IStatefulStamper (updateState, isStateChanged, resetStateChange, isOn, setState, getCurrentResistance).

docs.title: Example: Resistor Stamper Pattern
docs.text:
package gecko.core.circuit.matrix;

public class CustomResistorStamper implements IMatrixStamper {
    @Override
    public void stampMatrixA(final MatrixAccumulator a, final int nodeX, final int nodeY,
                             final int nodeZ, final double[] parameter, final double dt) {
        double admittance = getAdmittanceWeight(parameter[0], dt);
        a.add(nodeX, nodeX, admittance);
        a.add(nodeY, nodeY, admittance);
        a.add(nodeX, nodeY, -admittance);
        a.add(nodeY, nodeX, -admittance);
    }

    @Override
    public void stampVectorB(final double[] b, final int nodeX, final int nodeY, final int nodeZ,
                             final double[] parameter, final double dt, final double time,
                             final double[] previousValues) {
        // Purely passive element
    }

    @Override
    public double calculateCurrent(final double nodeVoltageX, final double nodeVoltageY,
                                   final double[] parameter, final double dt,
                                   final double previousCurrent) {
        return (nodeVoltageX - nodeVoltageY) / parameter[0];
    }

    @Override
    public double getAdmittanceWeight(final double parameterValue, final double dt) {
        return 1.0 / parameterValue;
    }
}

Register stampers in StamperRegistry keyed by CircuitTypCore (for example StamperRegistry.createDefault(SolverType.SOLVER_BE)).

docs.title: Writing Stamper Unit Tests
docs.text:
import gecko.core.circuit.matrix.DenseMatrixAccumulator;
import gecko.core.circuit.matrix.ResistorStamper;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;

class CustomResistorStamperTest {
    @Test
    void stampsAdmittanceEntries() {
        ResistorStamper stamper = new ResistorStamper();
        double[][] matrix = new double[3][3];
        DenseMatrixAccumulator acc = new DenseMatrixAccumulator(matrix, 3);

        stamper.stampMatrixA(acc, 0, 1, 2, new double[]{100.0}, 1e-6);

        assertEquals(0.01, matrix[0][0], 1e-12);
        assertEquals(0.01, matrix[1][1], 1e-12);
        assertEquals(-0.01, matrix[0][1], 1e-12);
        assertEquals(-0.01, matrix[1][0], 1e-12);
    }
}

docs.title: Coding Conventions
docs.text:
• Keep backend/gecko-simulation-core strictly free of UI toolkit dependencies (maven-enforcer-plugin enforces this boundary).
  • Add Javadoc comments to public API classes, constructors, and methods; explain non-obvious physics or solver constraints inline.
  • Avoid magic numbers in component models, canvas geometry, and stampers — extract named constants.
  • Follow checkstyle.xml and pmd-ruleset.xml rules for new code in backend/gecko-mcp and backend/gecko-rest-api.

docs.title: Run from Source
docs.text:
For contributors and developers who want to run from source:

git clone https://github.com/MartinRieser/GeckoCIRCUITS.git
cd GeckoCIRCUITS

run-gecko.bat        # Windows
./run-gecko.sh       # Linux / macOS

docs.title: What is GeckoCIRCUITS?
docs.text: GeckoCIRCUITS is an open-source power electronics circuit simulator written in Java 25 with a React/TypeScript schematic editor, Tauri 2 desktop shell, Spring Boot REST API, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. It supports multi-domain simulation across electrical, thermal, magnetic, mechanical, and control domains. Originally developed at ETH Zurich, it is used in education and research.

docs.title: What Java version do I need?
docs.text:
• Desktop Installers: Java 25 is bundled inside the desktop application (jlink runtime) — no separate Java install is required.
  • Running or Building from Source: JDK 25 or later (we recommend Eclipse Temurin).

docs.title: Which operating systems are supported?
docs.text: GeckoCIRCUITS runs natively on Windows, Linux, and macOS via desktop installers or from source (run-gecko.bat, run-gecko.ps1, ./run-gecko.sh).

docs.title: Is it really free?
docs.text: Yes. GeckoCIRCUITS is dual-licensed under GPL v3 (free for open-source and academic use) and a commercial license for proprietary applications.

docs.title: What solver does GeckoCIRCUITS use?
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS uses Modified Nodal Analysis (MNA) with fixed time-step solvers:

  • Backward Euler (BE) — Default, unconditionally stable first-order method
  • Trapezoidal (TRZ) — Second-order accuracy (can exhibit numerical ringing on stiff switching edges)
  • Gear-Shichman (GS) — Variable-order implicit integration for stiff systems

docs.title: How do I choose the right time step?
docs.text:
Rule of thumb: the time step should be at least 100x smaller than the switching period.

Switching Frequency Recommended Time Step 10 kHz < 1 µs 100 kHz < 100 ns 1 MHz < 10 ns

docs.title: Why is my simulation unstable?
docs.text:
Common causes:

  1. Time step too large — Reduce it (see table above)
  2. Algebraic loops — Add a small series resistance or inductance
  3. Ideal switches — Add snubber circuits or non-zero on/off resistance
  4. Stiff system — Try the Backward Euler solver instead of Trapezoidal

docs.title: Can I simulate thermal effects?
docs.text:
Yes. GeckoCIRCUITS supports coupled electro-thermal simulation:

  1. Enable thermal nodes on semiconductor components
  2. Define thermal resistance/capacitance networks (Rth, Cth)
  3. The simulator solves electrical and thermal equations simultaneously

See Thermal Simulation Tutorials.

docs.title: What's the maximum circuit size?
docs.text: There is no hard limit, though practical limits depend on system RAM and time step count. For very long simulations or small time steps, increase the JVM heap (-Xmx) when running gecko-rest-api.jar directly.

docs.title: Can I use GeckoCIRCUITS with MATLAB or Octave?
docs.text:
Yes, via the REST API (http://localhost:8080/gecko/api/v1) using webwrite/webread or HTTP requests. Legacy Java RMI (GeckoRemoteInterface) was retired with the Classic Swing UI.

See the MATLAB Integration Tutorial.

docs.title: Can I use it with Python?
docs.text:
Yes, through:

  • geckopy SDK — Built-in Python wrapper communicating with gecko-mcp.jar over stdio JSON-RPC 2.0
  • REST API — backend/gecko-rest-api HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket endpoints
  • Headless CLI — gecko.core.GeckoHeadless invoked via Spring Boot's PropertiesLauncher

See the Python Integration Tutorial.

docs.title: Can I use it with Simulink?
docs.text: Archival R2010a Simulink S-function files from ETH Zurich remain in resources/tutorials/7xx_scripting_automation/703_simulink_cosimulation/ for historical reference against the retired Classic classic-v1.0-final codebase. For current versions, integrate via MATLAB HTTP calls to the REST API or SCRIPT_BLOCK / NativeC C/C++ blocks inside the circuit.

docs.title: What is an .ipes file?
docs.text: The native GeckoCIRCUITS circuit file format. Modern .ipes files in this repository are plain UTF-8 line-oriented text describing components, coordinates, parameters, and wires; gzip-compressed .ipes / .ipes.gz files are also supported by the parser.

docs.title: Can I import SPICE netlists?
docs.text: Not directly. GeckoCIRCUITS uses its own .ipes format. Rebuild the circuit in the GeckoCIRCUITS editor or synthesize it programmatically via gecko_create_circuit / geckopy.

docs.title: Can I export simulation data?
docs.text:
Yes:

  • Export CSV waveforms directly from the Scope view in the editor
  • Or call POST /gecko/api/v1/simulations/{simulationId}/export from the REST API

docs.title: The application won't start
docs.text: See Troubleshooting for desktop launcher, Java 25, and simulation diagnostics.

docs.text: Open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common issues and solutions when running GeckoCIRCUITS desktop installers, building from source, or debugging simulations.

docs.title: Desktop app fails to start engine
docs.text:
In installed desktop builds, the Tauri shell spawns gecko-rest-api.jar on a bundled JDK 25 runtime and waits up to 90 seconds for GECKO_READY. If startup times out:

  1. Open the engine log directory (Help → Open Engine Logs, or <app log dir>/engine/):
  2. Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\com.geckocircuits.desktop\logs\engine\
  3. macOS: ~/Library/Logs/com.geckocircuits.desktop/engine/
  4. Linux: ~/.local/share/com.geckocircuits.desktop/logs/engine/
  5. Inspect engine.log (shell launcher output) and rest-api.log (Spring Boot server log).
  6. See Desktop Application for OS Gatekeeper/SmartScreen notes and WebView requirements.

docs.title: "Unsupported class file major version 69" when running from source
docs.text: GeckoCIRCUITS compiles targeting Java 25 (bytecode major version 69). Ensure java -version and JAVA_HOME point to JDK 25+ (for example Eclipse Temurin 25).

docs.title: OutOfMemoryError on large or long simulations
docs.text:
When launching the standalone REST API JAR directly with a large channel count or small time step, increase the heap limit:

java -Xmx4G -jar backend/gecko-rest-api/target/gecko-rest-api.jar

docs.title: Simulation runs but produces unexpected results
docs.text: Check Solution Time step too large Reduce dt below 1 / (100 × f_switch) Numerical ringing Switch from Trapezoidal to Backward Euler Missing ground Add a ground terminal (LK_GLOBAL_TERMINAL) to every electrical island Open nodes / floating wires Run DRC validation (gecko_validate_circuit or editor validation)

docs.title: Simulation diverges / NaN values
docs.text:
Usually caused by:

  1. Algebraic loops or ideal voltage-source parallels — Add small series resistance (e.g., 1 mΩ) to ideal voltage sources or small damping elements.
  2. Zero-valued parameters — Check that resistances, inductances, and capacitances are strictly positive where required.
  3. Time step too large for fast switching transitions.

docs.title: Simulation is slow
docs.text:
• Reduce simulation duration (tDURATION) while tuning topology or controller gains.
  • Increase time step (dt) as much as switching accuracy allows.
  • Adjust max plot points / signals recorded when fetching waveforms via MCP/REST.

docs.title: Maven build or test failures
docs.text:
# Clean rebuild and run all backend unit/integration tests
mvn clean verify

Ensure mvn -version shows Java 25 and Maven 3.8+.

docs.title: Frontend lint / type / test checks
docs.text:
npm --prefix frontend ci
npm --prefix frontend run lint
npx --prefix frontend tsc -p frontend/tsconfig.json --noEmit
npm --prefix frontend test

docs.title: Desktop Rust crate checks
docs.text:
On Windows, make sure the MSVC toolchain is installed (rustup toolchain install stable-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc):

cargo fmt --manifest-path desktop/Cargo.toml --all --check
cargo clippy --manifest-path desktop/Cargo.toml --workspace -- -D warnings
cargo test --manifest-path desktop/Cargo.toml -p gecko-engine

docs.title: Can't open an .ipes file
docs.text:
• Check whether the file is valid UTF-8 .ipes text (or a valid gzip-compressed .ipes archive).
  • Inspect structural errors via the REST validation endpoint (GET /gecko/api/v1/circuits/{circuitId}/validate) or geckopy (ckt.validate()).

docs.title: Still Stuck?
docs.text:
1. Check the FAQ
  2. Search existing issues
  3. Open a new issue with your OS, Java version, steps to reproduce, and engine.log / rest-api.log excerpts.

docs.title: 230 V AC (50 Hz) to 3.3 V DC (20 W) Power Supply Guide
docs.text:
A complete, beginner-friendly design and simulation tutorial for building an offline switched-mode power supply in GeckoCIRCUITS.

  • Project File: smps-230v-to-3v3.ipes

docs.title: 1. Design Overview
docs.text: Specification Target Value Notes Input Voltage 230 V RMS AC, 50 Hz European standard mains (\(V_{\text{peak}} \approx 325\text{ V}\)) Output Voltage 3.3 V DC Regulated logic / microcontroller bus Maximum Output Power 20 W \(I_{\text{out}} \approx 6.06\text{ A}\) Load Resistance 0.55 \(\Omega\) Sized for full 20 W load (\(R = V^2 / P\)) Switching Frequency 50 kHz Period \(T_{\text{sw}} = 20\,\mu\text{s}\) Output Ripple \(< 20\text{ mV}_{\text{pp}}\) Well filtered for digital circuitry

docs.title: 2. Block Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid Diagram Source (Click to expand if using the Markdown Preview Mermaid Support extension) 
graph LR
    AC["Mains Input<br/>230 V AC / 50 Hz"] --> XFMR["Step-Down Transformer<br/>(19 : 1 ratio)"]
    XFMR --> RECT["Full-Bridge Rectifier<br/>(4x Diodes)"]
    RECT --> DCLINK["DC-Link Capacitor<br/>(4700 µF → ~15 V DC)"]
    DCLINK --> BUCK["50 kHz Buck Stage<br/>(Switch + Diode + 33 µH)"]
    BUCK --> COUT["Output Filter<br/>(470 µF)"]
    COUT --> LOAD["Load Resistor<br/>(0.55 Ω / 20 W)"]

docs.title: Stage 1: Mains Input & Transformer
docs.text:
• Peak Mains Voltage:

$\(V_{\text{peak}} = 230\,\text{V} \times \sqrt{2} \approx 325.3\,\text{V}\)$

  • Transformer Secondary Voltage: Stepping down from \(230\,\text{V}\) to \(\sim 12\,\text{V}\) AC RMS (\(19 : 1\) turns ratio) yields a secondary peak voltage of:

$\(V_{\text{sec,peak}} \approx 12\,\text{V} \times \sqrt{2} \approx 17.0\,\text{V}\)$

docs.title: Stage 2: Rectifier & Intermediate DC Bus
docs.text:
• Rectifier Voltage Drop: Two diode forward conduction drops (\(\approx 2 \times 0.7\,\text{V} = 1.4\,\text{V}\)).
  • Peak Unloaded DC Voltage:

$\(V_{\text{dc,peak}} = 17.0\,\text{V} - 1.4\,\text{V} \approx 15.6\,\text{V}\)$

  • DC-Link Filter Capacitor (\(C_{\text{bulk}} = 4700\,\mu\text{F}\)): At full 20 W load (\(I_{\text{dc}} \approx 1.5\,\text{A}\) drawn from the intermediate bus), the bulk capacitor must supply current during the \(\sim 8\,\text{ms}\) interval between 100 Hz rectifier peaks:

$\(\Delta V_{\text{ripple}} = \frac{I_{\text{dc}} \cdot \Delta t}{C_{\text{bulk}}} = \frac{1.5\,\text{A} \times 0.008\,\text{s}}{4700 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{F}} \approx 2.5\,\text{V}\)$

This keeps the DC bus stiff between \(13.0\,\text{V}\) and \(15.6\,\text{V}\) (average \(\approx 14.3\,\text{V}\) to \(15.0\,\text{V}\)), preventing output sag. (A smaller \(1000\,\mu\text{F}\) capacitor discharges by \(>12\,\text{V}\), causing the bus and output to collapse to near 0 V at 100 Hz).

docs.title: Stage 3: High-Frequency Buck Converter (\(50\,\text{kHz}\))
docs.text:
• Duty Cycle (\(D\)):

$\(D = \frac{V_{\text{out}}}{V_{\text{in}}} = \frac{3.3\,\text{V}}{15.0\,\text{V}} = \mathbf{0.22}\quad (22\%)\)$

  • Switching Period (\(T_{\text{sw}}\)):

$\(T_{\text{sw}} = \frac{1}{50\,\text{kHz}} = 20\,\mu\text{s}\)$

  • Inductor Selection (\(L_1 = 33\,\mu\text{H}\)): Targeting an inductor ripple current \(\Delta I_L \approx 30\%\) of full load (\(1.8\,\text{A}\)):

$\(L = \frac{V_{\text{out}} \cdot (1 - D)}{\Delta I_L \cdot f_{\text{sw}}} = \frac{3.3\,\text{V} \cdot (1 - 0.22)}{1.8\,\text{A} \cdot 50\,000\,\text{Hz}} = \frac{2.574}{90\,000} \approx \mathbf{28.6\,\mu\text{H}} \quad \longrightarrow \text{Select } \mathbf{33\,\mu\text{H}}\)$

  • Output Capacitor Selection (\(C_1 = 470\,\mu\text{F}\)): For an ultra-clean output ripple \(\Delta V_{\text{out}} \le 20\,\text{mV}\):

$\(C = \frac{\Delta I_L}{8 \cdot f_{\text{sw}} \cdot \Delta V_{\text{out}}} = \frac{1.8\,\text{A}}{8 \cdot 50\,000\,\text{Hz} \cdot 0.02\,\text{V}} = \mathbf{225\,\mu\text{F}} \quad \longrightarrow \text{Select } \mathbf{470\,\mu\text{F}}\)$

docs.title: Stage 4: Load Resistor Sizing
docs.text:
• Full Load Resistance (\(R_{\text{load}}\)):

$\(I_{\text{out}} = \frac{20\,\text{W}}{3.3\,\text{V}} = 6.06\,\text{A} \implies R_{\text{load}} = \frac{3.3\,\text{V}}{6.06\,\text{A}} = \mathbf{0.545\,\Omega} \approx \mathbf{0.55\,\Omega}\)$

docs.title: Step 1: Mains & Transformer
docs.text:
1. Place the AC Voltage Source V_in vertically on the left.
  2. Place the Transformer TRANS.1 directly to the right. Wire V_in terminals to the transformer primary input pins.

docs.title: Step 2: Bridge Rectifier & DC-Link
docs.text:
1. Place 4 diodes arranged as a standard bridge:
  2. Two top diodes (D1, D2) pointing towards the top positive DC rail.
  3. Two bottom diodes (D3, D4) pointing away from the bottom negative rail.
  4. Connect transformer secondary pins to the bridge AC nodes.
  5. Place C_bulk vertically between the positive rail and the ground rail.

docs.title: Step 3: Buck Converter Power Train
docs.text:
1. Place S_1 horizontally on the top positive rail.
  2. Place D_fw vertically: anode to ground, cathode to the switch node between S_1 and L_1.
  3. Place L_1 horizontally immediately after S_1.
  4. Place C_1 vertically after L_1 to ground.
  5. Place R_load vertically after C_1 to ground.

docs.title: Step 4: PWM Control & Scope Probing
docs.text:
1. Place PWM_GEN and GATE.1 in the control region below.
  2. Wire PWM_GEN output pin to GATE.1 input pin.
  3. Open GATE.1 properties: assign its coupled switch to S_1.
  4. Place SCOPE.1:
  5. Wire Channel 1 to the top of R_load (label net as V_out).
  6. Insert an ammeter probe or connect Channel 2 to monitor I_L.

docs.text: Click the Gear icon (⚙) or Simulation ▾ in the top bar: * Duration: 0.05 s (50 ms, corresponding to 2.5 full 50 Hz line cycles). * Time Step (\(\Delta t\)): 1e-6 s (\(1\,\mu\text{s}\)).

1. Output Voltage (\(V_{\text{out}}\)):

  3. Inductor Current (\(I_L\)):

docs.title: 301 - Diode Rectifier
docs.text: Single-phase and three-phase diode bridge rectifiers for AC-DC conversion.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Diode rectifiers are the simplest form of AC-DC power conversion, using uncontrolled diodes to convert AC voltage to pulsating DC.

docs.title: Topics Covered
docs.text:
• Single-phase half-wave rectifier
  • Single-phase full-wave bridge
  • Three-phase diode bridge
  • Ripple calculation and filtering
  • Power factor considerations

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
Average DC Voltage:

\[ V_{DC} = \frac{2V_m}{\pi} \approx 0.637 \cdot V_m \]

RMS Voltage:

\[ V_{rms} = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}} \]

Ripple Factor:

\[ \gamma = \sqrt{\left(\frac{V_{rms}}{V_{DC}}\right)^2 - 1} \approx 0.483 \]

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
Average DC Voltage:

\[ V_{DC} = \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{\pi} V_{LL} \approx 1.35 \cdot V_{LL} \]

Ripple Frequency: \(6 \times \text{line frequency}\) (300 Hz for 50 Hz input)

docs.title: Simulation & Project Files
docs.text:
Pre-built and validated simulation project files are included directly in this tutorial directory:

  • Single-Phase Model: single-phase-rectifier.ipes
  • Three-Phase Model: three-phase-rectifier.ipes

docs.text: Setting Single-Phase Model Three-Phase Model Project File single-phase-rectifier.ipes three-phase-rectifier.ipes Input Source 230 V RMS / 50 Hz (\(V_m = 325.3\text{ V}\)) 400 V L-L RMS (\(V_{\text{ph,peak}} = 326.6\text{ V}\)) Diodes 4× D1..D4 (\(V_F = 0.7\text{ V}\)) 6× D1..D6 (\(V_F = 0.7\text{ V}\)) Output Filter \(C_1 = 1000\,\mu\text{F}\) \(C_1 = 470\,\mu\text{F}\) Load Resistance \(R_1 = 100\,\Omega\) \(R_1 = 50\,\Omega\) Simulation Step \(\Delta t\) \(10\,\mu\text{s}\) \(10\,\mu\text{s}\) Total Duration \(60\,\text{ms}\) (3 cycles) \(40\,\text{ms}\) (2 cycles) Monitored Signals v_ac, v_dc, i_load v_phase_a, v_dc, i_load

docs.title: How to Run in GeckoCIRCUITS
docs.text:
1. Open GeckoCIRCUITS desktop or launch via MCP.
  2. Load single-phase-rectifier.ipes or three-phase-rectifier.ipes.
  3. Press F5 (Run Simulation).
  4. Double-click the on-screen Scope block to inspect waveforms:
  5. In the single-phase circuit, observe the \(100\text{ Hz}\) DC voltage ripple charging to peak \(\approx 323.9\text{ V}\) (\(325.3\text{ V} - 2 \times 0.7\text{ V}\)).
  6. In the three-phase circuit, observe the significantly reduced ripple at \(6 \times 50\text{ Hz} = 300\text{ Hz}\) with average DC voltage around \(535\text{ V}\).

docs.title: 302 - PFC Basics
docs.text: Power Factor Correction fundamentals using boost converter topology.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: PFC circuits shape the input current to be sinusoidal and in phase with the voltage, achieving near-unity power factor and reducing harmonic distortion.

docs.title: Why PFC?
docs.text: Without PFC, rectifiers draw peaky current that: - Causes harmonic pollution on the grid - Reduces effective power delivery - Fails regulatory standards (IEC 61000-3-2)

docs.title: Operating Principle
docs.text:
1. Switch ON: Inductor charges, current rises
  2. Switch OFF: Inductor discharges through diode to output
  3. Current Shaping: PWM duty cycle modulated to make current follow voltage

docs.title: Average Current Mode Control
docs.text:
• Current loop tracks reference derived from voltage
  • Excellent current waveform
  • Complex implementation

docs.title: Critical Conduction Mode (CRM)
docs.text:
• Variable frequency operation
  • Zero-current switching
  • Simpler implementation
  • Higher peak currents

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
Duty Cycle (CCM):

\[ D = 1 - \frac{V_{in}(t)}{V_{out}} \]

Inductor Current Ripple:

\[ \Delta I_L = \frac{V_{in} \cdot D}{L \cdot f_{sw}} \]

Power Factor:

\[ PF = \frac{P}{S} = \frac{V_{rms} \cdot I_{rms} \cdot \cos\phi}{V_{rms} \cdot I_{rms}} \]

docs.title: Design Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Typical Value Notes Output Voltage 385-400V DC Above peak AC Switching Freq 65-130 kHz EMI tradeoffs Inductor 200-500µH Ripple control Output Cap 200-400µF Holdup time

docs.title: Interleaved PFC Architecture & Digital Control
docs.text:
This circuit incorporates advanced power electronics features:

  1. Two-Phase Interleaving (\(180^\circ\) Phase Shift):
  2. Two parallel boost stages (\(L_1 = 200\,\mu\text{H}\), \(L_2 = 200\,\mu\text{H}\)) switch at \(f_{sw} = 70\,\text{kHz}\).

  3. Gate signals gate1 and gate2 are interleaved by half a switching period (\(T_{sw}/2 \approx 7.14\,\mu\text{s}\)), which cancels high-frequency inductor current ripple at the input rectifier and output capacitor.

  4. Embedded Microcontroller Script PI Controller (CTRL_SCRIPT_PFC):

  5. Implements digital discrete-time PI feedback: 
    // Voltage loop error
error = V_ref - uOUT;
integrator += Ki * error * dt;
// Anti-windup clamping
if (integrator > 0.90) integrator = 0.90;
if (integrator < 0.05) integrator = 0.05;
duty = Kp * error + integrator;

  6. Sets duty cycle dynamically to regulate the output bus at precisely \(400\text{ V DC}\).

  7. Dynamic Load Step Verification:

  8. A secondary load switch (S_LOAD) switches on at \(t = 30\,\text{ms}\).
  9. Tests closed-loop transient recovery, showing the PI controller correcting for load droop within a few line cycles.

  5. Output voltage dip and rapid PI controller recovery when the load step triggers at \(t = 30\,\text{ms}\).

docs.title: 303 - Vienna Rectifier
docs.text: Three-level unidirectional PFC rectifier with excellent input current quality.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Vienna rectifier is a three-level, three-phase PFC topology offering: - High power factor (>0.99) - Low THD (<5%) - Reduced voltage stress on switches - Unidirectional power flow

docs.title: Circuit Configuration
docs.text: Three-phase input with bidirectional switches connected to DC bus midpoint:

docs.title: Switching States
docs.text: Input Current Upper Diodes Switch Lower Diodes Output Positive Conducting OFF Blocked +Vdc/2 Positive Blocked ON Blocked Neutral Negative Blocked ON Blocked Neutral Negative Blocked OFF Conducting -Vdc/2

docs.title: Three-Level Operation
docs.text:
• Voltage stress = Vdc/2 (not full Vdc)
  • Reduced dv/dt stress
  • Lower EMI emissions

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
DC Bus Voltage:

\[ V_{dc} = \sqrt{2} \cdot V_{LL} \cdot \frac{\pi}{3} \approx 1.1 \cdot V_{LL,rms} \]

Typical for 400V input: \(V_{dc} \approx 700\text{V}\)

docs.title: Design Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Value Notes Input Voltage 400V L-L Three-phase DC Bus 700V (±350V) Split capacitor Power 10-100 kW High power applications Switching Freq 20-50 kHz Lower than boost PFC Input Inductors 100-500µH Per phase

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Lower switch voltage stress (Vdc/2)
  • Excellent input current quality
  • Three-level output reduces filter requirements
  • No shoot-through risk (unidirectional switches)

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Unidirectional power flow only
  • More complex than 2-level boost PFC
  • Requires neutral point balancing

docs.text:
A complete, authentic 3-phase Vienna Rectifier simulation model is included directly in this directory:

  • Project File: vienna-rectifier.ipes

docs.title: Circuit Configuration & Operating Principles
docs.text:
1. Three-Phase Boost Stage:
  2. \(400\text{ V}\) line-to-line RMS (\(50\text{ Hz}\)) input through 3 phase inductors (\(L_a = L_b = L_c = 500\,\mu\text{H}\)).

  3. 3 bidirectional phase switches connect each phase leg directly to the split DC capacitor midpoint \(N_{mid}\).

  4. Split DC Bus with Neutral Clamping:

  5. Total bus voltage: \(700\text{ V DC}\) split across two matched capacitors \(C_1 = C_2 = 1000\,\mu\text{F}\) (\(\pm 350\text{ V}\) with respect to \(N_{mid}\)).

  6. Because each semiconductor switch only blocks half the DC bus voltage (\(350\text{ V}\) instead of \(700\text{ V}\)), faster, lower-loss 650 V GaN or SiC MOSFETs can be used.

  7. Input Current Shaping:

  8. The bidirectional switches clamp each phase inductor to neutral during part of the cycle, creating 3 voltage levels (\(-350\text{ V}, 0\text{ V}, +350\text{ V}\)) relative to neutral.
  9. This achieves near-unity power factor (\(> 0.99\)) with input current THD \(< 4\%\).

docs.title: 404 - Modular Multilevel Converter
docs.text: Scalable multilevel topology for HVDC and FACTS applications.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Modular Multilevel Converter (MMC) is the state-of-the-art topology for: - HVDC transmission (±320kV to ±525kV) - STATCOM systems - High-power motor drives - Battery energy storage systems (BESS)

docs.title: Submodule Types
docs.text:
• Half-Bridge SM (HBSM): Output is \(0\) or \(+V_c\) (Unipolar capability, lowest conduction losses).
  • Full-Bridge SM (FBSM): Output is \(-V_c, 0,\) or \(+V_c\) (Bipolar capability, DC short-circuit fault-blocking capability).

docs.title: Voltage Synthesis
docs.text:
• N submodules per arm
  • Insert/bypass SMs to create voltage steps
  • Output voltage = Vdc/2 - (inserted SMs × Vc)

docs.title: Current Path
docs.text:
• Upper + Lower arm currents combine at output
  • Circulating current flows within converter
  • Arm inductors limit circulating current

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
Submodule Voltage:

\[ V_{SM} = \frac{V_{dc}}{N} \]

Number of Levels:

\[ N_{levels} = N + 1 \quad \text{(per arm)} \]

Arm Current:

\[ i_{arm} = \frac{i_{dc}}{3} + \frac{i_{ac}}{2} + i_{circ} \]

Energy Storage:

\[ E_{stored} = 6 \cdot N \cdot \frac{1}{2}CV_{SM}^2 \]

docs.title: Hierarchical Control
docs.text:
1. System Level
  2. Active/reactive power control

  3. DC voltage control

  4. Converter Level

  5. Circulating current control

  6. Capacitor voltage balancing (average)

  7. Arm Level

  8. Individual SM capacitor balancing
  9. Sorting algorithm (NLM or PWM)

docs.title: Modulation Methods
docs.text:
Nearest Level Modulation (NLM): - Round reference to nearest level - Very low switching frequency - Used in HVDC

Phase-Shifted Carrier PWM: - Higher effective switching frequency - Better harmonic performance - Used in motor drives

docs.title: Design Parameters
docs.text: Parameter HVDC Motor Drive DC Voltage ±320-525kV 3-35kV Submodules/Arm 200-400 10-40 SM Capacitance 8-15mF 2-5mF Arm Inductance 50-100mH 1-10mH SM Type Half-bridge Full-bridge

  • Project File: mmc-converter.ipes

docs.title: MMC Phase Leg Architecture & Operation
docs.text:
1. High-Voltage DC Link (\(\pm 5\text{ kV}\) DC):

  2. Positive DC pole at \(+5.0\text{ kV}\) DC, negative DC pole at \(-5.0\text{ kV}\) DC (\(10.0\text{ kV}\) total DC bus), centered around neutral ground reference 0.

  3. Upper & Lower Half-Bridge Submodules (HBSM):

  4. Upper Arm:
    • Submodule switches S_u1 and S_u2 with energy storage capacitor \(C_{u} = 2000\,\mu\text{F}\).
    • Upper arm buffer inductor \(L_{arm,u} = 10.0\,\text{mH}\) connecting from upper arm node arm_up to AC output terminal ac_node.

  5. Lower Arm:

    • Submodule switches S_l1 and S_l2 with energy storage capacitor \(C_{l} = 2000\,\mu\text{F}\).
    • Lower arm buffer inductor \(L_{arm,l} = 10.0\,\text{mH}\) connecting from AC output terminal ac_node to lower arm node arm_lo.

  6. Submodule Insertion & Bypass States:

  7. Inserted State (\(v_{SM} = +V_c\)): S1=ON, S2=OFF. The capacitor is inserted into the arm path. Arm current flows through the capacitor, charging or discharging it depending on current polarity.

  8. Bypassed State (\(v_{SM} = 0\)): S1=OFF, S2=ON. Current flows entirely through S2, bypassing the capacitor and holding its stored voltage constant.

  9. Arm Inductor Function:

  10. Limits inter-arm circulating currents caused by instantaneous voltage mismatches between upper and lower inserted submodules.
  11. Decouples the DC bus from the synthesized AC grid terminal ac_node.

docs.title: 403 - NPC Multilevel Inverter
docs.text: Neutral-Point-Clamped three-level inverter topology.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The NPC inverter produces three voltage levels per phase, offering: - Reduced harmonic distortion - Lower dv/dt stress - Smaller output filters - Higher efficiency at medium voltage

docs.title: Switching States
docs.text: State S1 S2 S3 S4 Output P ON ON OFF OFF +Vdc/2 O OFF ON ON OFF 0 N OFF OFF ON ON -Vdc/2

docs.title: Voltage Stress
docs.text:
• Each switch blocks only Vdc/2
  • Enables use of lower voltage devices
  • Higher reliability

docs.title: Output Quality
docs.text:
• 3-level output waveform
  • Lower dv/dt (smaller steps)
  • Reduced EMI emissions
  • Smaller output filter

docs.title: The Challenge
docs.text:
• Capacitor voltage imbalance causes distortion
  • Imbalance occurs with non-unity power factor
  • Requires active control strategy

docs.title: Balancing Methods
docs.text:
1. Carrier-based PWM with offset
  2. Add zero-sequence component

  3. Simple implementation

  4. Space Vector PWM

  5. Select redundant vectors strategically

  6. Better utilization

  7. Direct voltage control

  8. Measure capacitor voltages
  9. Adjust modulation in real-time

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
Output Voltage Levels:

\[ V_{out} \in \{-V_{dc}/2, 0, +V_{dc}/2\} \]

Modulation Index:

\[ m_a = \frac{V_{ref,peak}}{V_{dc}/2} \]

Switching Frequency per Device: - Lower than 2-level (each switch operates part of cycle) - Reduces switching losses

docs.title: Design Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Typical Value DC Bus 600-1200V Split Capacitors 2× matched Clamping Diodes Fast recovery Switching Freq 2-10 kHz

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• Medium voltage drives (2.3-6.6 kV)
  • Grid-tied inverters (MW scale)
  • HVDC converters
  • Railway traction

docs.text:
A complete, simulated and verified 3-Level Neutral-Point-Clamped (NPC) Inverter project file is provided directly in this directory:

  • Project File: npc-inverter.ipes

docs.title: NPC Phase Leg Architecture & Commutation
docs.text:
1. Split DC Bus (\(800\text{ V DC}\)):
  2. Formed by two matched capacitors \(C_1 = C_2 = 1000\,\mu\text{F}\) with the midpoint tied to reference ground 0.

  3. Positive DC rail at \(+400\text{ V}\), negative DC rail at \(-400\text{ V}\).

  4. Four Series Switches & Neutral Clamping Diodes:

  5. S1 connected between \(+400\text{ V}\) and node n1.
  6. S2 connected between node n1 and switch output sw_out.
  7. S3 connected between switch output sw_out and node n2.
  8. S4 connected between node n2 and \(-400\text{ V}\).
  9. Clamping diode D_clamp1 connects neutral ground to n1.

  10. Clamping diode D_clamp2 connects n2 to neutral ground.

  11. Commutation States:

  12. State P (\(+400\text{ V}\)): S1=ON, S2=ON. Terminal connects to \(+400\text{ V}\). Diodes reverse biased.
  13. State O (\(0\text{ V}\)): S2=ON, S3=ON. Terminal clamps to neutral: if load current is positive, it circulates through S3 and D_clamp2; if negative, through S2 and D_clamp1.
  14. State N (\(-400\text{ V}\)): S3=ON, S4=ON. Terminal connects to \(-400\text{ V}\).

  15. Crucially, no switch ever experiences more than \(V_{dc}/2 = 400\text{ V}\) across its terminals.

  16. Output Filter & Load:

  17. Filter inductor \(L_1 = 2.0\,\text{mH}\) and capacitor \(C_{filt} = 10.0\,\mu\text{F}\).
  18. Output load \(R = 20\,\Omega\).

  6. Balanced split capacitor voltages (v_c1 and v_c2) holding steady at \(400\text{ V}\).

docs.title: 401 - Single-Phase Inverter
docs.text: PWM inverter fundamentals for DC-AC conversion.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Single-phase inverters convert DC to AC using PWM switching strategies, essential for: - UPS systems - Solar inverters (residential) - Motor drives (single-phase) - AC power supplies

docs.title: Half-Bridge Inverter
docs.text: Output: \(\pm V_{dc}/2\)

docs.title: Full-Bridge (H-Bridge) Inverter
docs.text: Output: \(\pm V_{dc}\)

docs.title: Bipolar PWM
docs.text:
• Compare sine reference to triangle carrier
  • S1-S4 switch together, S2-S3 switch together
  • Output levels: \(+V_{dc}, -V_{dc}\)

docs.title: Unipolar PWM
docs.text:
• Two reference signals (positive and negative)
  • Each leg switched independently
  • Output levels: \(+V_{dc}, 0, -V_{dc}\)
  • Lower harmonic content, reduced filter size

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
Modulation Index:

\[ m_a = \frac{V_{ref,peak}}{V_{carrier,peak}} \]

Fundamental Output Voltage (linear region):

\[ V_{out,1} = m_a \cdot V_{dc} \quad \text{(full-bridge)} \]

THD Calculation:

\[ THD = \frac{\sqrt{V_2^2 + V_3^2 + \dots + V_n^2}}{V_1} \]

docs.title: Design Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Typical Value DC Bus 400V (from PFC) Switching Freq 10-50 kHz Output Filter L 1-5 mH Output Filter C 2-10 µF Modulation Index 0.8-0.95

docs.title: Simulation & Project File
docs.text:
A complete, simulated and verified Single-Phase H-Bridge Inverter project file is provided directly in this directory:

  • Project File: single-phase-inverter.ipes

docs.title: Power Stage & Modulation Specifications
docs.text:
1. H-Bridge Switching Matrix:
  2. 4 switches (S1, S2, S3, S4) driven by complementary gate signals.
  3. S1 and S4 conduct together for positive phase output \(+V_{dc}\); S2 and S3 conduct together for negative phase output \(-V_{dc}\).

  4. \(V_{dc} = 400.0\text{ V DC}\) standard industrial DC bus.

  5. LC Low-Pass Filter Design:

  6. Filter inductor \(L_1 = 2.0\,\text{mH}\) and filter capacitor \(C_1 = 10.0\,\mu\text{F}\).
  7. Resonant cutoff frequency: $\(f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{L_1 C_1}} = \frac{1}{2\pi \sqrt{2.0\times 10^{-3} \times 10.0\times 10^{-6}}} \approx 1.125\,\text{kHz}\)$

  8. Attenuates the \(20\,\text{kHz}\) switching ripple by \(> 40\,\text{dB}\) while preserving the \(50\,\text{Hz}\) fundamental sine wave.

  9. Output & Load:

  10. Pure resistive load \(R_1 = 20\,\Omega\).
  11. Output voltage: \(230\text{ V RMS}\) at \(50\text{ Hz}\) (\(V_{\text{peak}} \approx 325\text{ V}\)).
  12. Output current: \(\approx 11.5\text{ A RMS}\) (\(16.3\text{ A peak}\)).

docs.text:
1. Open single-phase-inverter.ipes in GeckoCIRCUITS.
  2. Press F5 to start simulation.

  4. Clean sinusoidal AC output voltage (v_ac) centered at 0 V with peak amplitude \(\approx 325\text{ V}\).

docs.text: Three-phase voltage source inverter (VSI) for motor drives and grid-tied applications.

docs.text: State S1 S3 S5 Vector V0 0 0 0 Zero V1 1 0 0 Active V2 1 1 0 Active V3 0 1 0 Active V4 0 1 1 Active V5 0 0 1 Active V6 1 0 1 Active V7 1 1 1 Zero

docs.title: SVPWM Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Calculate reference vector in \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) frame
  2. Identify sector (1-6)
  3. Calculate dwell times for adjacent vectors
  4. Generate switching sequence

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
DC Bus Utilization:

  • Sine PWM:
\[ V_{LL,max} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} V_{dc} \approx 0.866 \cdot V_{dc} \]
  • SVPWM:
\[ V_{LL,max} = \frac{V_{dc}}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 1.15 \cdot V_{LL,max(\text{SPWM})} \]

15% more DC bus utilization with SVPWM

Clarke Transform:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} v_\alpha \\ v_\beta \end{bmatrix} = \frac{2}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_a \\ v_b \\ v_c \end{bmatrix} \]

docs.title: Power Stage & Modulation Architecture
docs.text:
1. Two-Level 6-Switch Bridge:
  2. 3 phase legs with complementary switch pairs:
    • Phase A: Upper S1, Lower S4
    • Phase B: Upper S3, Lower S6
    • Phase C: Upper S5, Lower S2

  3. \(700.0\text{ V DC}\) DC bus voltage (typical for grid-tied inverters and industrial 400 V motor drives).

  4. Sinusoidal Pulse-Width Modulation (SPWM):

  5. Three reference sinusoids shifted by \(120^\circ\) (\(0^\circ, -120^\circ, +120^\circ\)) at fundamental frequency \(f_0 = 50\text{ Hz}\).

  6. Modulated against a \(10\text{ kHz}\) high-frequency triangular carrier.

  7. Output LC Filter & Star Load:

  8. 3-phase inductors \(L_a = L_b = L_c = 2.0\,\text{mH}\).
  9. 3-phase filter capacitors \(C_a = C_b = C_c = 10.0\,\mu\text{F}\).
  10. Balanced star-connected resistive load \(R_a = R_b = R_c = 15.0\,\Omega\) connected to virtual neutral star point star_n.
  11. Attenuates 10 kHz switching harmonics while delivering clean 3-phase sinusoidal currents.

docs.title: Tutorial: Boost Converter
docs.text:
Design and simulate a boost (step-up) DC-DC converter.

Difficulty: Beginner (⅓) | Duration: 30 minutes

Circuit file: resources/tutorials/2xx_dcdc_converters/202_boost_converter/boost_simple.ipes

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand boost converter operation
  • Calculate output voltage and component values
  • Simulate and verify the design
  • Analyze voltage and current waveforms

docs.title: Topology
docs.text: The boost converter steps up DC voltage:

docs.title: Operating Principle
docs.text:
Switch ON (0 < t < D·T): Inductor charges from V_in, diode is reverse-biased, capacitor supplies load.

\[V_L = V_{in}, \quad \frac{di_L}{dt} = \frac{V_{in}}{L}\]

Switch OFF (D·T < t < T): Inductor discharges through diode to load and capacitor.

\[V_L = V_{in} - V_{out}, \quad \frac{di_L}{dt} = \frac{V_{in} - V_{out}}{L}\]

docs.title: Key Equations
docs.text:
Voltage conversion ratio (CCM):

\[\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{1}{1-D}\]

Minimum inductance for CCM:

\[L_{min} = \frac{D(1-D)^2 R}{2f_{sw}}\]

Output voltage ripple:

\[\frac{\Delta V_{out}}{V_{out}} = \frac{D}{R C f_{sw}}\]

Inductor current ripple:

\[\Delta i_L = \frac{V_{in} \cdot D}{L \cdot f_{sw}}\]

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Input voltage 12 V Output voltage 24 V Output power 24 W Switching frequency 100 kHz Max voltage ripple 1%

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Duty cycle:

\[D = 1 - \frac{V_{in}}{V_{out}} = 1 - \frac{12}{24} = 0.5\]

Load resistance:

\[R = \frac{V_{out}^2}{P_{out}} = \frac{24^2}{24} = 24\ \Omega\]

Minimum inductance:

\[L_{min} = \frac{0.5 \times 0.5^2 \times 24}{2 \times 100k} = 15\ \mu H\]

Choose L = 100 uH (well above minimum for low ripple).

Output capacitor:

\[C = \frac{D}{R \times \frac{\Delta V}{V} \times f_{sw}} = \frac{0.5}{24 \times 0.01 \times 100k} = 20.8\ \mu F\]

Choose C = 47 uF.

docs.text:
1. Open boost-converter.ipes in GeckoCIRCUITS desktop or simulate via MCP gecko_simulate.
  2. Press F5 to run the simulation.
  3. Open the Scope window to inspect:
  4. Output voltage smoothly rising and stabilizing at \(24.0\text{ V DC}\).
  5. Inductor current continuously flowing in CCM with average value \(4.8\text{ A}\).
  6. Diode current pulsating during the OFF time \((1-D)T_s\) to deliver power to the load.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Duty Cycle Variation
docs.text: Change D from 0.3 to 0.7 in steps of 0.1. Plot \(V_{out}\) vs \(D\) and verify: $\(V_{out} = \frac{V_{in}}{1 - D}\)$

docs.title: Exercise 2: CCM/DCM Boundary
docs.text: Reduce the load power (increase \(R\) to \(100\,\Omega\)) until the inductor current touches zero. Observe the transition to discontinuous conduction mode.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Component Sizing
docs.text: Change \(L_1\) to \(50\,\mu\text{H}\). Observe increased current ripple \(\Delta I_L = 2.4\text{ A}\) and higher capacitor voltage ripple.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
Boost Converter Limitations

  • Output is always higher than input (\(V_{out} > V_{in}\))
  • As \(D\) approaches 1, practical duty cycle is limited by diode and inductor series resistances
  • The boost converter has a Right-Half-Plane (RHP) zero at \(\omega_z = \frac{R(1-D)^2}{L}\), limiting the control bandwidth in closed-loop designs
  • Continuous input current makes boost topologies ideal for PFC and solar MPPT applications

\[V_{out} = -\frac{D}{1-D} \times V_{in}\] D V_out/V_in Mode 0.25 -0.33 Step-down 0.50 -1.00 Unity 0.75 -3.00 Step-up

docs.title: Topology
docs.text: The SEPIC (Single-Ended Primary-Inductor Converter) provides non-inverted output:

docs.title: Voltage Ratio
docs.text:
Same as buck-boost magnitude, but non-inverted:

\[ V_{out} = \frac{D}{1-D} \times V_{in} \]

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Non-inverted output
  • Continuous input current (good for battery/solar)
  • Can step up or step down

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Two inductors and coupling capacitor
  • Higher component count than buck-boost
  • Pulsating output current

docs.title: Voltage Ratio
docs.text: \[ V_{out} = -\frac{D}{1-D} \times V_{in} \]

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Continuous input AND output current
  • Low ripple at both ports
  • Can couple L1 and L2 on same core

docs.title: Coupling Capacitor (SEPIC/Cuk)
docs.text:
\[ C_{coupling} = \frac{I_{out}}{f_{sw} \times \Delta V_C} \]

Typically 1-10 uF ceramic. Must handle RMS ripple current.

docs.title: Inductors
docs.text: \[ L_1 \geq \frac{V_{in} \times D}{f_{sw} \times \Delta i_{L1}} \] \[ L_2 \geq \frac{V_{out} \times (1-D)}{f_{sw} \times \Delta i_{L2}} \]

docs.title: Tutorial 201: Buck Converter
docs.text: The buck converter is the fundamental step-down DC-DC topology, efficiently converting a higher voltage to a lower voltage using PWM control.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Difficulty  Intermediate Duration 30-40 minutes Prerequisites PWM Basics

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will:

  • Understand buck converter operation in CCM and DCM
  • Apply the volt-second balance principle
  • Calculate output voltage, inductor current ripple, and capacitor voltage ripple
  • Design a buck converter for given specifications

docs.title: Circuit Topology
docs.text:
Components:

  • S - High-side switch (MOSFET/IGBT)
  • D - Freewheeling diode (Schottky recommended)
  • L - Output inductor
  • C - Output capacitor
  • R - Load resistance

docs.title: Operating Principle
docs.text:
Switch ONSwitch OFF
  • Current path: \(V_{in} \to S \to L \to C/R \to \text{GND}\)
  • Inductor voltage: \(V_L = V_{in} - V_{out}\) (positive)
  • Current increases: \(\frac{di_L}{dt} = \frac{V_{in} - V_{out}}{L}\)
  • Current path: \(L \to C/R \to \text{GND} \to D \to L\)
  • Inductor voltage: \(V_L = -V_{out}\) (negative)
  • Current decreases: \(\frac{di_L}{dt} = \frac{-V_{out}}{L}\)

docs.title: Output Voltage (Volt-Second Balance)
docs.text:
In steady state, the average inductor voltage is zero:

\[ V_{out} = D \times V_{in} \]

Key Insight

Output voltage is directly proportional to duty cycle!

docs.title: Inductor Current Ripple
docs.text: \[ \Delta I_L = \frac{V_{out} \times (1 - D)}{f_s \times L} \]

docs.title: Output Voltage Ripple
docs.text: \[ \Delta V_{out} = \frac{\Delta I_L}{8 \times f_s \times C} \]

docs.title: Critical Inductance (CCM Boundary)
docs.text: \[ L_{crit} = \frac{V_{in} \times (1-D) \times D}{2 \times f_s \times I_{out,min}} \]

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Unit Input Voltage 48 V Output Voltage 12 V Output Current 5 A Switching Frequency 100 kHz Max Voltage Ripple 1% Max Current Ripple 30%

docs.title: Step-by-Step Design
docs.text:
1. Calculate Duty Cycle:

\[ D = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{12}{48} = 0.25 \]

2. Calculate Load Resistance:

\[ R = \frac{V_{out}}{I_{out}} = \frac{12}{5} = 2.4\,\Omega \]

3. Calculate Inductance (for 30% ripple):

\[ \Delta I_L = 0.3 \times 5 = 1.5\,\text{A} \] \[ L = \frac{V_{out} \times (1-D)}{f_s \times \Delta I_L} = \frac{12 \times 0.75}{100k \times 1.5} = 60\,\mu\text{H} \]

4. Calculate Capacitance (for 1% ripple):

\[ C = \frac{\Delta I_L}{8 \times f_s \times \Delta V_{out}} = \frac{1.5}{8 \times 100k \times 0.12} = 15.6\,\mu\text{F} \]

docs.title: Building the Circuit
docs.text:
1. Add voltage source (Vin = 48V)
  2. Add switch with PWM gate signal (D = 0.25, fs = 100kHz)
  3. Add freewheeling diode
  4. Add inductor (L = 68µH)
  5. Add capacitor (C = 22µF)
  6. Add load resistor (R = 2.4Ω)
  7. Connect SCOPE to measure Vout and IL

docs.title: Tutorial: Flyback Converter
docs.text:
Design and simulate an isolated flyback converter.

Difficulty: Intermediate (⅔) | Duration: 30 minutes

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand flyback operation and energy transfer
  • Design the coupled inductor (flyback transformer)
  • Handle leakage inductance and voltage spikes
  • Simulate transient and steady-state behavior

docs.title: Topology
docs.text: The flyback is an isolated version of the buck-boost converter:

docs.title: Operating Principle
docs.text:
Switch ON: Energy stores in magnetizing inductance Lm. Secondary diode is reverse-biased.

\[V_{Lm} = V_{in}, \quad \Delta i_{Lm} = \frac{V_{in} \cdot D}{L_m \cdot f_{sw}}\]

Switch OFF: Stored energy transfers to secondary through the coupled inductor. Diode conducts.

\[V_{Lm} = -\frac{V_{out}}{n}, \quad n = \frac{N_s}{N_p}\]

docs.title: Voltage Conversion
docs.text:
\[V_{out} = n \cdot \frac{D}{1-D} \cdot V_{in}\]

Where n = Ns/Np is the turns ratio.

docs.title: Key Design Equations
docs.text:
Magnetizing inductance:

\[L_m = \frac{V_{in}^2 \cdot D^2}{2 \cdot P_{out} \cdot f_{sw}}\]

Turns ratio:

\[n = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} \cdot \frac{1-D}{D}\]

Switch voltage stress:

\[V_{DS,max} = V_{in} + \frac{V_{out}}{n} + V_{spike}\]

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Input voltage 48V DC Output voltage 5V DC Output power 25W Switching frequency 100 kHz Max duty cycle 0.45

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Turns ratio:

\[n = \frac{5}{48} \times \frac{1-0.45}{0.45} = 0.127 \approx 1:8 \text{ (Np:Ns)}\]

Magnetizing inductance (for CCM):

\[L_m = \frac{48^2 \times 0.45^2}{2 \times 25 \times 100k} = 93.3\ \mu H\]

Output capacitor:

\[C = \frac{I_{out} \cdot D}{f_{sw} \cdot \Delta V_{out}} = \frac{5 \times 0.45}{100k \times 0.05} = 450\ \mu F\]

docs.title: Leakage Inductance
docs.text:
Real transformers have imperfect coupling (k < 1). The leakage inductance causes:

  • Voltage spikes on the switch at turn-off
  • Energy loss if not recovered
  • EMI concerns

docs.title: Snubber Circuit
docs.text:
An RCD snubber clamps the voltage spike:

\[R_{snub} = \frac{V_{clamp}^2}{P_{leak}}, \quad C_{snub} = \frac{V_{clamp}}{R_{snub} \cdot f_{sw} \cdot \Delta V_{clamp}}\]

docs.title: Tutorial: Forward Converter
docs.text:
Design and simulate an isolated forward converter.

Difficulty: Intermediate (⅔) | Duration: 30 minutes

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
The forward converter is an isolated version of the buck converter:

Unlike the flyback, energy transfers during the switch ON time.

docs.title: Operating Principle
docs.text:
Switch ON: Power transfers through transformer to secondary. Output diode D1 conducts.

\[V_{sec} = n \cdot V_{in}, \quad V_L = n \cdot V_{in} - V_{out}\]

Switch OFF: Transformer resets. Freewheeling diode D2 conducts. Inductor supplies load.

\[V_L = -V_{out}\]

docs.title: Voltage Conversion
docs.text:
\[V_{out} = n \cdot D \cdot V_{in}\]

Where n = Ns/Np.

docs.title: Key Difference from Flyback
docs.text: Feature Forward Flyback Energy transfer During ON time During OFF time Output filter LC filter needed Capacitor only Output ripple Lower (LC filtered) Higher Core utilization Unipolar (needs reset) Unipolar Power level Medium (50-500W) Low-Medium (5-150W)

docs.title: Core Reset
docs.text:
The forward converter needs a mechanism to reset the transformer core each cycle. With third winding:

\[D_{max} = \frac{N_p}{N_p + N_r}\]

For Np = Nr: D_max = 0.5

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Input voltage 48V DC Output voltage 12V DC Output power 100W Switching frequency 200 kHz Max duty cycle 0.45

docs.title: Calculations
docs.text:
Turns ratio:

\[n = \frac{V_{out}}{D \cdot V_{in}} = \frac{12}{0.45 \times 48} = 0.556 \approx 1:1.8\]

Output inductor:

\[L = \frac{(n \cdot V_{in} - V_{out}) \cdot D}{f_{sw} \cdot \Delta i_L} = 16\ \mu H\]

Output capacitor:

\[C = \frac{\Delta i_L}{8 \cdot f_{sw} \cdot \Delta V_{out}} = 8.7\ \mu F\]

docs.title: Simulation & Project File
docs.text:
A complete, simulated and verified Isolated Forward Converter project file is provided directly in this directory:

  • Project File: forward-converter.ipes

docs.title: Forward Converter Architecture & Core Demagnetization
docs.text:
Unlike the flyback converter which stores energy in the magnetic core during the ON time and delivers it during the OFF time, the forward converter transfers energy directly to the secondary during the switch ON time:

  1. Transformer Primary & Demagnetization Clamp:
  2. \(48.0\text{ V DC}\) input source.
  3. Primary switch S_1 switches at \(50\text{ kHz}\) with duty ratio \(D = 0.35\) (safely below the maximum theoretical limit \(D_{max} = 0.50\) to guarantee complete flux reset).

  4. Core reset is guaranteed by an RCD snubber clamp (\(R_{clamp} = 500\,\Omega\), \(C_{clamp} = 10\,\text{nF}\)) connected across S_1. During the switch OFF time, magnetizing current circulates into \(C_{clamp}\), demagnetizing the core and clamping switch voltage to \(V_{in} + V_{reset}\).

  5. Secondary Rectifier & Buck Filter:

  6. Forward rectifier diode D_fwd conducts during switch ON, feeding energy to filter inductor \(L_1 = 50\,\mu\text{H}\).
  7. Freewheeling diode D_fw conducts during switch OFF, maintaining continuous inductor current into output capacitor \(C_1 = 100\,\mu\text{F}\) and load \(R_1 = 10.0\,\Omega\).
  8. Nominal output voltage: $\(V_{out} = n \cdot D \cdot V_{in} = 1.0 \times 0.35 \times 48.0\text{ V} \approx 16.8\text{ V DC}\)$

docs.title: 903 - Inductor Saturation
docs.text: Non-linear inductance modeling and saturation effects.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Inductor saturation occurs when the core's magnetic flux density approaches Bsat, causing: - Dramatic inductance drop - Current spike - Potential device damage - Control instability

docs.title: B-H Relationship
docs.text:
\[B = \mu_0 \mu_r(H) \cdot H\]

At saturation (core behaves like air):

\[\mu_r \rightarrow 1\]

docs.title: Inductance vs Current
docs.text:
\[L(i) = \frac{N^2 \cdot \mu_0 \mu_r(i) \cdot A_e}{l_e}\]

As i increases → H increases → μr decreases → L decreases

docs.title: Piecewise Linear Model
docs.text:
Simple region-based saturation model:

\[ L(i) = \begin{cases} L_{nom} & |i| < I_{sat} \\ L_{sat} & |i| \geq I_{sat} \end{cases} \]

docs.title: Smooth Saturation Model
docs.text:
More realistic continuous saturation roll-off:

\[ L(i) = \frac{L_0}{1 + (i/I_{sat})^n} \]

Where \(n\) controls transition sharpness (typically \(2 \dots 6\)).

docs.title: Jiles-Atherton
docs.text: Physics-based model including: - Anhysteretic magnetization - Domain wall motion - Energy loss (hysteresis)

docs.title: DC-DC Converter
docs.text:
Normal operation (CCM): - Triangle current waveform - Predictable ripple

Saturated operation: - Current spike during on-time - Potential switch damage - EMI increase

docs.title: Current at Saturation
docs.text:
\[I_{sat} = \frac{B_{sat} \cdot l_e}{\mu_0 \mu_r \cdot N}\]

With air gap:

\[I_{sat} = \frac{B_{sat} \cdot l_g}{\mu_0 \cdot N}\]

docs.title: Method 1: Air Gap
docs.text:
Add gap to reduce effective permeability:

\[\mu_{eff} = \frac{\mu_r}{1 + \mu_r \cdot l_g/l_e}\]

Benefits: - Stores energy in gap - Soft saturation characteristic - Stable inductance vs temperature

docs.title: Method 2: Larger Core
docs.text:
Increase Ae to reduce B for given flux:

\[B = \frac{L \cdot I_{peak}}{N \cdot A_e}\]

docs.title: Method 3: Distributed Gap Materials
docs.text: Powder cores (Kool Mμ, MPP, etc.): - Inherent distributed gap - Soft saturation - Higher core losses

docs.text: Parameter Before Sat After Sat Inductance 100 µH 10 µH di/dt 50 A/µs 500 A/µs Peak current 10 A unlimited

docs.text: During load step: 1. Current increases toward new operating point 2. If current exceeds Isat, L drops suddenly 3. di/dt increases dramatically 4. Current overshoots

docs.title: Simulation Project: Linear vs. Saturating Inductor Comparison
docs.text: The companion project file inductor-saturation.ipes compares a linear inductor against an authentic non-linear saturating choke driven in parallel by a common voltage step excitation in GeckoCIRCUITS.

docs.title: Circuit & Simulation Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Description Circuit File inductor-saturation.ipes Validated saturation comparison model Excitation Voltage (U.1) \(40\text{ V DC}\) pulse Step voltage driving parallel branches Branch 1 (Linear Inductor) R.1 (\(1.0\,\Omega\)) + L.3 (\(500\,\mu\text{H}\)) Linear reference choke (isNonlinear false) Branch 2 (Saturating Inductor) R.3 (\(1.0\,\Omega\)) + L.4 (Non-linear) Saturating power choke (isNonlinear true) Saturation Characteristic (L.4) \(0\text{ A} \to 500\,\mu\text{H}\), \(7\text{ A} \to 500\,\mu\text{H}\), \(10\text{ A} \to 150\,\mu\text{H}\), \(30\text{ A} \to 100\,\mu\text{H}\) Non-linear inductance vs. current lookup curve Saturation Knee (\(I_{sat}\)) \(7.0\text{ A}\) Transition current where core enters saturation Simulation Step (\(\Delta t\)) \(1.0\,\mu\text{s}\) High temporal resolution Simulation Duration \(0.005\text{ s}\) (\(5\text{ ms}\)) Complete current transient through saturation knee

docs.title: Current Slope Acceleration Physics
docs.text:
For the linear inductor L.3, the current rises monotonically according to:

\[ i_{linear}(t) = \frac{V}{R} \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right), \quad \tau = \frac{L_0}{R} = \frac{500\,\mu\text{H}}{1\,\Omega} = 500\,\mu\text{s} \]

For the saturating inductor L.4: - When \(i < 7.0\text{ A}\): \(L(i) = 500\,\mu\text{H}\), and the current slope matches the linear choke: \(\frac{di}{dt} = \frac{V - R i}{500\,\mu\text{H}}\). - When \(i > 7.0\text{ A}\): The core saturates, and inductance drops to \(100\,\mu\text{H}\). The current slope surges by a factor of 5:

\[ \left.\frac{di}{dt}\right|_{sat} = \frac{V - R i}{100\,\mu\text{H}} \approx 5 \times \left.\frac{di}{dt}\right|_{unsaturated} \]

This causes a sharp upward curvature in the current waveform, demonstrating the severe current spikes caused by core saturation.

docs.title: 901 - Magnetic Domain
docs.text: Permeance-capacitance modeling for magnetic circuits.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: GeckoCIRCUITS uses the permeance-capacitance analogy for magnetic circuit simulation, enabling: - Core saturation modeling - Leakage inductance effects - Coupled inductors and transformers - Non-linear magnetic behavior

docs.title: Permeance-Capacitance Model
docs.text: Magnetic Electrical Unit MMF (F) Voltage (V) A-turns / V Flux (Φ) Charge (Q) Wb / C dΦ/dt Current (I) V / A Permeance (P) Capacitance (C) H / F Reluctance (R) 1/C 1/H / 1/F

docs.title: Why This Analogy?
docs.text: The permeance-capacitance model: - Allows integration with electrical circuit - Handles non-linear permeability naturally - Supports multiple windings on single core - Models leakage paths explicitly

docs.title: Permeance (Magnetic Capacitor)
docs.text:
\[P = \frac{\mu_0 \mu_r A}{l}\]

Where: - μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m - μᵣ = relative permeability - A = cross-sectional area - l = magnetic path length

docs.title: Winding (Gyrator)
docs.text:
Converts electrical current to MMF:

\[ F = N \cdot i \] \[ v = N \cdot \frac{d\Phi}{dt} \]

docs.title: Air Gap
docs.text:
\[ P_{gap} = \frac{\mu_0 A_{eff}}{l_g} \]

With fringing factor for accurate modeling.

docs.title: Winding-to-Core Dual Domain Interface
docs.text: The dual-domain interface models: - Electrical Port: Winding with \(N\) turns, terminal voltage \(v(t)\), and current \(i(t)\). - Magnetic Port: Magnetomotive force \(F = N \cdot i\), driving core flux \(\Phi\) through core permeance \(P_{core}\) and air gap permeance \(P_{gap}\). - Coupling Principle: The rate of change of magnetic flux induces back-EMF according to Faraday's law \(v = N \cdot \frac{d\Phi}{dt}\).

docs.title: B-H Curve
docs.text:
Non-linear permeability:

\[ B = f(H) = \mu_0 \mu_r(H) \cdot H \]

docs.title: Jiles-Atherton Model
docs.text: Physics-based hysteresis model with parameters: - Ms = saturation magnetization - a = domain wall density - k = pinning coefficient - c = reversibility - α = domain coupling

docs.title: Piecewise Linear
docs.text: Simpler approach with: - Initial permeability μᵢ - Saturation flux Bsat - Saturated permeability μsat ≈ μ₀

docs.title: Steinmetz Equation
docs.text:
\[P_v = k \cdot f^\alpha \cdot B^\beta\]

Typical values: - Ferrite: α ≈ 1.3, β ≈ 2.5 - Iron powder: α ≈ 1.5, β ≈ 2.0

docs.title: Improved GSE (iGSE)
docs.text:
For non-sinusoidal waveforms:

\[P_v = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T k_i \left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right|^\alpha (\Delta B)^{\beta-\alpha} dt\]

  3. Material (ferrite, iron powder)
  4. Dimensions (A, l)
  5. Saturation characteristics
  6. Add windings and connect to electrical circuit
  7. Add leakage permeance if needed

docs.title: Magnetic Coupling Physics
docs.text:
The coupling factor \(k\) between windings \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) defines the mutual inductance:

\[ M = k \sqrt{L_1 L_2} = 0.98 \sqrt{5.0\text{ mH} \cdot 2.0\text{ mH}} = 3.10\text{ mH} \]

The leakage inductance referred to the primary is:

\[ L_{\sigma} = (1 - k^2) L_1 = (1 - 0.98^2) \cdot 5.0\text{ mH} \approx 0.198\text{ mH} \]

docs.title: Two-Mass System
docs.text:
Models shaft compliance:

Equations:

\[J_1 \frac{d\omega_1}{dt} = \tau_m - \tau_s\] \[J_2 \frac{d\omega_2}{dt} = \tau_s - \tau_L\] \[\tau_s = k(\theta_1 - \theta_2) + b(\omega_1 - \omega_2)\]

docs.title: Constant Torque
docs.text:
\[\tau_L = \tau_0\]

Applications: Conveyors, hoists, cranes

docs.title: Quadratic (Fan/Pump)
docs.text:
\[\tau_L = k \cdot \omega^2\]

Applications: Fans, pumps, blowers

docs.title: Linear (Friction)
docs.text:
\[\tau_L = b \cdot \omega\]

Viscous friction model

docs.title: Constant Power
docs.text:
\[\tau_L = \frac{P_0}{\omega}\]

Applications: Winders, machine tools

docs.title: PMSM (Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor)
docs.text:
Electrical equations (dq frame):

\[v_d = R_s i_d + L_d \frac{di_d}{dt} - \omega_e L_q i_q\] \[v_q = R_s i_q + L_q \frac{di_q}{dt} + \omega_e L_d i_d + \omega_e \psi_m\]

Torque:

\[\tau_e = \frac{3}{2} p [\psi_m i_q + (L_d - L_q)i_d i_q]\]

docs.title: BLDC (Brushless DC)
docs.text:
Trapezoidal back-EMF model:

\[e_{ph} = k_e \cdot \omega \cdot f(\theta_e)\]

Where f(θe) is trapezoidal function of electrical angle.

docs.title: Induction Motor
docs.text:
Rotor flux model:

\[\frac{d\psi_r}{dt} = \frac{L_m}{\tau_r}i_s - \frac{1}{\tau_r}\psi_r + j\omega_{slip}\psi_r\]

Torque:

\[\tau_e = \frac{3}{2}p\frac{L_m}{L_r}Im\{\psi_r^* i_s\}\]

docs.title: Ideal Gear Ratio
docs.text: \[\omega_2 = \frac{\omega_1}{n}\] \[\tau_2 = n \cdot \tau_1\]

docs.title: Reflected Inertia
docs.text:
\[J_{eq} = J_1 + \frac{J_2}{n^2}\]

Inertia seen from motor side

docs.title: Gear Efficiency
docs.text: \[\tau_2 = \eta \cdot n \cdot \tau_1 \quad \text{(motoring)}\] \[\tau_2 = \frac{n \cdot \tau_1}{\eta} \quad \text{(regenerating)}\]
