docs.title: Simulation Project: Two-Mass Electromechanical Drivetrain
docs.text: The companion project file mechanical-systems.ipes models a compliant two-mass rotational drivetrain in GeckoCIRCUITS, simulating torsional oscillations, shaft compliance, and speed response under step torque excitation.

docs.title: Circuit & Simulation Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Mechanical Value Electrical Analogy Description Circuit File mechanical-systems.ipes Validated electromechanical model Complete simulation project Motor Drive Torque (\(\tau_m\)) \(50.0\text{ Nm}\) \(V_{drive} = 50.0\text{ V}\) (TAU_M) Step motor torque Internal Source Resistance \(0.5\text{ Nm}\cdot\text{s/rad}\) \(R_{int} = 0.5\,\Omega\) (R_INT) Motor torque generation compliance Motor Rotor Inertia (\(J_1\)) \(0.05\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\) \(C_1 = 0.05\text{ F}\) (J1_MOTOR) Motor rotor mass Shaft Torsional Stiffness (\(k\)) \(1000.0\text{ Nm/rad}\) \(L_{shaft} = 1.0\text{ mH}\) (K_SHAFT) Elastic shaft compliance (\(1/k\)) Shaft Damping (\(b_s\)) \(0.1\text{ Nm}\cdot\text{s/rad}\) \(R_{shaft} = 10.0\,\Omega\) (B_SHAFT) Torsional internal damping Load Inertia (\(J_2\)) \(0.15\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\) \(C_2 = 0.15\text{ F}\) (J2_LOAD) Driven machine inertia Load Viscous Friction (\(b_L\)) \(0.2\text{ Nm}\cdot\text{s/rad}\) \(R_{load} = 5.0\,\Omega\) (B_LOAD) Load resistance (\(1/b_L\)) Simulation Step (\(\Delta t\)) \(10.0\,\mu\text{s}\) Fast MNA solver step 15,001 time steps Simulation Duration \(0.15\text{ s}\) (\(150\text{ ms}\)) Captures startup transient and torsional settling

docs.title: Torsional Resonance Frequency
docs.text:
The mechanical natural resonance frequency of the two-mass system is:

\[ f_{res} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k(J_1 + J_2)}{J_1 J_2}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{1000 \cdot (0.05 + 0.15)}{0.05 \cdot 0.15}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{26666.7} \approx 25.99\text{ Hz} \]

During acceleration, motor angular velocity \(\omega_{motor}\) and load angular velocity \(\omega_{load}\) oscillate out-of-phase at \(26\text{ Hz}\) before damping out into synchronized steady-state velocity:

\[ \omega_{ss} = \frac{\tau_m}{b_L + b_{int}} = \frac{50.0}{0.2 + 0.5} \approx 71.4\text{ rad/s} \quad (682\text{ RPM}) \]

docs.title: Monitored Probe Signals
docs.text: Signal Analogous Unit Description omega_motor \(\text{rad/s}\) (Volts) Motor rotor angular velocity \(\omega_1(t)\) omega_load \(\text{rad/s}\) (Volts) Driven load angular velocity \(\omega_2(t)\)

docs.title: How to Run Simulation
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS GUIMCP Interface (Command Line)
  1. Open mechanical-systems.ipes in GeckoCIRCUITS desktop.
  2. Click Start Simulation (or press F5).
  3. Open the Scope window and inspect omega_motor and omega_load to observe the \(26\text{ Hz}\) torsional ringing during startup.
# Validate circuit integrity
python -c "from scripts.desktop.mcp_client import GeckoMcpClient; c = GeckoMcpClient(); c.start(); print(c.call_tool('gecko_validate_circuit', {'circuit_path': 'docs/tutorials/magnetics/mechanical-systems.ipes'})); c.close()"

# Run simulation
python -c "from scripts.desktop.mcp_client import GeckoMcpClient; c = GeckoMcpClient(); c.start(); print(c.call_tool('gecko_simulate', {'circuit_path': 'docs/tutorials/magnetics/mechanical-systems.ipes', 'total_time': 0.15, 'time_step': 1e-5})); c.close()"

docs.title: Simulation Exercises
docs.text:
1. Measure the measured oscillation period between velocity peaks and verify \(T_{res} \approx 1 / 26\text{ Hz} \approx 38.5\text{ ms}\).
  2. Increase shaft stiffness \(k\) by \(4\times\) (\(L_{shaft} = 250\,\mu\text{H}\)) and observe how \(f_{res}\) doubles to \(52\text{ Hz}\).
  3. Vary the inertia ratio \(\sigma = J_{load} / J_{motor}\) from \(3.0\) to \(10.0\) and observe the increasing overshoot and settling time.
  4. Add a notch filter in the speed controller tuned to \(f_{res}\) to suppress mechanical resonance excitation.

docs.title: 902 - Transformer Design
docs.text: High-frequency transformer modeling with leakage and parasitics.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Transformer modeling in power electronics requires: - Magnetizing inductance - Leakage inductance - Winding capacitance - Core losses

docs.title: Practical Model
docs.text: Where: - \(L_m\) = magnetizing inductance - \(R_{fe}\) = core loss equivalent resistance - \(L_{\sigma p}, L_{\sigma s}\) = primary and secondary leakage inductances - \(R_p, R_s\) = primary and secondary winding resistances

docs.title: Parameter Extraction
docs.text:
Magnetizing Inductance:

\[ L_m = N_1^2 \cdot P_{core} \]

Leakage Inductance:

\[ L_{lk} = N^2 \cdot P_{leak} \]

docs.title: Step 1: Core Selection
docs.text:
Area product method:

\[ A_p = A_e \cdot A_w = \frac{P_{out}}{K_f \cdot K_u \cdot J \cdot B_{max} \cdot f} \]

Where: - \(A_e\) = core cross-section - \(A_w\) = window area - \(K_f\) = waveform factor - \(K_u\) = window utilization - \(J\) = current density - \(B_{max}\) = peak flux density

docs.title: Step 2: Turns Calculation
docs.text:
Primary Turns:

\[ N_1 = \frac{V_1}{4 \cdot f \cdot B_{max} \cdot A_e} \]

Secondary Turns:

\[ N_2 = \frac{N_1}{n} \]

docs.title: Step 3: Wire Selection
docs.text:
Current density (typical 3-5 A/mm² for natural cooling):

\[ A_{wire} = \frac{I_{rms}}{J} \]

Skin depth at frequency \(f\):

\[ \delta = \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\pi f \mu}} \]

docs.title: Step 4: Leakage Inductance
docs.text:
Depends on winding arrangement: - Interleaved: lower leakage - Separated: higher leakage

\[ L_{lk} \approx \frac{\mu_0 N^2 MLT}{3 h_w} \cdot \left(n_p \cdot b_p + \frac{n_i \cdot b_i}{3}\right) \]

docs.title: Primary-Secondary (P-S)
docs.text:
• Simple construction
  • High leakage inductance
  • Suitable for flyback

docs.title: Interleaved (P-S-P-S)
docs.text:
• Reduced leakage
  • Lower proximity effect
  • More complex

docs.title: Sandwich (P-S-P)
docs.text:
• Moderate leakage
  • Good balance

docs.title: Inter-winding Capacitance
docs.text:
\[ C_{ps} = \frac{\epsilon_0 \epsilon_r A_{overlap}}{d_{insulation}} \]

Important for: - Common-mode noise - High dv/dt applications

docs.title: Intra-winding Capacitance
docs.text:
Affects self-resonance frequency:

\[ f_{res} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_{lk} C_{self}}} \]

docs.title: Setting Up
docs.text:
1. Use coupled inductor component
  2. Set:
  3. Turns ratio
  4. Magnetizing inductance
  5. Leakage inductance (referred to primary)
  6. Winding resistances
  7. For detailed analysis:
  8. Use permeance network
  9. Add saturation to core permeance

docs.title: Simulation Project: Practical Transformer Equivalent Circuit
docs.text: The companion project file transformer-design.ipes models the practical transformer equivalent circuit in GeckoCIRCUITS, incorporating primary/secondary leakage inductances, copper winding resistances, core magnetizing inductance, and shunt core loss resistance.

docs.title: Circuit & Simulation Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Description Circuit File transformer-design.ipes Validated practical transformer model Primary Voltage (\(V_{pri}\)) \(230\text{ V RMS}\) (\(325.27\text{ V peak}\)), \(50\text{ Hz}\) Grid AC voltage source (V_AC) Turns Ratio (\(N_1 : N_2\)) \(10.0 : 2.5\) (\(4:1\) step-down) Ideal 4-terminal transformer core (XFMR) Primary Resistance (\(R_p\)) \(0.5\,\Omega\) Primary copper resistance (R_P) Primary Leakage (\(L_{\sigma p}\)) \(50.0\,\mu\text{H}\) Primary leakage inductance (L_SIGMA_P) Magnetizing Inductance (\(L_m\)) \(50.0\text{ mH}\) Core magnetizing inductance (L_M) Core Loss Resistance (\(R_{fe}\)) \(10.0\,\text{k}\Omega\) Eddy current and hysteresis core loss equivalent (R_FE) Secondary Leakage (\(L_{\sigma s}\)) \(3.125\,\mu\text{H}\) Secondary leakage inductance (\(L_{\sigma p} / n^2\)) (L_SIGMA_S) Secondary Resistance (\(R_s\)) \(0.03125\,\Omega\) Secondary copper resistance (\(R_p / n^2\)) (R_S) Secondary Load (\(R_{load}\)) \(5.0\,\Omega\) Secondary resistive load (R_LOAD) Simulation Step (\(\Delta t\)) \(1.0\,\mu\text{s}\) Fine temporal resolution Simulation Duration \(0.04\text{ s}\) (\(40\text{ ms}\)) Two complete \(50\text{ Hz}\) line periods (40,001 time steps)

docs.title: Voltage Transfer & Regulation Analysis
docs.text:
For an ideal transformer, the secondary voltage would be:

\[ V_{sec,ideal} = \frac{V_{pri}}{n} = \frac{230\text{ V}}{4} = 57.5\text{ V RMS} \quad (81.32\text{ V peak}) \]

Under loaded conditions (\(R_{load} = 5\,\Omega\)), the secondary current reflects back to the primary, causing internal voltage drops across the primary impedance \(Z_p = R_p + j\omega L_{\sigma p}\) and secondary impedance \(Z_s = R_s + j\omega L_{\sigma s}\). At \(50\text{ Hz}\), the leakage reactances are negligible compared to load resistances, so voltage regulation is dominated by the copper winding resistances:

\[ R_{eq,sec} = R_s + \frac{R_p}{n^2} = 0.03125\,\Omega + \frac{0.5\,\Omega}{16} = 0.0625\,\Omega \] \[ V_{sec,loaded} \approx V_{sec,ideal} \cdot \frac{R_{load}}{R_{load} + R_{eq,sec}} = 57.5\text{ V} \cdot \frac{5.0}{5.0625} \approx 56.79\text{ V RMS} \quad (80.3\text{ V peak}) \]

docs.title: Monitored Probe Signals
docs.text: Signal Description Expected Value v_pri Primary AC voltage across supply \(325.27\text{ V peak}\), \(50\text{ Hz}\) sinusoidal v_sec Secondary voltage across \(R_{load}\) \(\approx 80.3\text{ V peak}\), in-phase with primary

docs.title: How to Run Simulation
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS GUIMCP Interface (Command Line)
  1. Open transformer-design.ipes in GeckoCIRCUITS desktop.
  2. Click Start Simulation (or press F5).
  3. Open the Scope window and inspect v_pri and v_sec to verify the \(4:1\) step-down transformation and voltage regulation.
# Validate circuit integrity
python -c "from scripts.desktop.mcp_client import GeckoMcpClient; c = GeckoMcpClient(); c.start(); print(c.call_tool('gecko_validate_circuit', {'circuit_path': 'docs/tutorials/magnetics/transformer-design.ipes'})); c.close()"

# Run simulation
python -c "from scripts.desktop.mcp_client import GeckoMcpClient; c = GeckoMcpClient(); c.start(); print(c.call_tool('gecko_simulate', {'circuit_path': 'docs/tutorials/magnetics/transformer-design.ipes', 'total_time': 0.04, 'time_step': 1e-6})); c.close()"

docs.title: Simulation Exercises
docs.text:
1. Measure no-load magnetizing current by setting \(R_{load} = 1\text{ M}\Omega\). Verify that \(I_{mag} \approx V_{pri} / (\omega L_m) = 230 / (2\pi \cdot 50 \cdot 0.05) \approx 14.6\text{ mA RMS}\).
  2. Increase primary and secondary leakage inductances by \(10\times\) (\(L_{\sigma p} = 500\,\mu\text{H}\)) and operate at \(10\text{ kHz}\). Observe the inductive phase lag and voltage regulation drop.
  3. Compare the practical model with an ideal transformer without parasitics.
  4. Calculate core power loss: \(P_{fe} = V_{pri}^2 / R_{fe} = 230^2 / 10000 = 5.29\text{ W}\).

docs.title: Option A: Using geckopy (Repository Python SDK)
docs.text:
import geckopy

ckt = geckopy.open("resources/projects/buck_sampled_50v_to_10v.ipes")
ckt.set_parameter("R_load", "resistance", 12.0)
res = ckt.simulate(duration=0.01, dt=1e-6)
print(res.metrics)

docs.title: Option B: Using the REST API (requests)
docs.text:
Start the server (run-gecko.bat or ./run-gecko.sh) so it listens on http://localhost:8080/gecko:

import time
import requests

base = "http://localhost:8080/gecko/api/v1"
resp = requests.post(f"{base}/simulations", json={
    "circuitFile": "resources/projects/buck_sampled_50v_to_10v.ipes",
    "simulationTime": 0.01,
    "timeStep": 1e-6,
    "solverType": "backward-euler",
})
resp.raise_for_status()
sim_id = resp.json()["simulationId"]

while True:
    status = requests.get(f"{base}/simulations/{sim_id}").json()
    if status["status"] in ("COMPLETED", "FAILED", "CANCELLED"):
        print(f"Simulation finished: {status['status']}")
        break
    time.sleep(0.1)

docs.title: 701 - Script Blocks & Legacy GeckoSCRIPT
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS separates in-circuit custom scripting (executed every simulation time step inside a circuit) from external automation:

  • In-circuit control logic: Use the Script Block (SCRIPT_BLOCK, component typ 61), supported natively in the desktop editor, REST API, MCP server (gecko_set_script_code), and headless simulation engine (ScriptBlockCalculator) via a pure-Java interpreter without GraalVM dependencies.
  • External parameter sweeps & batch runs: Use the Python SDK (geckopy) or the REST API.

Legacy GeckoSCRIPT (Retired in v1.0+)

Standalone GeckoSCRIPT (Tools > GeckoSCRIPT, GraalVM JavaScript macros with runSimulation() / setParameter() and CLI --script) was part of the Classic Swing GUI, which is archived on git tag classic-v1.0-final. Use Python (geckopy) or the REST API for external automation in current versions.

docs.title: Using SCRIPT_BLOCK (typ 61)
docs.text: A Script Block evaluates custom expressions at every simulation time step using wired control inputs (xIN[0], xIN[1], ...) and drives output signals (yOUT[0], ...).

docs.title: Inspecting or Updating a Script Block via Python (geckopy)
docs.text:
import geckopy

ckt = geckopy.open("resources/tutorials/7xx_scripting_automation/701_gecko_script_basics/GeckoSCRIPT.ipes")
ckt.set_script_code(
    block_name="SCRIPT.1",
    source_code="yOUT[0] = (xIN[0] > 0.5) ? 1.0 : 0.0;",
)
report = ckt.validate()
assert report.is_valid
res = ckt.simulate()

You can inspect or patch SCRIPT_BLOCK code from MCP assistants via gecko_set_script_code and gecko_validate_circuit (see MCP Interface).

docs.title: Headless CLI Batch Execution
docs.text:
To run a circuit containing script blocks directly from the command line without opening the GUI:

java -Dloader.main=gecko.core.GeckoHeadless \
     -cp backend/gecko-rest-api/target/gecko-rest-api.jar \
     org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.PropertiesLauncher \
     --circuit resources/tutorials/7xx_scripting_automation/701_gecko_script_basics/buck_control.ipes \
     --output results.csv --quiet

docs.title: 704 - Custom Control Blocks & NativeC
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS provides two supported ways to integrate custom algorithmic control blocks into simulations, depending on whether you want external compiled C/C++ firmware or a built-in Java calculator in gecko-simulation-core:

Approach Best For Documentation NativeC Block (NATIVE_C, typ 88) Running microcontroller C/C++ control firmware via shared libraries (.dll / .so / .dylib) without modifying GeckoCIRCUITS NativeC C/C++ Blocks Core Java Calculator (AbstractControlCalculatable) Adding first-class built-in control blocks to backend/gecko-simulation-core Control Calculators API, Developer Guide

Legacy Classic UI Java Blocks (Retired)

Runtime in-GUI compilation of standalone .java files inheriting AbstractControlBlock belonged to the retired Classic Swing application (archived at git tag classic-v1.0-final). Current releases do not ship a runtime Java compiler or AbstractControlBlock; use NativeC (NATIVE_C) for user-supplied compiled blocks or SCRIPT_BLOCK (typ 61) for inline scripted control logic.

docs.title: Option 1: Firmware-in-the-Loop with NativeC (NATIVE_C)
docs.text:
With the C Library Block (typ 88), you compile your C or C++ control algorithm into a shared library against gecko_c_block.h using your own toolchain (gcc, clang, or MSVC). GeckoCIRCUITS loads it per simulation run using JDK 25's Foreign Function & Memory (FFM) API:

#include "gecko_c_block.h"

void gecko_init(void) {
    /* Optional: reset controller state at t = 0 */
}

void gecko_step(const double* xIN, int n_in,
                double* yOUT, int n_out,
                double t, double dt) {
    if (n_out > 0 && n_in > 1) {
        double error = xIN[0] - xIN[1];
        yOUT[0] = 2.0 * error;
    }
}

See NativeC C/C++ Blocks for the full ABI specification (gecko_init, gecko_step, gecko_deinit), Windows/Linux/macOS build commands, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Option 2: Core Simulation Java Calculators
docs.text:
When extending GeckoCIRCUITS itself with a new built-in block, control logic lives in backend/gecko-simulation-core/src/main/java/gecko/core/control/calculators/ as a subclass of AbstractControlCalculatable (or AbstractSingleInputSingleOutputCalculator / AbstractTwoInputsOneOutputCalculator):

package gecko.core.control.calculators;

public final class ClampGainCalculator extends AbstractSingleInputSingleOutputCalculator {
    private final double gain;
    private final double maxOutput;

    public ClampGainCalculator(final double gain, final double maxOutput) {
        super();
        this.gain = gain;
        this.maxOutput = maxOutput;
    }

    @Override
    public void calculateYOUT(final double deltaT) {
        double y = gain * _inputSignal[0][0];
        _outputSignal[0][0] = Math.max(-maxOutput, Math.min(maxOutput, y));
    }
}

See Control Calculators API and the Developer Guide for signal wiring, InitializableAtSimulationStart, and unit testing instructions.

docs.title: 702 - MATLAB Integration
docs.text:
Integrate GeckoCIRCUITS circuit simulation into MATLAB or GNU Octave workflows using the REST API (http://localhost:8080/gecko/api/v1/...), or load exported CSV waveforms directly for plotting and control analysis.

Legacy RMI Removed

The legacy Java RMI interface (GeckoRemoteInterface, --remote, --mmf, and GeckoCustomMMF) belonged to the retired Classic Swing application (archived at git tag classic-v1.0-final). Current releases use the HTTP REST API instead, requiring no Java classpath setup in MATLAB.

docs.title: Step 1: Start the GeckoCIRCUITS Engine
docs.text:
Launch the desktop app or run the REST server from a checkout:

# Windows
run-gecko.bat

# Linux / macOS
./run-gecko.sh

# Or run the built REST API JAR directly
java -jar backend/gecko-rest-api/target/gecko-rest-api.jar

Verify the server responds:

health = webread('http://localhost:8080/gecko/api/health');
disp(health);

opts = weboptions('MediaType', 'application/json', 'Timeout', 30);

% Submit simulation using a circuit file and parameter overrides
req = struct( ...
    'circuitFile', 'resources/projects/buck_sampled_50v_to_10v.ipes', ...
    'simulationTime', 0.005, ...
    'timeStep', 1e-6, ...
    'solverType', 'backward-euler', ...
    'parameters', struct('R_load.resistance', 10.0) ...
);

sim = webwrite([baseUrl '/simulations'], req, opts);

% Poll until completion
while strcmp(sim.status, 'PENDING') || strcmp(sim.status, 'RUNNING')
    pause(0.1);
    sim = webread([baseUrl '/simulations/' sim.simulationId], opts);
end

if ~strcmp(sim.status, 'COMPLETED')
    error('Simulation failed: %s', sim.errorMessage);
end

% Fetch results and compute waveform characteristics
results = webread([baseUrl '/simulations/' sim.simulationId '/results'], opts);

docs.title: Post-Processing via /analysis/characteristics
docs.text:
charReq = struct('simulationId', sim.simulationId, 'signalName', 'V_out');
metrics = webwrite([baseUrl '/analysis/characteristics'], charReq, opts);
fprintf('Vout avg = %.3f V, rms = %.3f V, ripple = %.4f\n', ...
    metrics.average, metrics.rms, metrics.ripple);

docs.title: Duty / Load Sweep Example
docs.text:
You can submit multiple runs individually or submit a single batch sweep using POST /gecko/api/v1/simulations/batch:

baseUrl = 'http://localhost:8080/gecko/api/v1';
opts = weboptions('MediaType', 'application/json', 'Timeout', 30);

loads = [2, 5, 10, 20, 50];
vout_avg = zeros(size(loads));

for i = 1:length(loads)
    req = struct( ...
        'circuitFile', 'resources/projects/buck_sampled_50v_to_10v.ipes', ...
        'simulationTime', 0.005, ...
        'timeStep', 1e-6, ...
        'parameters', struct('R_load.resistance', loads(i)) ...
    );
    sim = webwrite([baseUrl '/simulations'], req, opts);
    while strcmp(sim.status, 'PENDING') || strcmp(sim.status, 'RUNNING')
        pause(0.1);
        sim = webread([baseUrl '/simulations/' sim.simulationId], opts);
    end
    m = webwrite([baseUrl '/analysis/characteristics'], ...
        struct('simulationId', sim.simulationId, 'signalName', 'V_out'), opts);
    vout_avg(i) = m.average;
end

figure;
plot(loads, vout_avg, 'b-o', 'LineWidth', 1.5);
xlabel('Load Resistance (Ohm)');
ylabel('Average Output Voltage (V)');
grid on;

docs.title: Python Integration
docs.text: Automate GeckoCIRCUITS simulations from Python and integrate with NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib using the built-in geckopy SDK, the REST API, or the headless CLI.

docs.title: Integration Methods
docs.text: Method Best For Transport geckopy SDK (recommended) In-process scripts, parameter sweeps, SciPy optimization, DRC validation gecko-mcp.jar over JSON-RPC 2.0 stdio REST API (requests) Remote servers, async/batch sweeps, WebSocket/SSE progress streaming HTTP (http://localhost:8080/gecko/api/v1) Headless CLI Shell/CI batch CSV generation without a long-lived server gecko.core.GeckoHeadless via PropertiesLauncher

docs.title: Method 1: Using geckopy (Recommended)
docs.text: The repository includes geckopy/ (Circuit, SimulationResult, Metrics, Waveforms, ValidationReport), which communicates directly with backend/gecko-mcp/target/gecko-mcp.jar (or the bundled desktop JAR).

docs.title: Build the MCP Server JAR (if running from source)
docs.text: mvn -pl backend/gecko-mcp -am package -DskipTests

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
import geckopy

# Open an existing circuit file (.ipes)
ckt = geckopy.open("resources/projects/buck_sampled_50v_to_10v.ipes")

# Pre-flight Design Rule Check (DRC)
report = ckt.validate()
if not report.is_valid:
    print("Validation errors:", report.errors)

# Modify parameters and run headless simulation
ckt.set_parameter("R_load", "resistance", 12.0)
result = ckt.simulate(duration=0.01, dt=1e-6, solver="backward-euler")

print("Metrics:", result.metrics)
waveforms = ckt.get_waveforms(duration=0.01, dt=1e-6, max_points=2000)

docs.title: Parameter Sweep & Optimization with NumPy/SciPy
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
import geckopy

ckt = geckopy.open("resources/projects/buck_sampled_50v_to_10v.ipes")

def objective(resistance: float) -> float:
    ckt.set_parameter("R_load", "resistance", float(resistance))
    metrics = ckt.measure_metrics()
    v_out = metrics.get("v_out", {}).get("steady_state_dc", 0.0)
    return abs(v_out - 10.0)

opt = minimize_scalar(objective, bounds=(2.0, 20.0), method="bounded")
print(f"Best R_load = {opt.x:.2f} Ohm, error = {opt.fun:.4f} V")

docs.title: Method 2: REST API (requests)
docs.text:
Start the REST server (run-gecko.bat, ./run-gecko.sh, or java -jar backend/gecko-rest-api/target/gecko-rest-api.jar). All endpoints are served under the /gecko context path.

import time
import requests

BASE_URL = "http://localhost:8080/gecko/api/v1"

# 1. Submit an asynchronous simulation
resp = requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/simulations", json={
    "circuitFile": "resources/projects/buck_sampled_50v_to_10v.ipes",
    "simulationTime": 0.01,
    "timeStep": 1e-6,
    "solverType": "backward-euler",
    "parameters": {"R_load.resistance": 10.0},
})
resp.raise_for_status()
sim_id = resp.json()["simulationId"]

# 2. Poll status until completion
while True:
    status = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/simulations/{sim_id}").json()
    if status["status"] in ("COMPLETED", "FAILED", "CANCELLED"):
        break
    time.sleep(0.1)

# 3. Fetch results and signal analysis
results = requests.get(f"{BASE_URL}/simulations/{sim_id}/results").json()
metrics = requests.post(f"{BASE_URL}/analysis/characteristics", json={
    "simulationId": sim_id,
    "signalName": "V_out",
}).json()
print("Characteristics:", metrics)

For multi-point sweeps in one call, see POST /gecko/api/v1/simulations/batch in the REST API Reference.

import subprocess

cmd = [
    "java",
    "-Dloader.main=gecko.core.GeckoHeadless",
    "-cp", "backend/gecko-rest-api/target/gecko-rest-api.jar",
    "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.PropertiesLauncher",
    "--circuit", "tools/parity/circuits/rc-lowpass.ipes",
    "--output", "rc_out.csv",

]
subprocess.run(cmd, check=True)

docs.title: Notes on .ipes File Format
docs.text: .ipes files are plain-text line-oriented UTF-8 circuit files (<ElementLK>, <ElementCONTROL>, tDURATION, etc.). Some historical or exported files may also be gzip-compressed (.ipes or .ipes.gz). Both geckopy and CircuitFileParser handle plain-text and gzip-compressed .ipes files automatically; prefer geckopy / REST endpoints over hand-editing raw .ipes files so DRC rules and terminal wiring stay valid.

docs.text: Power semiconductor loss calculation and thermal modeling for reliable converter design in GeckoCIRCUITS.

docs.title: Available Tutorials and Project Files

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Calculate conduction and switching losses in IGBTs, MOSFETs, and diodes
  • Model thermal impedance networks (Foster and Cauer representations)
  • Simulate transient and steady-state semiconductor junction temperatures
  • Size heatsinks for natural and forced-air convection cooling
  • Inspect thermal waveforms and loss metrics via GeckoCIRCUITS GUI and MCP tools

docs.title: Thermal Resistance Chain
docs.text: \[ T_j = T_a + P_{loss} \cdot (R_{th,jc} + R_{th,ch} + R_{th,ha}) \]

docs.title: Loss Equations
docs.text:
Conduction Loss: - IGBT: \(P_{cond} = V_{ce0} \cdot I_c + R_{on} \cdot I_c^2\) - Diode: \(P_{cond} = V_f \cdot I_d + R_d \cdot I_d^2\)

Switching Loss:

\[ P_{sw} = (E_{on} + E_{off}) \cdot f_{sw} \cdot \left(\frac{V_{dc}}{V_{ref}}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{I_c}{I_{ref}}\right) \]

  • DC-AC Inverter Tutorials

docs.title: 503 - Heatsink Design
docs.text: Thermal resistance calculation and heatsink selection.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Heatsink design ensures junction temperature stays within safe limits under all operating conditions.

docs.title: Required Heatsink Thermal Resistance
docs.text: \[R_{th,ha} = \frac{T_{j,max} - T_a}{P_{loss}} - R_{th,jc} - R_{th,ch}\]

docs.title: Example Calculation
docs.text:
Given: - Tj,max = 125°C (design limit) - Ta,max = 50°C (ambient) - Ploss = 50W - Rth,jc = 0.5 K/W - Rth,ch = 0.2 K/W (with thermal paste)

Required:

\[R_{th,ha} = \frac{125 - 50}{50} - 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.8 \text{ K/W}\]

docs.title: Natural Convection
docs.text: Type Rth Range Application TO-220 clip 10-30 K/W <5W Extruded profile 1-10 K/W 5-50W Large finned 0.3-2 K/W 50-200W

docs.title: Forced Air Cooling
docs.text:
Thermal resistance with airflow:

\[R_{th}(v) = R_{th,natural} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{v_0}{v}}\]

Where v₀ ≈ 0.5 m/s (natural convection equivalent)

docs.title: Liquid Cooling
docs.text: Type Rth Range Cold plate 0.05-0.2 K/W Microchannel 0.02-0.1 K/W Jet impingement 0.01-0.05 K/W

docs.title: TIM Thermal Resistance
docs.text: \[R_{th,ch} = \frac{t_{TIM}}{k_{TIM} \cdot A} + R_{contact}\]

docs.title: Material Comparison
docs.text: TIM Type k (W/m·K) Rth (typical) Thermal grease 1-5 0.1-0.3 K/W Phase change 3-5 0.1-0.2 K/W Thermal pad 1-6 0.2-0.5 K/W Solder 50 0.01-0.05 K/W

docs.title: Thermal Coupling
docs.text:
Devices share heatsink → thermal interaction:

\[\begin{bmatrix} T_{j1} \\ T_{j2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Z_{11} & Z_{12} \\ Z_{21} & Z_{22} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} P_1 \\ P_2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} T_a \\ T_a \end{bmatrix}\]

Self-heating: Z₁₁, Z₂₂ Cross-coupling: Z₁₂ = Z₂₁

docs.title: Step 1: Loss Budget
docs.text:
• Calculate losses at worst-case operating point
  • Include all devices on heatsink

docs.title: Step 2: Thermal Budget
docs.text:
• Determine maximum ambient temperature
  • Set junction temperature target
  • Calculate required Rth,ha

docs.title: Step 3: Heatsink Selection
docs.text:
• Select heatsink meeting Rth requirement
  • Add margin for:
  • Manufacturing variation (10-20%)
  • TIM degradation over life
  • Altitude derating

docs.title: Step 4: Verification
docs.text:
• Simulate thermal transient
  • Check at startup (maximum losses)
  • Check at overload conditions

docs.title: Single Device
docs.text:
1. Enable thermal on device
  2. Set Rth,jc from datasheet
  3. Set Rth,ch (interface)
  4. Add thermal node for heatsink
  5. Set Rth,ha and Cth,ha

docs.title: Multiple Devices
docs.text:
1. Connect devices to common thermal node
  2. Set individual Rth,jc
  3. Single heatsink Rth,ha
  4. Enable thermal coupling if needed

docs.title: Simulation Project: Heatsink Sizing & Thermal Verification
docs.text: The companion project file heatsink-design.ipes models a complete power stage with thermal budgeting, semiconductor loss injection, and heatsink thermal mass in GeckoCIRCUITS.

docs.title: Circuit & Simulation Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Description Circuit File heatsink-design.ipes Validated heatsink design model Input Voltage (\(V_{in}\)) \(300\text{ V DC}\) Operating DC supply Ambient Temperature (\(T_a\)) \(50.0^\circ\text{C}\) Worst-case high ambient environment (Temp.1) Power Loss (\(P_{loss}\)) \(50\text{ W}\) Average dissipated heat flux Junction-to-Case Resistance (\(R_{th,jc}\)) \(0.5\text{ K/W}\) Internal semiconductor die thermal barrier Case-to-Heatsink Resistance (\(R_{th,ch}\)) \(0.2\text{ K/W}\) Thermal interface material (TIM / thermal grease) Heatsink Thermal Resistance (\(R_{th,ha}\)) \(0.8\text{ K/W}\) Sized for \(T_j \le 125^\circ\text{C}\) design budget (Rth.ha) Heatsink Thermal Capacitance (\(C_{th,h}\)) \(25.0\text{ J/K}\) Heatsink aluminum thermal mass (Cth.6) Simulation Step (\(\Delta t\)) \(1.0\,\mu\text{s}\) Fast MNA solver step Simulation Duration \(0.01\text{ s}\) (\(10\text{ ms}\)) High-resolution initial transient verification

docs.title: Thermal Verification
docs.text:
Using the steady-state thermal chain formula:

\[ T_{sink} = T_a + P_{loss} \cdot R_{th,ha} = 50^\circ\text{C} + 50\text{ W} \cdot 0.8\text{ K/W} = 90.0^\circ\text{C} \] \[ T_j = T_{sink} + P_{loss} \cdot (R_{th,jc} + R_{th,ch}) = 90.0^\circ\text{C} + 50\text{ W} \cdot (0.5 + 0.2)\text{ K/W} = 125.0^\circ\text{C} \]

The selected heatsink (\(0.8\text{ K/W}\)) guarantees the junction temperature remains strictly within the \(125^\circ\text{C}\) safe design envelope.

docs.title: How to Run Simulation
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS GUIMCP Interface (Command Line)
  1. Open heatsink-design.ipes in GeckoCIRCUITS desktop.
  2. Click Start Simulation (or press F5).
  3. Open the Scope window and inspect the thermal nodes Tj and TSink.
# Validate circuit integrity
python -c "from scripts.desktop.mcp_client import GeckoMcpClient; c = GeckoMcpClient(); c.start(); print(c.call_tool('gecko_validate_circuit', {'circuit_path': 'docs/tutorials/thermal/heatsink-design.ipes'})); c.close()"

# Run simulation
python -c "from scripts.desktop.mcp_client import GeckoMcpClient; c = GeckoMcpClient(); c.start(); print(c.call_tool('gecko_simulate', {'circuit_path': 'docs/tutorials/thermal/heatsink-design.ipes', 'total_time': 0.01, 'time_step': 1e-6})); c.close()"

docs.title: Simulation Exercises
docs.text:
1. Natural vs Forced Convection: Change \(R_{th,ha}\) from \(0.8\text{ K/W}\) (forced air at \(2\text{ m/s}\)) to \(2.5\text{ K/W}\) (natural convection). Observe the dramatic increase in \(T_j\) exceeding the \(150^\circ\text{C}\) maximum limit.
  2. Thermal Mass Dynamics: Double \(C_{th,h}\) to \(50.0\text{ J/K}\) and observe how the heatsink temperature rate-of-rise slows down during a cold start.
  3. Transient Overload: Apply a \(2\times\) power pulse (\(100\text{ W}\)) for \(100\text{ ms}\) and evaluate whether the thermal capacitances prevent \(T_j\) from exceeding \(T_{j,max}\).

docs.title: 502 - Junction Temperature
docs.text: Thermal network modeling and transient analysis.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Junction temperature directly affects: - Semiconductor reliability (Arrhenius law) - Conduction losses (RDS(on) increases) - Switching characteristics - Safe Operating Area (SOA)

docs.title: Electrical-Thermal Analogy
docs.text: Thermal Electrical Unit Temperature T Voltage V °C / V Heat Flow P Current I W / A Thermal Resistance Rth Resistance R K/W / Ω Thermal Capacitance Cth Capacitance C J/K / F

docs.title: Foster Network
docs.text:
• Series connection of parallel \(R_i \parallel C_i\) branches
  • Parameters obtained directly from datasheet transient thermal impedance curve fitting
  • Cannot be cascaded directly (internal nodes have no physical temperature meaning)
  • Mathematically efficient for fast simulation

docs.title: Cauer Network
docs.text:
• Ladder network with series thermal resistances and shunt thermal capacitances to ambient ground
  • Physically meaningful nodes corresponding to semiconductor material layers (junction, silicon die, solder, copper baseplate, heatsink, ambient)
  • Can be cascaded modularly (junction \(\to\) case \(\to\) heatsink \(\to\) ambient)
  • Mathematically transformed from Foster coefficients or derived from finite element analysis (FEA)

docs.title: Datasheet Parameters
docs.text: From semiconductor datasheet: - \(R_{th,j-c}\) (junction to case) - \(R_{th,c-h}\) (case to heatsink) - depends on mounting / thermal grease - Transient thermal impedance curve \(Z_{th}(t)\)

docs.title: Extracting Foster Parameters
docs.text:
From \(Z_{th}\) curve fitting:

\[ Z_{th}(t) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i \cdot (1 - e^{-t/\tau_i}) \]

Where \(\tau_i = R_i \times C_i\)

docs.title: Steady-State
docs.text: \[ T_j = T_a + P_{loss} \cdot (R_{th,jc} + R_{th,ch} + R_{th,ha}) \]

docs.title: Transient Response
docs.text:
For step power change:

\[ T_j(t) = T_a + P \cdot Z_{th}(t) \]

docs.title: Periodic Power
docs.text:
Average temperature + ripple:

\[T_{j,avg} = T_a + P_{avg} \cdot R_{th,total}\] \[\Delta T_{j,ripple} = P_{peak} \cdot Z_{th}(t_{on})\]

docs.title: Maximum Junction Temperature
docs.text: Device Tj,max Recommended Max Si MOSFET 150-175°C 125°C Si IGBT 150-175°C 125°C SiC MOSFET 175-200°C 150°C GaN HEMT 150°C 125°C

docs.title: Derating
docs.text:
Temperature margin for reliability:

\[T_{j,design} = T_{j,max} - \Delta T_{margin}\]

Typical margin: 25-50°C

docs.title: 501 - Loss Calculation
docs.text: Semiconductor conduction and switching loss modeling.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Accurate loss calculation is essential for: - Thermal design and heatsink sizing - Efficiency optimization - Component selection - Reliability prediction

docs.title: Total Semiconductor Losses
docs.text: \[P_{total} = P_{cond} + P_{sw}\]

docs.title: Conduction Losses
docs.text:
MOSFET:

\[P_{cond,MOS} = I_{rms}^2 \cdot R_{DS(on)}\]

IGBT:

\[P_{cond,IGBT} = V_{CE(sat)} \cdot I_{avg} + r_{CE} \cdot I_{rms}^2\]

Diode:

\[P_{cond,D} = V_F \cdot I_{avg} + r_D \cdot I_{rms}^2\]

docs.title: Switching Losses
docs.text:
\[P_{sw} = (E_{on} + E_{off}) \cdot f_{sw}\]

Where switching energies depend on: - Current at switching instant - Voltage being switched - Temperature (increases with temp)

docs.title: RDS(on) vs Temperature
docs.text:
\[R_{DS(on)}(T) = R_{DS(on)}(25°C) \cdot \left[1 + \alpha(T - 25)\right]\]

Typical α ≈ 0.004 to 0.006 /°C (doubles at 150°C)

docs.title: Switching Energy vs Temperature
docs.text: \[E_{sw}(T) = E_{sw}(25°C) \cdot \left[1 + \beta(T - 25)\right]\]

docs.title: Setting Up Loss Parameters
docs.text:
1. Open semiconductor properties
  2. Enable thermal model
  3. Enter datasheet values:
  4. RDS(on) or VCE(sat)
  5. Eon, Eoff at reference conditions
  6. Temperature coefficients

docs.title: Data Entry Table
docs.text: Parameter MOSFET IGBT Diode V_on - VCE(sat) VF R_on RDS(on) rCE rD E_on Eon Eon Qrr×V E_off Eoff Eoff - E_rr - - Err

docs.title: High-Side MOSFET
docs.text:
Conduction:

\[P_{cond,HS} = D \cdot I_L^2 \cdot R_{DS(on)}\]

Switching:

\[P_{sw,HS} = \frac{1}{2}V_{in} \cdot I_L \cdot (t_r + t_f) \cdot f_{sw}\]

docs.title: Low-Side Diode/MOSFET
docs.text:
Conduction:

\[P_{cond,LS} = (1-D) \cdot I_L \cdot V_F\]

docs.title: Inductor Losses
docs.text:
DC Copper Loss:

\[P_{Cu,DC} = I_{DC}^2 \cdot R_{DC}\]

AC Copper Loss (skin effect):

\[P_{Cu,AC} = I_{AC,rms}^2 \cdot R_{AC}\]

Core Loss (Steinmetz):

\[P_{core} = k \cdot f^{\alpha} \cdot B^{\beta} \cdot V_{core}\]

docs.text: The companion project file loss-calculation.ipes implements an authentic buck-boost converter with active semiconductor loss calculation and electro-thermal feedback in GeckoCIRCUITS.

docs.text: Parameter Value Description Circuit File loss-calculation.ipes Complete validated simulation model Input Voltage (\(V_{in}\)) \(300\text{ V DC}\) High-voltage DC rail Switching Frequency (\(f_{sw}\)) \(20\text{ kHz}\) Period \(T_{sw} = 50\,\mu\text{s}\) Duty Cycle (\(D\)) \(0.40\) Gate drive command Switch Device (IGBT.1) \(R_{on} = 44\,\text{m}\Omega\), \(V_f = 0.8\text{ V}\), \(k_{on} = 97\,\mu\text{J/A}\), \(k_{off} = 120\,\mu\text{J/A}\) Thermal loss calculator Pv.1 coupled to thermal network Diode Device (D.1) \(R_{on} = 33\,\text{m}\Omega\), \(V_f = 0.8\text{ V}\) Thermal loss calculator Pv.2 Thermal Network 4-layer Foster RC network \(R_{th,jc}\) chain coupled to heatsink \(R_{th,ha} = 0.8\text{ K/W}\) Ambient Temperature (\(T_a\)) \(25^\circ\text{C}\) Thermal voltage source Temp.1 Simulation Step (\(\Delta t\)) \(1.0\,\mu\text{s}\) 10,001 time steps Total Duration \(0.01\text{ s}\) (\(10\text{ ms}\)) Captures switching cycle losses and initial thermal transient

docs.title: How to Run Simulation
docs.text:
GeckoCIRCUITS GUIMCP Interface (Command Line)
  1. Open loss-calculation.ipes in GeckoCIRCUITS desktop.
  2. Click Start Simulation (or press F5).
  3. Open the Scope window and observe Tj temperature trajectory alongside switching pulses.
# Validate circuit integrity
python -c "from scripts.desktop.mcp_client import GeckoMcpClient; c = GeckoMcpClient(); c.start(); print(c.call_tool('gecko_validate_circuit', {'circuit_path': 'docs/tutorials/thermal/loss-calculation.ipes'})); c.close()"

# Run simulation
python -c "from scripts.desktop.mcp_client import GeckoMcpClient; c = GeckoMcpClient(); c.start(); print(c.call_tool('gecko_simulate', {'circuit_path': 'docs/tutorials/thermal/loss-calculation.ipes', 'total_time': 0.01, 'time_step': 1e-6})); c.close()"

docs.title: Simulation Exercises
docs.text:
1. Measure losses at different load currents (\(10\text{ A}\) vs \(30\text{ A}\)) and plot the quadratic conduction loss curve.
  2. Compare switching losses at \(20\text{ kHz}\) vs \(50\text{ kHz}\) to verify the linear frequency scaling \(P_{sw} \propto f_{sw}\).
  3. Analyze the loss breakdown between IGBT.1 and freewheeling diode D.1.
  4. Correlate total dissipated power with the resulting steady-state junction temperature rise: \(\Delta T_j = P_{loss} \cdot R_{th,total}\).
